World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: The story of Zarzaparilla, an Indigenous root beer from Veracruz
World.content:
Mexico’s truest beauty can often be found in its widely diverse, uniquely regional variations of culture and flavors. No two places in Mexico are exactly alike. Whether it’s the way a certain salsa is prepared, the protein of choice used to stuff a tamal or the techniques that may differ from coast to coast, pueblo to pueblo, the country reflects an endless multiverse of realities inside its kitchens. As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me while driving across the desert terrain, you can spend two lifetimes in Mexico and even then, you still wouldn’t uncover all of its secrets and taste all of its idiosyncrasies.

It was a revelation, then, when I learned about zarzaparilla — about its historic origins and regional importance — from one of my uncles who grew up in Veracruz. In the simplest terms, zarzaparilla (referred to simply as zarza by locals) is what modern consumers would likely associate with root beer. But centuries before making its way into European markets via the Spanish — who in the 16th century first encountered the Indigenous remedy in the mountains of what is now Veracruz, and then exported it to Seville, Spain — zarza was a native drink with purported medicinal qualities made from local roots and ingredients that combated syphilis and, according to the American Homebrewers Association, far predates root beer.

A root beer revelation

In an effort to learn more about it, I drove 45 minutes to the source, on a southbound road from my home in Veracruz past two Pueblos Mágicos — first Coatepec, then Xico — until I reached Mexico’s cradle of zarza: Teocelo (or, in Nahuatl, “Tiger God”).

The mountain town of around 11,000 can only be reached through narrow, curving roads that carve through the subtropical terrain at a high elevation — with humid and wet conditions that allow all sorts of vegetation and crops to flourish in the surrounding areas (coffee, in particular, is a notable product from this part of Mexico).

It’s here that zarzaparilla (also confusingly spelled “sarsaparilla”) gained notoriety as a beverage among Spaniards and mestizos, becoming a local commercial industry of sorts that would expand beyond the region. Today, zarzaparilla can be found throughout Mexico, particularly within Veracruz and its neighboring states. But back then, it was — much like jalapeños were until they became commonplace elsewhere — a specialty product known only to those in the greater Xalapa vicinity.

The origins of ‘zarza’

In snooping around the tiny pueblo, it’s easy to find where it all started: Zarzaparilla Flores (a family-owned business that is not to be mistaken for a separate branch of family operations, Zarzaparilla Flores Doña Chabe, which is literally next door, but technically unaffiliated). The original Zarzaparilla Flores is said to have opened in 1920 inside what used to be a storage building for the nearby train yard, which served as a prominent trade route during the Porfiriato era from Xico to the United States. Due to the train, lots of immigrants and outsiders were able to pass through town, bringing a transient mixture of passersby who helped give zarzaparilla its fame beyond Veracruz.

Today, a third-generation family member runs the business — with antique family photos dating back to the Mexican Revolution bedecking the walls (one photo of the original shop owner, Don Manuel Flores, and his wife hangs stoically beneath two old rifles).

Rubén Olivares is the current face of operations. He married into the Flores family and has taken over the zarzaparilla tradition with pride.

A family tradition and recipe

“This region used to be known for cultivating pineapples and oranges, and that created a local exporting economy early on,” Olivares says. “But over time, with climate change and different farming methods, everything shifted, and pineapple exports migrated further south, due to the hotter temperatures down there. And this area, which has always been colder and at higher altitudes, began to grow coffee and other ingredients that were good for making zarzaparilla.”

Without revealing the specifics of their family recipe, he tells me their zarzaparilla is a mix of ginger, cardamom, star anise, cinnamon, lime, jamaica, egg whites and more. They also sell hidromiel (mead) and other liquors made from fermented oranges, arrowhead plants, cherry and crucetillo (a shrub that in the past was used to treat venomous snakebites).

The family’s zarza recipe has remained the same for more than a century and was patented in 1920 by Don Manuel Flores, but according to Olivares, Don Manuel only sold a few liters of it at the time. The family now regularly brews batches of around 1,000 liters and ships it all over Mexico. Predominantly made as a syrupy concentrate, the molasses-like mixture is put into various sizes of plastic bottles and jugs, which consumers can mix with any ratio of filtered or mineral water to their liking.

How the drink conquered the ‘Wild West’

In the 19th and 20th centuries, the beverage was viewed as a medicinal remedy and was brought to the U.S. According to The Seattle Times, “Sarsaparilla was widely consumed all across 19th-century America, easy to find in the local saloon if the one-road town one rode into had no dedicated apothecary or pharmacy, and was supposedly quite popular with cowboys and ranchers looking to tame a rumbling tummy or put a little pep in their step, much as people use kombucha today.” Eventually — and it’s unclear when, why or how — zarzaparilla (made from “dried root bark of several plants in the genus Smilax,” which grew plentifully in Veracruz) was replaced by sassafras, and zarzaparilla became known as root beer. (In 1960, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration banned real sassafras in commercial root beer as safrole in high amounts was found to be carcinogenic.)

Throughout it all, zarza remained the dominant beverage of choice in and around the town of its origin in Veracruz. The Flores family is no longer the only one making it, either: A Google Maps search will reveal no fewer than five other zarzaparilla businesses in the town of about 23 square miles (for comparison’s sake, Mexico City is estimated at 573 square miles, yet according to Google, unfortunately has no official zarzaparilla-dedicated outlets).

Travel attractions in Teocelo

Teocelo has other worthwhile features besides zarza: It’s the site of the Fiesta Patronal, a weekend-long celebration that includes parades, fireworks and religious celebrations in honor of the burial of Jesus after his crucifixion. At the pueblo’s main entrance, there’s a bee sanctuary that produces all kinds of honey products you likely won’t find anywhere else, at least not in abundance — jugs of honey wine, salsa macha made with honey and “honey butter” (akin to peanut butter, with a similarly thick consistency) in variations that range from almond and walnut to berry or garlic.

Note: The honey shop, known as La Mielada, or “The Honeydew,” also has an accompanying restaurant that serves honeyed meats and breads, with an affordable selection of beverages like the aforementioned honey wine or my personal favorite, a mug of locally cultivated coffee with large dollops of organic honey mixed in — a pure delight of sweet and bitter flavors. For outdoor-seeking adventurers, the surrounding area also offers waterfalls, hikes, cabins and whitewater rapids.

To be sure, there’s no shortage of offerings — and mugs of zarza — to enjoy for a weekend in the chilly mountain locale.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let’s start today’s column with a quick quiz:

Pop Quiz Question #1: What is currently the top Mexican export to the United States?

If you are like most people, you are thinking of one of three categories: alcoholic beverages (think tequila, mezcal, Corona beer), food (perhaps avocados, jalapenos, tomatoes) or automobiles. All of those answers are incorrect.

Pop Quiz Question #2: Which country sells more AI servers and equipment to the United States, Mexico or Taiwan?

Of course, most people answer Taiwan. That would also be incorrect.

Mexico’s server-related exports to the US have overtaken autos, underscoring how AI data-center demand is reshaping its export base. Source: @financialtimes https://t.co/QtrH6mKZ0I pic.twitter.com/pyRYc40ktb — (((The Daily Shot))) (@SoberLook) August 7, 2026

Sometimes just one picture, or in this case — one chart recently published by the Financial Times — can be incredibly insightful. Above, you’ll see a chart comparing Mexican exports of two product categories from 2010 to the present day. The blue line shows vehicles, which Mexico has been exporting for over 60 years. Last year, nearly 80% of Mexico’s light vehicle exports went to the United States. The red line shows server-related hardware (think AI data centers). The x-axis shows the years from 2010 to 2026. The y-axis shows monthly exports in billions of US dollars.

As can be clearly seen, exports of server-related hardware have absolutely exploded in the past two years, to the point where they are now surpassing vehicles. Last month alone, over US $15 billion of these products were exported. Think about that for a minute. The news is filled on a daily basis with headlines telling us that Trump has decided not to renew the USMCA or that Trump commented that “we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” Other headlines lead us to believe that tariffs are being slapped on most Mexican goods, significantly hurting Mexico in the process. Neither is true.

That being said, much of the conversation often seems to revolve around two categories of products highly influenced by two distinct voting groups in the U.S. The first is union members and more specifically the members of the United Auto Workers, who have an obvious interest in keeping as much vehicle production as possible in the country. The second is U.S. farmers, who naturally want to keep food production domestic. As a result of these two powerful and influential groups, those segments are what we most often hear about — more specifically cars and tomatoes. And in fact, the U.S. currently has a 17% “antidumping” tariff on Mexican tomatoes and a relatively small and extremely complex-to-calculate tariff on Mexican vehicles. Fun fact: One of the final projects my senior year of college was to analyze the impact of U.S. tomato tariff practices and policies on Mexico. (Yes, I am aware of what an exceptionally boring topic that is for a final project!)

Perhaps not surprisingly, server equipment from Mexico has a 0% tariff from the United States. The most in-demand product on the planet right now has firmly established Mexico in its supply chain, and investment, jobs and exports are all booming in this area. Taiwanese companies are investing heavily in Mexico. It’s all happening very fast. It’s quite exciting and going to be very interesting to continue to follow.

So while most headlines would have you believe that the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship is in shambles, the reality is as follows:

1. Mexico moves past Taiwan as the top AI server exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-moves-past-taiwan-as-top-ai-server-exporter-to-united-states/

2. Mexico is now by far the leading exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-in-numbers-mexico-exports-us-china-canada/

3. Inflation is now lower in Mexico than in the U.S. for the first time: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/inflation-mexico-lower-united-states-why-thats-such-a-big-deal-a-perspective-from-our-ceo/

4. Mexico’s export revenue is up 25% so far this year: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/mexico-export-revenue-this-year/

So what’s the bottom line here? Follow the data, not the noise, and stay tuned to what is the most dynamic segment in the world, growing fast and furious right here in Mexico.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Missed the deadline? Here’s how to get your cell phone service back
World.content:
The first enforced deadline for compliance with mandatory cell phone registration came and went on Aug. 15 and approximately 2.6 million phone lines were suspended, prompting chaos and confusion for users whose now-unregistered phone numbers end in “0.”

Mexico’s Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (CRT) announced on Thursday that nearly 9.7 million users whose number ends in “0” successfully registered their cell phones before the deadline.

The CRT also said that just over 2.3 million users whose lines had been suspended managed to reactivate their phone service by Aug. 19. Another 2.6 million mobile phones are expected to be reactivated in the coming days, while the CRT expects 2.5 million “unused” lines to be decommissioned.

Those who failed to register before the deadline faced plenty of online misinformation, but those whose service was suspended can still recover their service because their phone number was not canceled.

To reactivate the service, users must complete the registration process via their phone company. Prepaid lines must also be registered to remain active.

You can register through the phone company’s registration portal and by verifying your identity. Links to all providers’ platforms can be found on the CRT website here.

You can also complete the process in person at one of your company’s customer service centers, where staff is on hand to assist with the registration.

Mexican mobile phone owners must provide a CURP (Unique Population Registry Code) and a valid official ID, such as the INE-issued voter ID.

Foreigners must also register their phone lines (if it is a Mexican provider) by using the corresponding identity or immigration document, such as a resident visa or a passport.

Procedures vary slightly depending on the phone company, but the process is free.

It is important to note that suspended lines can still make calls to emergency numbers, citizen services and their phone company. They will also continue to receive earthquake alerts and they can be used to complete the registration process.

The government mandated cell phone registration procedures in an effort to eliminate anonymous mobile lines, stop criminal extortion and curb the use of untraceable “burner” prepaid SIM cards.

The CRT had originally established a June 30 deadline for all cell phones to be registered, but when it became apparent that a significant number of users would see their lines suspended, the deadline was extended.

The official schedule to register cell phones now depends on the final digit of your phone number. If your phone number ends in “1,” you must register by Aug. 31. If it ends in “2,” your deadline is Sept. 15, and so on through the end of the year as shown in the graphic above.

In its Aug. 20 report, the CRT said a total of 73.2 million lines — or 60.5% of the total lines expected to be connected in the country — were registered. By the end of the registration process, it expects a purge of around 25 million lines.

With reports from El Universal, Wired and LatinUS

World.title: Mexico’s urban sprawl is steadily reshaping life in its biggest cities
World.content:
A new study has found that 69 Mexican metropolitan areas nearly doubled their urban populations from 1990 to 2020, but much of that growth occurred farther from the heart of downtown, leaving their central areas with 2.5 million fewer residents.

The study, published July 25 by researchers at Tecnológico de Monterrey’s Center for the Future of Cities (CFC) and the Complexity Science Hub in Vienna, Austria, examined census data from 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020.

It found that population distribution shifted steadily toward intermediate, distant and peripheral areas.

More than 40% of residents in the metro areas studied lived in central areas in 1990. By 2020, that share had fallen to 22%, according to the research.

Researchers said limited affordable housing in established urban areas — where land and construction costs are higher — helped push growth outward. Cheaper peripheral land and housing policies that favored development outside consolidated areas also contributed to the shift.

Researchers also cited rising car ownership and transportation planning that lagged behind new development as factors that reinforced the pattern.

As a result, a larger share of residents lived farther from jobs, schools, health care and other services — with increased travel times and distances needed to get to those locations from their homes.

In Mexico City, the population of areas nearest the historic center fell by about 166,000 residents during the period, even as the broader metropolitan area grew.

Monterrey’s population within 5 kilometers of its center fell from about 485,000 in 1990 to 377,000 in 2020, while Guadalajara lost more than 200,000 residents in the same radius.

Researchers estimated that the average distance between where residents lived and their city’s center increased 28% as populations moved outward.

The study does not establish whether outward moves were voluntary or involuntary, nor does it identify the income or job location of individual households that moved. It also does not establish gentrification, rent increases or replacement by wealthier residents as a factor in the departures.

Its authors instead focused on documenting the shift.

Alberto Meouchi, head of the Mexico City office of Tec de Monterrey’s CFC, told Wired en Español that a return of all residents to traditional city centers was unrealistic.

He said cities could instead develop multiple centers that bring housing, jobs, services and transportation closer together.

With reports from TecScience, Animal Político, La Silla Rota and Wired

World.title: What I learned from a summer in San Miguel de Allende: 10 reflections from an MND intern
World.content:
Nine weeks ago, I set foot on Mexican soil for the first time in my life. I spent the next two months discovering a small part of the country by traveling, exploring San Miguel, and trying to understand daily life and culture here.

Now it’s time for me to head back to the United States and embark on my senior year of college. I’ll go back feeling like the same person, but with a fresh perspective on life in another country.

Here are my 10 reflections as I end my summer internship with Mexico News Daily.

1. From what I saw, Mexico is nothing like how it is often portrayed in the United States. The only people I saw holding guns were police. I never felt unsafe or witnessed any drug use. What I found instead was gorgeous cities, incredible nature and a warm, friendly populace. I was here in the summer, and it was not even that hot! Mexico gets a bad rap and some of it is justified, but like any large place, the reality is more complicated than any single narrative. Mexico has some of the best destinations in the Western Hemisphere that get overlooked because of its perception in American media.

2. Mexico did not change me, per se. I’m going back to the United States next week feeling like I’m still the same person I was when I left. Would six months in Mexico instead of two have changed that? I don’t know. I could have gone out and interacted with people more. I could have drank more margaritas or gone out of my comfort zone, but I chose to be myself. I still had amazing experiences, travelled around the country and ate some amazing food, but I could have done more to give myself a truly transformative experience.

3. Nothing demonstrated the immaculate vibes of Mexico quite like El Tri’s loss to England in the round of 16. Given soccer’s culture of hooliganism and frequent riots after big game losses in North American sports, I expected a similar reaction from Mexico’s famously passionate fans. But after the final whistle grew, music started blasting out of speakers and people began dancing. I was shocked. This was a monumental opportunity for Mexico soccer and they lost. Most fans would be crushed and would let it ruin their week. But the Mexican fans danced and sang.

4. Mexico has lots of scary bugs. I hate bugs. On the couple of excursions I made to San Miguel de Allende’s botanical gardens, I witnessed some of the creepiest looking beetles I’ve ever seen in my life — never mind the giant hornets, massive red ants, or constant threat of scorpions (which I’m thankful I never saw.) Coming face to face with freaky bugs may have been my least favorite part of my Mexico experience.

5. Catholicism is visible everywhere in Mexico, but it does not create a society as conservative as one might think. While in San Miguel, I attended the local pride parade and in Mexico City I saw pride flags everywhere. Many people take their religious beliefs seriously, but Mexicans are generally understanding and welcoming.

6. The lack of polarization was a breath of fresh air. While riding on a long bus to Mexico City, I was getting to know my coworker and travelling companion, María. We disagreed on a lot of political issues and even on ideologies, but it never had any effect on our relationship. I can be “woke” while she is not. With the extremism ever-present in the U.S., this might be a dealbreaker. But in Mexico, it’s just differences I have with a friend.

7. This one may be obvious, but the food lives up to the hype.

8. Mexico is generally more laid back than their northern neighbors. As a night owl and a late riser, I tended to like that. But when I had to wait a long time for food at restaurants and there is less urgency in customer service, I sometimes found myself missing American customer service. Even the local McDonalds felt like it took forever.

9. As a massive introvert, I really enjoyed living by myself away from almost everyone I knew, but it had its drawbacks. I was too shy to go to bars most of the time, even though the bar scene in San Miguel is active late into the night. Most nights I did not have many regrets, but by the end, part of me wished I had made more friends.

10. Mexico may not have changed who I am, but it has had a major impact on my life. Living in a different country taught me new ways to communicate and new ways to think. I got a front-row seat to the lives completely different from my own, which was equal parts fascinating and harrowing. I’ll never forget Hierve el Agua or Monte Albán in Oaxaca, or witnessing Mexico beat Ecuador with hundreds of thousands of people in the Zócalo in Mexico City. I’m going back the same person, but these nine weeks will have a lasting impact on me.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Despite surging peso, further interest rate cuts remain unlikely for the foreseeable future
World.content:
The Bank of Mexico adopted a guarded approach in its Aug. 6-7 monetary policy meeting, indicating it is likely to keep its benchmark interest unchanged, even as inflation is easing.

In minutes from the meeting released on Thursday, the central bank cited an uncertain global backdrop and lingering inflation risks in its decision to maintain a 6.5% interest rate, deeming it “adequate to face the current economic risks.”

It further justified maintaining the rate by assessing “the observed levels of the [peso-dollar] exchange rate, the absence of demand pressures in the economy and the degree of monetary restriction implemented.”

The board said it believed the monetary policy stance “is adequate to meet the challenges of the macroeconomic environment, including those arising from the international context.”

Still, four of the five members of Banxico’s Governing Board said the persistence of inflation in services remains a concern, prompting the cautious stance. A balance of risks skewed to the upside and the continued weakness of the Mexican economy also impacted the decision.

Policymakers view inflation in services (i.e., restaurants, hotels and air travel) as a key concern as it has remained above 4% since late 2021. It is viewed as one of the primary obstacles to bringing overall inflation back to the bank’s 3% target.

Board members attributed lingering price pressures in the service sector to businesses adjusting prices slowly while facing elevated costs for labor and living expenses

Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, down from 3.37% in June, marking its lowest level since May 2020. However, core inflation — which excludes some volatile food and energy prices — registered at 3.95%, down slightly from 4.03% in June.

Banxico, as the Banco de México is also known, now says it doesn’t expect headline inflation to converge to its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027, requiring sustained monetary discipline. In the short term, analysts surveyed by Banxico expect year-end headline inflation of 4.00%.

A strong peso has helped curb inflation. The currency — hovering at and below 17 to the U.S. dollar since last week — has strengthened nearly 6% in 2026, helped considerably by a weaker dollar, though ⁠Mexico’s solid macroeconomic fundamentals are a factor as well.

The minutes noted that the economy expanded in the second quarter (+1.5%) after contracting in the first, but some members warned that weakness persists in various components of demand.

Regarding the international environment, the board highlighted tensions in the Middle East that continue to pose upside risks to inflation, cautioning that the prolonged conflict has tested the buffers that “have mitigated the rise in oil prices.”

With reports from Reuters, El Economista, Forbes México and Mexico Business News

World.title: Freak Waves on Lake Titicaca Destroy 200 Tonnes of Trout
World.content:
Peru · AGRICULTURE

Key Facts — Location Southern sector of Lake Titicaca, Puno region, Peru

— Damage About 200 tonnes of trout lost

— Cause Strong winds, intense gusts, waves up to five metres, and rain

— Affected areas El Faro de Pomata and Huaylluni, among others

— Reporting COER Puno, the regional emergency operations centre, reported on the zones

Waves of up to five metres tore through the floating cages before dawn.

A jetty on Lake Titicaca at Puno. Anomalous waves from 18 August 2026 destroyed an estimated 200 tonnes of farmed trout. (Photo: Kataleya Torrsh, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Freak waves on Lake Titicaca destroyed about 200 tonnes of trout in farming cages early Tuesday, according to state news agency Andina. The anomalous swell, known locally as oleaje anómalo, hit the southern sector of the lake in Peru’s Puno region.

What Happened on Lake Titicaca

From the early hours of Tuesday 18 August 2026, unusual waves battered trout farming cages on Lake Titicaca. The event was recorded in the southern sector, with the heaviest damage in the lakeside ring.

Strong winds and intense gusts hit the altiplano, the high plateau of the central Andes. They combined with rain and waves of up to about five metres.

This created the anomalous swell that tore through the floating cages.

The Scale of the Loss

Meanwhile, losses are estimated at about 200 tonnes of trout, according to Andina and other outlets. This is a significant blow for local fish farmers who rely on the lake for their livelihood.

Trout are farmed in floating cages moored in the lake. When strong swell hits, it tears the nets, and the fish escape or die.

Affected Areas in Puno

The damage was concentrated in the lakeside strip of Lake Titicaca. Areas reported include El Faro de Pomata, in the district of Pomata, province of Chucuito.

Huaylluni and other parts of the lakeside were also affected. COER Puno, the regional emergency operations centre, reported on the affected zones.

However, no full list of affected sites is available.

Why Lake Titicaca Is Vulnerable

In addition, lake Titicaca sits at about 3,800 metres in the Andes, on the border between Peru and Bolivia. Puno is the Peruvian side, and the lake’s high altitude makes it prone to strong winds.

The altiplano, where the lake is located, is known for its intense weather. Strong winds are common, and when they combine with rain, they can create dangerous wave conditions.

The Impact on Trout Farming

Trout farming is a key activity on Lake Titicaca, with floating cages anchored in the water. The recent waves have damaged these cages, leading to the loss of fish.

For local producers, this means a sudden and severe reduction in their stock. The full economic impact is still being assessed, but the loss of 200 tonnes is substantial.

Weather Conditions Behind the Waves

As a result, the waves were caused by strong winds and intense gusts on the altiplano. These winds, combined with waves of up to about five metres and rain, created the anomalous swell.

Such weather events are not uncommon in the region, but their intensity this time was exceptional. The result was significant damage to the fish farms.

Response From Local Authorities

COER Puno, the regional emergency operations centre, has been monitoring the situation. They reported on the affected zones, but no government response or emergency declaration has been verified.

In the meantime, local communities are dealing with the aftermath. The focus is on assessing the damage and supporting the affected producers.

What This Means for the Region

Overall, the destruction of 200 tonnes of trout is a major setback for the local fishing industry. It highlights the vulnerability of Lake Titicaca to extreme weather events.

For the people of Puno, this event is a reminder of the power of nature. The lake, which is a source of livelihood, can also be a source of sudden disaster.

Looking Ahead After the Waves

As the waters calm, the focus will be on recovery. Producers will need to repair their cages and restock their fish.

Meanwhile, the event serves as a lesson about the risks of farming in such a dynamic environment. Lake Titicaca remains a vital resource, but it demands respect.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the freak waves on Lake Titicaca?

The waves came from strong winds and intense gusts on the altiplano. Rain fell too, and the swell reached about five metres.

How much trout was lost in the incident?

About 200 tonnes of trout were lost, according to state news agency Andina and other outlets. The fish either escaped or died when the nets were torn by the waves.

Where did the damage occur on Lake Titicaca?

The damage was in the southern sector of the lake, in the Puno region of Peru. Specific areas include El Faro de Pomata and Huaylluni, among others in the lakeside strip.

Is Lake Titicaca prone to such events?

The lake sits at about 3,800 metres in the Andes, where strong winds are common. However, the combination of winds, rain, and large waves made this event particularly severe.

Sources: Andina; COER Puno; Peruvian regional media.

Dmar Córdoba Salamanca, a critic of the 2016 peace accord, will run Colombia’s Historical Memory Centre. The journalist and lawyer was named director of the Centro Nacional de Memoria Histórica on 21 August 2026, according to Colombian outlets.

A New Director for the Historical Memory Centre

Dmar Córdoba Salamanca has been appointed to lead the Historical Memory Centre, a state body that investigates Colombia’s armed conflict. He is a journalist and lawyer by training.

Colombian media describe him as a critic of the 2016 peace accord. He has also questioned whether Colombia had an armed conflict at all.

The Centre’s Role in Colombia’s Conflict

Meanwhile, the Historical Memory Centre preserves academic and documentary work on the armed conflict. It compiles testimony and records of human rights violations and supports memorialisation.

This work is vital for victims who seek recognition and reparations. The centre’s role is to ensure their stories are not forgotten.

A Controversial Appointment

Córdoba Salamanca’s views have sparked concern among commentators in 2026. They warn of historical revisionism and argue that such a director undermines trust in the centre.

In fact, earlier appointments of directors who denied the conflict fractured confidence. Those appointments drew rejection from victims’ organisations and social groups.

The Legal Stakes of the Conflict Debate

In addition, whether Colombia’s violence constituted an armed conflict is not a technical quibble. The legal recognition underpins victims’ rights, reparations and the peace accord itself.

Therefore, a director who questions this could affect how the centre operates. His stance may influence the legal framework that protects victims.

Replacing María Valencia Gaitán

Córdoba Salamanca replaces María Valencia Gaitán, who ran the centre during Gustavo Petro’s government. She is the granddaughter of liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán.

Her tenure saw the centre focus on documenting the conflict. Now, the leadership changes hands under a new administration.

A New Political Era

As a result, abelardo de la Espriella took office as president of Colombia on 7 August 2026. His government has already made its mark on memory institutions.

Meanwhile, the appointment of Córdoba Salamanca signals a shift in approach. It remains to be seen how this will affect the centre’s work.

Victims’ Trust at Risk

Commentary in 2026 warns that a director who denies the conflict erodes trust. Victims rely on the Historical Memory Centre to validate their experiences.

For example, the centre’s testimony archives are crucial for legal claims. Without trust, victims may feel abandoned by the state.

Historical Revisionism Concerns

Overall, observers argue that the new director could promote historical revisionism. This would undermine the centre’s mission to preserve the truth.

Despite this, the appointment is now official. The centre’s future direction will depend on how Córdoba Salamanca interprets his role.

The Path Ahead for the Historical Memory Centre

The Historical Memory Centre faces a challenging period under its new leadership. The director’s views on the conflict will shape its priorities.

In short, the coming months will reveal whether the centre continues its core work. For now, victims and observers watch closely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Dmar Córdoba Salamanca?

He is a journalist and lawyer who has been named director of Colombia’s Historical Memory Centre. Colombian outlets describe him as a critic of the 2016 peace accord.

What does the Historical Memory Centre do?

It is a state body that investigates and preserves academic and documentary work on Colombia’s armed conflict. It compiles testimony and records of human rights violations and supports memorialisation.

Why is the director’s stance on the armed conflict important?

The legal recognition of an armed conflict underpins victims’ rights, reparations and the peace accord. A director who questions this could affect how the centre operates and how victims are supported.

Who did Córdoba Salamanca replace?

He replaces María Valencia Gaitán, who ran the centre during Gustavo Petro’s government. She is the granddaughter of liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán.

Sources: Colombian press; Centro Nacional de Memoria Histórica.

World.title: JEP Presses Colombia’s Government on Restorative Sentences
World.content:
Colombia · JUSTICE

Key Facts — Request date On 21 August 2026, JEP magistrate Alejandro Ramelli asked Justice Minister Iván Cancino for an urgent meeting.

— Purpose The meeting would discuss making restorative sentences operational, including projects and resource coordination.

— Definition Restorative sentences, known as sanciones propias, are non-custodial sanctions imposed after admission of responsibility.

— Duration The JEP’s guidance sets a minimum of five years and a maximum of eight years of compliance.

— Context The JEP is Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, created by the 2016 peace accord.

The request follows the tribunal’s push to make its non-custodial sanctions operational, a key step in Colombia’s peace process.

Illustrative photo: central Bogotá. The JEP’s restorative sentences run for a minimum of five years and a maximum of eight. (Photo: Baiji, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The JEP has pressed Colombia’s government on restorative sentences, requesting an urgent meeting with the justice minister. On 21 August 2026, magistrate Alejandro Ramelli asked Iván Cancino to discuss how to make these sanctions operational.

The Urgent Meeting Request

Alejandro Ramelli of the JEP asked Justice Minister Iván Cancino for a meeting on 21 August 2026. The request is urgent, according to the tribunal.

The discussion would focus on carrying out the JEP’s restorative sentences. This includes the projects involved and the coordination of resources and implementation.

What Are Restorative Sentences?

Restorative sentences are known in Spanish as sanciones propias. They are non-custodial sanctions imposed after someone admits responsibility.

These sentences combine restrictions on rights and freedoms with reparative work. The JEP’s guidance sets a minimum of five years and a maximum of eight years of compliance.

Understanding Non-Custodial Sanctions

A non-custodial sanction means the person does not go to prison. Instead, their movement and activity are restricted while they carry out work that repairs harm.

This approach aims to repair the damage caused by the conflict. It also allows offenders to contribute to society in a meaningful way.

The JEP’s Role in Peace

The JEP is Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace. This tribunal was created by the 2016 peace accord to try the gravest crimes of the armed conflict.

Its work is central to the peace process. Therefore, making restorative sentences operational is a key step.

Making Sentences Operational

The request concerns making those sanctions operational. This involves the projects that offenders would work on.

In addition, it requires coordinating resources and implementation. The meeting would address these practical details.

The Importance of Coordination

Coordination between the JEP and the government is crucial. Without it, restorative sentences may not be carried out effectively.

For example, resources must be allocated to support reparative projects. Meanwhile, oversight is needed to ensure compliance.

What Restorative Sentences Mean for Victims

Restorative sentences focus on repairing harm to victims. This is different from traditional prison sentences.

Instead of incarceration, offenders work on projects that benefit communities. As a result, victims may see tangible reparations.

Next Steps in the Process

The meeting has been requested but has not yet taken place. However, the urgency suggests that progress is needed soon.

Once the meeting occurs, the JEP and government can plan the implementation. This will be a significant step for the peace process.

The Future of Restorative Sentences

Restorative sentences are a cornerstone of Colombia’s transitional justice. They offer an alternative to prison while promoting reconciliation.

In short, their success depends on effective coordination. The upcoming meeting is a chance to make that happen.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are restorative sentences in Colombia?

Restorative sentences, or sanciones propias, are non-custodial sanctions imposed by the JEP after someone admits responsibility. They combine restrictions on rights with reparative work, lasting between five and eight years.

Who requested the meeting about restorative sentences?

Alejandro Ramelli, a magistrate of the JEP, requested an urgent meeting with Justice Minister Iván Cancino on 21 August 2026. The meeting would discuss making the sentences operational.

What does non-custodial mean?

Non-custodial means the person does not go to prison. Instead, their movement and activity are restricted while they carry out work that repairs harm.

Why is the JEP important?

The JEP is Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, created by the 2016 peace accord. It tries the gravest crimes of the armed conflict and oversees restorative sentences.

Sources: JEP communications; Colombian press.

World.title: Rocha Moya Is Back as Sinaloa Governor After 112 Days Away
World.content:
Mexico · POLITICS

Key Facts — Return date Rubén Rocha Moya resumed the governorship on Friday 21 August 2026.

— Absence length He was away on licence for about 112 days.

— Opposition stance PAN leaders rejected the legitimacy of his administration on 21 August 2026.

— Homicide trend Sinaloa recorded 1,654 intentional homicides in 2025, up 66.5% from 2024.

— Federal position President Claudia Sheinbaum said on 11 August 2026 that the return was his decision.

The governor’s return lands amid a record homicide surge and a political battle over the legitimacy of his administration.

Culiacán, capital of Sinaloa. Rocha Moya resumed the governorship on Friday 21 August 2026, after 112 days away. (Photo: Carlos Valenzuela, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Rubén Rocha Moya has returned as governor of Sinaloa after a 112-day leave of absence. He resumed his post on Friday 21 August 2026, announcing the move on X.

Rocha Moya Returns to Office

In short, rubén Rocha Moya is back as the constitutional governor of Sinaloa. He stated on X that he had taken up the exercise of his post that day.

His return ends a licencia, a formal leave of absence that lets an elected official step aside without resigning. The leave lasted about 112 days, just under four months.

Why He Stepped Aside

Rocha Moya had stepped aside to face investigations triggered by United States accusations of alleged links between his government and organised crime. He denies these allegations.

During his absence, he appeared before Mexico’s federal attorney general’s office, the Fiscalía General de la República. The nature of those proceedings has not been detailed.

Opposition Rejects His Mandate

Meanwhile, on the day of his return, the PAN’s Sinaloa president spoke out. Wendy Barajas Cortés categorically rejected the political and moral legitimacy of Rocha’s administration.

Her statement came on 21 August 2026. Meanwhile, national PAN leader Jorge Romero Herrera said the party does not recognise Rocha Moya’s government at all.

He added that any acts of the state administration will have no validity for the PAN.

Call for Analysis of Desaparición de Poderes

Romero Herrera urged an analysis of a possible desaparición de poderes in Sinaloa. This is a constitutional mechanism by which Mexico’s Senate can declare a state’s powers to have ceased and appoint an interim governor.

However, no such measure has been initiated. The PAN only urged that it be analysed, not that it be enacted.

Federal Government’s Stance

As a result, president Claudia Sheinbaum said on 11 August 2026 that whether Rocha Moya resumed office was exclusively his decision. She noted that the United States had not yet sent the evidence Mexico requested on the trafficking allegations.

In addition, the federal government has not publicly commented on the PAN’s call for a desaparición de poderes. The focus remains on the governor’s own choice to return.

Homicide Surge in Sinaloa

Sinaloa closed 2025 with 1,654 intentional homicides, a 66.5% increase on the 993 recorded in 2024. The daily average rose from 2.72 to 4.56 victims.

This surge has been driven by fighting between cartel factions, according to official data. The violence has marked the state during Rocha Moya’s absence.

Peak and Recent Trends

For example, june 2025 was the peak, with 210 to 212 intentional homicides. In June 2026, the figure was 116, well below that peak but still above pre-crisis levels.

By contrast, January 2026 recorded 106 intentional homicides, a 27.9% reduction on January 2025. That figure was about 6.7% of the national total.

Cumulative Violence Statistics

From September 2024 to February 2026, Sinaloa recorded 2,680 homicide victims. This reflects the intense conflict between cartel factions over that period.

Even so, the recent decline in homicides offers a glimmer of hope. The numbers remain high compared to pre-crisis levels.

Challenges Ahead for Rocha Moya

Overall, rocha Moya returns to a state facing both a security crisis and a political legitimacy battle. The PAN’s rejection could complicate his administration’s ability to govern.

Despite this, the governor’s constitutional status is clear. He is back, and the focus now shifts to how he addresses the violence and the opposition’s challenges.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did Rocha Moya return as governor?

Rubén Rocha Moya resumed the governorship on Friday 21 August 2026. He announced the move on X, saying he had taken up the exercise of his post that day.

Why did Rocha Moya take a leave of absence?

He stepped aside to face investigations triggered by United States accusations of alleged links between his government and organised crime. He denies these allegations.

What is a desaparición de poderes?

It is a constitutional mechanism by which Mexico’s Senate can declare a state’s powers to have ceased and appoint an interim governor. The PAN has urged that this be analysed, but it has not been initiated.

How has violence in Sinaloa changed recently?

Sinaloa recorded 1,654 intentional homicides in 2025, a 66.5% increase from 2024. However, June 2026 saw 116 homicides, well below the peak of June 2025.

Sources: La Jornada; EFE; Infobae; Luz Noticias; Mexican security data.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 22, 2026
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 22, 2026

If You Only Go to One Place Saturday Night in Barra Funda Saturday is São Paulo’s biggest club night, and Barra Funda is its engine. D-Edge — a global top-100 club with a Funktion-One system — leads, with Clash Club and the big room at Audio a short walk away. Doors are late and the headliners land around 2 am, so eat first and pace yourself. Check tonight’s line-ups online, buy ahead, and rideshare in and out.

Tonight at a Glance —Roberto Carlos · Espaço Unimed The biggest name in the city, 8.30 pm, tonight and Sunday. —MPB4 “60 Anos” · Blue Note The quartet’s second night, two sets at 8 pm and 10.30 pm, from R$110 (US$21). —Luedji Luna · Sesc Pinheiros 8 pm to 9.30 pm, Rua Paes Leme 195. R$70 (US$14) full, R$35 (US$7) meia. —CPM 22 · Audio Rock, not techno — Barra Funda’s big room goes to the São Paulo hardcore veterans tonight. —Also on: Humberto Gessinger at Tokio Marine Hall (10 pm), Ivan Lins at The Cavern Club (9.30 pm), Budah at Cine Joia (8 pm), Thaíde at Sesc Vila Mariana (8 pm).

Tonight, Saturday 22 August 2026, São Paulo is at full weekend tilt, and the strength is in the concert halls rather than the clubs. Roberto Carlos plays the Espaço Unimed, MPB4’s 60th-anniversary run gives its second night at the Blue Note, Luedji Luna returns to Sesc Pinheiros, and CPM 22 turn Audio over to rock. Barra Funda still runs late for anyone who wants a dancefloor. Pick your tempo — a seated show, a forró floor, or a club till sunrise.

Saturday is São Paulo’s biggest club night, led by Barra Funda. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

The big rooms — Roberto Carlos plays the Espaço Unimed in Água Branca at 8.30 pm, tonight and again on Sunday — the largest booking in the city. Humberto Gessinger brings the Engenheiros do Hawaii songbook to the Tokio Marine Hall at 10 pm, Ivan Lins plays The Cavern Club at 9.30 pm, Budah is at Cine Joia at 8 pm and Thaíde at Sesc Vila Mariana at 8 pm. Buy ahead where you can.

MPB4 — “60 Anos” at Blue Note — Av. Paulista 2073. One of Brazil’s most important vocal groups closes a two-night stand with sets at 8 pm and 10.30 pm, from around R$110 (US$21). Impeccable harmonies and a songbook that runs through the history of MPB, in a polished, seated room — the two sets mean there is usually room to get in.

Luedji Luna at Sesc Pinheiros — Rua Paes Leme 195. The Bahian singer closes a two-night run, 8 pm to 9.30 pm, at R$70 (US$14) full, R$35 (US$7) meia-entrada and R$21 (US$4) on a Sesc credencial plena. Book through the Sesc site or the box office; we could not confirm availability either way, so check before you travel.

Clubs, forró and the rest — Audio in Barra Funda gives its big room to CPM 22 tonight, so the electronic night there is off; D-Edge and Clash Club a short walk away run their usual late Saturday sessions. In Pinheiros, Canto da Ema has its forró floor, and Milton Guedes plays Bourbon Street in Moema at 10 pm, where the promoter reports last tickets.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (8 pm) — A seated show: MPB4 at Blue Note, Luedji Luna at Sesc Pinheiros, or Budah at Cine Joia. Eat first.

Prime time (8.30–10 pm) — Roberto Carlos at the Espaço Unimed, Milton Guedes at Bourbon Street, or the forró floor at Canto da Ema.

Late (midnight+) — Barra Funda: CPM 22 at Audio, D-Edge and Clash Club for the dancefloors, headliners around 2 am.

Alternative crawl — Vila Madalena’s bars are heaving on a Saturday and easy to move between on foot.

Getting home — Lines 1, 2, 3 and 15 of the metro run through the night from Saturday into Sunday; other lines close around midnight. Rideshare surge peaks 2–5 am, so budget for it and wait in a lit, busy spot.

Scenes & Sounds

Electronic and clubs — D-Edge and Clash Club in Barra Funda, plus Blitz Haus on Augusta. Audio is on rock tonight.

Where: Barra Funda, Rua Augusta.

MPB and samba-canção — MPB4 at Blue Note, Ná Ozzetti’s Maysa tribute at Casa de Francisca, Luedji Luna at Sesc Pinheiros. Where: Blue Note (Paulista), Casa de Francisca (Sé), Sesc Pinheiros.

Forró — Canto da Ema’s floor is at its weekly fullest. Where: Canto da Ema (Pinheiros).

Rock and hip-hop — CPM 22 at Audio, Humberto Gessinger at Tokio Marine Hall, Thaíde at Sesc Vila Mariana, Budah at Cine Joia.

Where: Barra Funda, Bom Retiro, Vila Mariana, Liberdade.

Big names — Roberto Carlos plays the Espaço Unimed at 8.30 pm, tonight and Sunday.

Where: Espaço Unimed (Água Branca).

Pick Your Night

The event: Roberto Carlos at the Espaço Unimed, 8.30 pm.

A legend, seated: MPB4’s 60th-anniversary show at Blue Note.

Romantic and intimate: Ná Ozzetti sings Maysa at Casa de Francisca.

Rock instead: CPM 22 at Audio in Barra Funda.

Worth checking: Luedji Luna at Sesc Pinheiros, 8 pm — two nights only.

Where to Go

D-Edge — Barra Funda São Paulo’s design-icon electronic club with a Funktion-One sound system — a global top-100 club, and the anchor of the city’s Saturday night. Tonight: Saturday electronic night; the line-up is published on the club’s own channels. Doors are typically around 11 pm with the headliner near 2 am. Best time: Friday and Saturday, late — the room fills after 1 am. Cost: Typically R$40 (US$8) to R$120 (US$23) depending on the night. Comanda card — don’t lose it. Address: Al. Olga 170, Barra Funda Website: www.d-edge.com.br Getting there: Metro Marechal Deodoro, 15-minute walk. Better to rideshare — the street is industrial and dark. Good to know: Buy tickets online. No flip-flops.

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York jazz club, polished and central, overlooking Avenida Paulista. Tonight: MPB4, “60 Anos” — two sets, 8 pm and 10.30 pm. From around R$110 (US$21). Best time: Wednesday to Sunday. Arrive 30 minutes early — seating is first-come. Cost: Couvert from around R$40 (US$8) to R$180 (US$35) depending on the act. Address: Av. Paulista 2073, 2º andar (Conjunto Nacional), Consolação Website: bluenotesp.com Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), 200 m from the door. Good to know: The later set is usually quieter; book the one you want.

Casa de Francisca — Sé/Centro An intimate listening room inside the gorgeous Palacete Teresa, mixing MPB, jazz, samba and instrumental. The city’s loveliest place to hear live music. Tonight: Ná Ozzetti and Marcelo Ghelfi sing Maysa — samba-canção and bossa. The house has not published a start time for this one; its shows usually begin between 9 pm and 10 pm, so confirm when you reserve. Best time: Tuesday to Sunday; arrive early to eat and get a good seat. Cost: Couvert usually R$40 (US$8) to R$70 (US$14). Cash and card. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva 22, Sé (Palacete Teresa) Website: casadefrancisca.art.br Getting there: Metro Sé (red/blue lines), 5-minute walk. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Small rooms — reservations strongly recommended.

Canto da Ema — Pinheiros One of São Paulo’s classic forró houses, going since 2000, with live bands and a floor that fills with dancers. Tonight: Live forró on the house’s busiest night of the week. The band time is not published in advance — check Sympla before you go. Best time: Wednesday to Sunday, with Friday and Saturday the busiest floors. Dance classes run on some nights before the show. Cost: Tickets from R$55 (US$11) on Sympla; dance classes are charged separately at R$28 (US$5). Card accepted. Address: Av. Brigadeiro Faria Lima 364, Pinheiros Getting there: Metro Faria Lima (yellow line), about an eight-minute walk — not Fradique Coutinho, which is further. Good to know: No dance experience needed — the crowd is friendly and mixed.

Bourbon Street Music Club — Moema A São Paulo institution modelled on a New Orleans jazz hall — jazz, blues, soul and, tonight, pop-rock. Tonight: Milton Guedes, from 10 pm. The promoter reports last tickets; buy on the official site. Best time: Most nights; arrive early to settle in and eat. Cost: Ticket or couvert varies by act, typically R$50 (US$10) to R$120 (US$24). Address: Rua dos Chanés 127, Moema Website: bourbonstreet.com.br Getting there: Metro Eucaliptos (green line) is nearby; rideshare is easiest at night. Good to know: Set times can run late — check when you book.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Barra Funda: The club district and tonight’s headline — D-Edge, Clash Club and Audio. Industrial and dark on foot, so rideshare door-to-door.

Pinheiros / Vila Madalena: Bohemian and bar-heavy, with Canto da Ema and a heaving Saturday bar crawl. Busy and walkable.

Paulista / Consolação: Blue Note and the Augusta clubs, a short walk to everything. Safe and well-lit.

Moema: Leafy and upmarket, home to Bourbon Street and good dinner options. Safe and walkable.

Sé / Centro: Casa de Francisca and the historic core. Grand by day, very quiet after dark — rideshare door-to-door.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Peak night — Saturday is the biggest night for São Paulo’s queer scene, one of the world’s largest. Expect major parties around Barra Funda, Augusta and Frei Caneca; check listings for tonight’s line-up.

Everyday-friendly spaces — The Augusta and Frei Caneca corridors are broadly mixed and welcoming, and tonight’s music rooms are all easy, inclusive options.

Money & How Paying Works Comanda card: Clubs like D-Edge give you a card on entry; settle at the exit. Losing it means a steep fixed fee. Concert tickets: Buy through official sellers (eventim for Blue Note); meia-entrada (half price) needs ID. Couvert: Music rooms add a per-person charge — around R$110 (US$22) at Blue Note tonight, R$40 (US$8) to R$70 (US$14) at Casa de Francisca. Cash, card and Pix: Widely accepted, but carry R$100 (US$20) to R$200 (US$40) in cash for smaller bars and the club cloakroom.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: lines 1, 2, 3 and 15 run through the night from Saturday into Sunday; the other lines close around midnight. If your route needs one of those, plan a rideshare home.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable. Surge peaks between 2 and 5 am, when the clubs empty — expect 2x or more, and wait in a lit spot.

Barra Funda clubs: The security team will often help you into your car. Wait inside until the app says the car is arriving; the streets are industrial and dark.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Centro: The Sé area empties and quietens after dark — rideshare door-to-door from Casa de Francisca.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do the Barra Funda clubs actually get going?

Late. Doors are around 11 pm, but the rooms fill after 1 am and headliners often play around 2 am. Eat dinner first, and don’t arrive at opening expecting a crowd.

I want live music, not a club — what’s best tonight?

MPB4’s 60th-anniversary show at Blue Note (two sets, easy to get into) or Ná Ozzetti’s Maysa tribute at Casa de Francisca (intimate and romantic). Both are seated and central.

I’ve just landed at GRU tonight. Can I still go out?

Easily — it’s Saturday, so the city runs till dawn. The Barra Funda clubs are about a 40-minute rideshare from the airport and only really start after midnight, so you have time to drop your bags first.

What’s the dress code?

Clubs like D-Edge skew dark and casual-cool — no beach flip-flops, but no strict door either. Smart-casual for Blue Note and Casa de Francisca; jeans are fine.

Sources: d-edge.com.br, bluenotesp.com, casadefrancisca.art.br, Sesc São Paulo (agenda)

What’s On Tonight

Liniker — “Bye Bye Caju” — Farmasi Arena, Av. Embaixador Abelardo Bueno 3401, Barra da Tijuca. The tour bids farewell to Caju, the album that won three Latin Grammys in 2025 and made Liniker one of the defining Brazilian artists of the decade, and marks ten years of her career. Expect a grand production — a 25-piece band with horns, strings and a backing chorus, plus the ten dancers of the Balé Caju Negro. Gates open at 5 pm and the show starts at 8 pm. After a sold-out São Paulo opening at the Nubank Parque in July, last tickets for some sectors are still on sale via Eventim, though Cadeira N3 has gone — buy before you travel.

Lapa at Saturday peak — If you’re staying central, Lapa is at its loudest. Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio 20) runs samba, gafieira and choro across three floors from 8 pm to 3 am, with Grupo Mvúka at 8.30 pm and Flavia Saolli at 11.30 pm. Carioca da Gema (Av. Mem de Sá 79) opens at 8.30 pm and gives its main set at 10 pm to Andrezão do Cacique, marking 91 years since the birth of Candeia. The two are about 600 m apart. On the same few blocks, Flávio Venturini plays Circo Voador at 8 pm (from R$90 / US$18 meia), Mari Roots and Trio Forrozão play Fundição Progresso at 8 pm (from R$30 / US$6 meia), and Trio Nordestino plays the Clube dos Democráticos at 9 pm (R$45 / US$9).

Bossa and jazz in Copacabana — Celso Fonseca brings “Tudo é Bossa” to Blue Note Rio (Av. Atlântica 1910), two sessions at 8 pm and 10.30 pm, from R$60 (US$12) meia — songs of his own alongside Caymmi, Baden Powell and Vinicius. For something smaller, Cris Delanno sings bossa at Vinícius Bar in Ipanema at 8 pm (R$70 / US$14 meia), and Victor Biglione and Marcos Ariel play the Cave Music Lounge in Leme at 8 pm (R$70 / US$14). A quieter counterpoint to the arena and the samba houses.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Going to Liniker — Leave early; Barra traffic is heavy and gates open at 5 pm for an 8 pm show. Arrange your ride home before you go in.

Staying central (8 pm) — Rio Scenarium opens and Circo Voador and Fundição Progresso both start; kiosks along Mem de Sá sell cold beer under the Arcos.

Main event (10 pm–late) — Carioca da Gema gives its main set; Rio Scenarium fills and runs to 3 am.

Bossa alternative — Blue Note Rio’s late session starts at 10.30 pm in Copacabana.

Free option — CCS Movimento, Av. Mem de Sá 215A, opens at 7 pm with DJs and no cover.

After the arena — If you’ve energy left, Lapa runs latest, but it’s a long ride from Barra. Copacabana is closer for a nightcap.

Scenes & Sounds

Big concert — Liniker’s farewell “Bye Bye Caju” at the Farmasi Arena is the night’s event. Where: Farmasi Arena (Barra da Tijuca).

Samba houses — Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema carry Lapa at full weekend strength, both with named acts tonight.

Where: Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio 20), Carioca da Gema (Av. Mem de Sá 79).

Bossa and jazz — Celso Fonseca at Blue Note Rio, Cris Delanno at Vinícius Bar, Victor Biglione and Marcos Ariel at the Cave Music Lounge.

Where: Blue Note Rio (Av. Atlântica 1910), Vinícius Bar (Rua Vinícius de Moraes 39, Ipanema), Cave Music Lounge (Leme).

Gafieira and choro — Rio Scenarium’s upper floors mix ballroom gafieira and choro into the samba. Where: Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio 20).

Forró and gafieira — Trio Nordestino at the Clube dos Democráticos and Mari Roots with Trio Forrozão at Fundição Progresso, both in Lapa.

Where: Rua Riachuelo 91 and Rua dos Arcos 24, Lapa.

Clubs — Lapa’s clubs are in full weekend swing, latest of all. Where: Lapa.

Pick Your Night

The event: Liniker at the Farmasi Arena — the pick of the night, if you can get out to Barra.

The full house: Rio Scenarium — three floors, seven spaces, doors 8 pm to 3 am.

The safe bet: Carioca da Gema — Andrezão do Cacique’s Candeia tribute, about 600 m from Scenarium.

Something quieter: Celso Fonseca’s bossa at Blue Note Rio, Copacabana.

Free and open-air: CCS Movimento on Av. Mem de Sá — DJs from 7 pm, no cover. (Pedra do Sal’s roda runs Mondays and Fridays, not tonight.)

Where to Go

Farmasi Arena — Barra da Tijuca Rio’s largest indoor arena, in the Barra Olympic cluster and configurable up to 18,000 — tonight the stage for Liniker’s farewell tour, with a 25-piece band and the ten-strong Balé Caju Negro. Tonight: Liniker, “Bye Bye Caju”. Gates 5 pm, show 8 pm. Under-18s only with a parent or legal guardian, per the venue; the promoter has said 16- and 17-year-olds may enter unaccompanied. Best time: Arrive early — Barra traffic is heavy and the gates open three hours before. Cost: Cadeira N3 from R$147.50 (US$29) meia — now sold out; Cadeira N1 from R$322.50 (US$63) meia; pista from R$347.50 (US$68) meia, R$695 (US$135) full; VIP package R$1,195 (US$232). Address: Av. Embaixador Abelardo Bueno 3401, Barra da Tijuca Tickets: eventim.com.br Getting there: BRT to Parque Olímpico, or rideshare (budget extra time and money for Barra traffic). Good to know: If you bought on EVENTIM.Pass, the entry QR code only appears in the app 24 hours before — set it up in advance. Other delivery methods are unaffected.

Rio Scenarium — Centro/Lapa A magical three-floor 19th-century mansion packed with antiques and seven distinct spaces — one of Rio’s great samba-and-gafieira houses, at its Saturday peak. Tonight: Grupo Mvúka on the Palco Scenarium at 8.30 pm and Flavia Saolli at 11.30 pm, with DJ Gustavo Jr between them. Doors 8 pm, running to 3 am. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday; Friday and Saturday are the fullest. Cost: From R$30 (US$6) meia-entrada, R$45 (US$9) advance. Card and cash. Address: Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro Website: rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk to Rua do Lavradio. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Buy online to skip the queue on a busy Saturday.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa Lapa’s most awarded samba house, going since 2000. Live samba, chorinho and MPB in an intimate, air-conditioned room. Tonight: Andrezão do Cacique, “Homenagem 91 anos de Candeia”. Doors 8.30 pm, main set from 10 pm. Best time: Saturday is its biggest night; it fills up, so go early or reserve. Cost: Cover R$35 (US$7) on Fridays and Saturdays, against R$30 (US$6) Tuesday to Thursday. Card and cash. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Lapa/Centro Website: barcariocadagema.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door at night. Good to know: About 600 m from Rio Scenarium, an eight-minute walk — easy to pair.

Blue Note Rio — Copacabana The Rio outpost of the New York jazz club, on the Copacabana beachfront — polished, seated, and the city’s most reliable room for jazz, bossa and MPB. Tonight: Celso Fonseca, “Tudo é Bossa” — two sessions, 8 pm and 10.30 pm. Songs of his own with Ronaldo Bastos alongside Caymmi, Baden Powell and Vinicius. Best time: The later session is usually the quieter room. Arrive 30 minutes early for seating. Cost: From R$60 (US$12) meia-entrada. Card and cash. Address: Av. Atlântica 1910, Copacabana Getting there: Metro Cardeal Arcoverde, then a short walk down to the beachfront, or rideshare to the door. Good to know: Book the session you want — the two sets sell separately.

Vinícius Bar — Ipanema A small bossa-nova room on the corner where “Garota de Ipanema” was written. Live music every night, close quarters, and a crowd that listens. Tonight: Cris Delanno sings bossa nova, from 8 pm. Best time: Early — the room is small and fills from the first set. Cost: From R$70 (US$14) meia-entrada, plus the bill. Card and cash. Address: Rua Vinícius de Moraes 39, Ipanema Getting there: Metro General Osório, a five-minute walk. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Reserve — there are only a few dozen seats.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Barra da Tijuca: Sprawling, car-dependent beach zone, home to the Farmasi Arena. Great for the show, but far from the rest of the nightlife — plan your transport.

Lapa: Rio’s nightlife heart under the Arcos, at its Saturday peak — Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Circo Voador and Fundição Progresso within a few blocks. Rideshare door-to-door late.

Copacabana / Ipanema: Blue Note Rio on the beachfront and Vinícius Bar on the Ipanema corner, plus an easy base and the closest nightlife to Barra. Walkable and lively.

Centro / Saúde: The old port and Rua do Lavradio, where Rio Scenarium and the Dolores Club sit. Alive for the samba, quiet otherwise, so travel by car.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. Charming and low-key; rideshare up and down.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Peak night, and a fitting headline — Saturday is the biggest night for Rio’s queer scene, and Liniker — a Black trans artist and one of the country’s most celebrated — headlines the Farmasi Arena. Beyond the show, expect parties in Copacabana, the port and Lapa.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Lapa’s samba houses are broadly mixed and welcoming, and all of tonight’s rooms are easy, inclusive options.

Money & How Paying Works Concert tickets: Buy Liniker through Eventim only. If your ticket is an EVENTIM.Pass, the entry QR code appears in the app 24 hours before — don’t rely on a screenshot. Couvert and cover: Lapa houses charge a per-person music cover, higher on a Saturday. It’s on your bill, separate from food and drinks. Cash for the small places: street kiosks and the smaller bars use cash. Carry about R$150 (US$29) in small notes. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. It is customary rather than compulsory, and you can ask for it to be removed.

Getting Home Safe

From the arena: Book your ride before the show ends, or expect a long surge-priced wait as the arena empties. The BRT is an option earlier in the night.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and the safest way home from Lapa and Barra late at night. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Lapa at night: Busy and fun around the Arcos on a Saturday, but keep your phone and wallet secure and stick to the main, well-lit streets.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Geography: Barra to Lapa is roughly an hour by car. Decide where you’re ending the night before you start it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still get Liniker tickets?

As of this weekend, yes — last tickets for some sectors are still on sale via Eventim, after the São Paulo dates sold out. Buy before you head to Barra, and set up the Eventim app, since your entry QR code only appears there 24 hours before the show.

Can I do Liniker and Lapa in one night?

It’s a stretch. The arena is in Barra, about an hour from Lapa, and the show runs late. If you want both, keep it loose — the samba houses run until 4 am, but the ride across town is long and pricey after midnight.

I’ve just landed at GIG (Galeão) tonight. Where should I go?

If you’re not at the arena, head to Lapa — Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema run into the early hours and are about a 30–40 minute rideshare from Galeão. Carry some cash and take a rideshare door-to-door.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not at all. The music does the work and the crowds are welcoming. A smile, a cold beer, and cash for the cover or the drinks are all you need.

Sources: eventim.com.br (Liniker), farmasiarena.com.br, rioscenarium.com.br, barcariocadagema.com.br, bluenoterio.com.br

World.title: IDB Calls the Guyana Outlook Highly Uncertain on Oil Risk
World.content:
Guyana · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Report Inter-American Development Bank’s Caribbean Economics Quarterly, released mid-August 2026

— Coverage Bahamas, Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago

— Growth Guyana projected to average about 14% between 2026 and 2030

— Suriname Growth slowed to 1.5% in 2025, projected to recover to 3.9% in 2026

— Risk Oil shocks may cause Dutch disease, hurting other industries

An oil exporter, and still exposed to the price of the thing it sells.

Guyana’s economy now turns on offshore oil. The IDB calls the outlook highly uncertain, with oil prices driven by geopolitical tensions. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)
