The Guyana outlook is highly uncertain, according to an Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) report released in mid-August 2026. Persistent geopolitical tensions continue to push up international oil prices, creating risks for the country’s economy.

IDB Report Highlights Uncertainty

The Inter-American Development Bank’s Caribbean Economics Quarterly, titled Fiscal Resilience, Debt Reduction and Domestic Resource Mobilization in the Caribbean, covers six nations. It includes the Bahamas, Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica, Suriname and Trinidad and Tobago.

The report warns that Caribbean governments face a difficult international financial environment. High global interest rates, volatile energy markets and external shocks can quickly pressure national budgets.

Oil Prices and Geopolitical Tensions

An IDB-linked report dated 21 August 2026 describes the Guyana outlook as highly uncertain. Persistent geopolitical tensions continue to push up international oil prices.

However, the wider Caribbean analysis notes that oil prices are expected to stay low over the medium term and could fall further. This would temper the oil boom in Guyana.

Dutch Disease Risks

The report warns that oil shocks can create Dutch disease risks. These shocks can also pass through to fuel and electricity prices, even though Guyana is a net oil exporter.

Dutch disease occurs when an oil or mining boom pushes up a country’s currency and costs. As a result, other industries become uncompetitive.

Potential Game Changers

The IDB identifies the biggest potential game changers for the region. These include shifts in demand from advanced economies, especially the United States.

In addition, geopolitical tensions and changes in China’s demand for commodities are key factors. Therefore, the Guyana outlook depends on global developments.

Guyana’s Growth Prospects

Despite the uncertainty, the Guyana outlook includes strong growth projections. An IDB Caribbean Quarterly cited in January 2026 projects Guyana’s growth to average about 14% between 2026 and 2030.

This growth is driven by rising oil output and non-oil expansion. Guyana became one of the world’s fastest-growing economies after ExxonMobil started producing oil offshore.

Suriname’s Contrasting Outlook

For Suriname, the report says near-term risks lean to the downside because of the geopolitical context. Still, the medium-term outlook remains favourable.

Suriname’s outlook is anchored in expected oil-driven growth and improved fiscal and external dynamics. Suriname’s growth slowed to about 1.5% in 2025, from 1.7% in 2024, because gold production contracted.

Recovery Projections for Suriname

Suriname is projected to recover to about 3.9% in 2026 and settle near 4%. Meanwhile, the Guyana outlook remains tied to oil price movements.

The report’s warnings highlight the delicate balance for oil-dependent economies. Even so, the medium-term prospects for both countries are shaped by global commodity trends.

Implications for the Caribbean

Overall, the IDB report stresses the need for fiscal resilience in the Caribbean. Debt reduction and domestic resource mobilization are central themes.

As a result, governments must prepare for external shocks. The Guyana outlook serves as a reminder that even booming economies face vulnerabilities.

What the Guyana Outlook Depends On

In short, the Guyana outlook is highly uncertain, but growth remains strong. The IDB’s analysis points to both opportunities and risks.

While oil prices may fall, geopolitical tensions could keep them elevated. Therefore, policymakers must stay vigilant.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Guyana outlook according to the IDB?

The Guyana outlook is described as highly uncertain because persistent geopolitical tensions push up international oil prices. However, growth is projected to average about 14% between 2026 and 2030.

What is Dutch disease?

Dutch disease is when an oil or mining boom pushes up a country’s currency and costs. This makes other industries uncompetitive.

Which countries does the IDB report cover?

The report covers the Bahamas, Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica, Suriname and Trinidad and Tobago. It was released in mid-August 2026.

What are the main risks for Guyana?

Oil shocks can create Dutch disease risks and pass through to fuel and electricity prices. Additionally, shifts in demand from advanced economies and China’s commodity demand are potential game changers.

Sources: Inter-American Development Bank; Caribbean press.

World.content:
Paraguay · DEFENCE

Key Facts — Arrival Fifth Super Tucano received on 21 August 2026

— Contract Six aircraft total, not five

— Financing Loan from Brazil’s development bank BNDES

— Purpose Intercept illegal flights, including drug trafficking

— Context Paraguay sits on smuggling routes between Bolivia, Brazil, and Argentina

The new planes arrive late, but Paraguay is closing a gap in its fight against drug flights.

An Embraer A-29 Super Tucano. Paraguay received its fifth aircraft on Friday 21 August 2026, with a sixth due by the end of September. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Paraguay Receives Its Fifth Super Tucano to Chase Drug Flights, marking a key step in modernizing its air defenses. The aircraft arrived on Friday 21 August 2026.

The Fuerza Aérea Paraguaya received it at a ceremony headed by President Santiago Peña.

A New Arrival in the Fight Against Drug Flights

The fifth Super Tucano touched down in Paraguay on Friday 21 August 2026, welcomed by President Santiago Peña. This Brazilian-made light attack aircraft is designed to intercept illegal flights, including those used for drug trafficking.

The ceremony was led by the Fuerza Aérea Paraguaya, the country’s air force. It marks a significant addition to Paraguay’s efforts to secure its skies.

The Super Tucano: A Versatile Aircraft

The Super Tucano is an Embraer A-29, a light attack and advanced training aircraft built in Brazil. It is small and propeller-driven, making it slow enough to intercept other small aircraft.

In addition, it is cheap to run compared with a jet, which makes it practical for patrol missions. This aircraft type is well-suited for the region’s smuggling challenges.

Contract Details and Financing

The contract covers six aircraft in total, not five, as some might assume. Reported contract values differ, with defence-focused sources giving US$96,681,379, financed through a loan from Brazil’s development bank BNDES.

Other outlets cite about US$95 million or US$105 million for the six aircraft. Therefore, the exact price remains unclear, but the financing is known to involve BNDES.

Delivery Schedule and Delays

The original plan was to deliver all six by around March 2026, but that slipped. Four arrived in late June and early July 2025, and the last two were rescheduled to July and August 2026.

Meanwhile, the sixth aircraft is expected by the end of September 2026. Despite the delays, the fifth has now arrived, and the fleet is nearly complete.

Why Paraguay Needs the Super Tucano

Paraguay sits on smuggling routes between Bolivia, Brazil and Argentina. Light aircraft are a common way to move cargo across the region.

The Super Tucano is intended to intercept these illegal flights in Paraguayan airspace. As a result, the aircraft play a crucial role in combating drug trafficking.

They provide a cost-effective solution to a persistent problem.

The Role of Light Attack Aircraft

A light attack aircraft like the Super Tucano is small and propeller-driven. That lets it fly slowly enough to intercept other small planes.

This makes it an effective tool for air policing. Moreover, its operational costs are lower than a jet’s, making it an economical choice for continuous patrols.

Therefore, it fits Paraguay’s needs well.

Looking Ahead to the Sixth Super Tucano

With the fifth Super Tucano now in service, attention turns to the sixth and final aircraft. It is expected by the end of September 2026, completing the contract.

Once all six are operational, Paraguay will have a more robust capability to monitor its airspace. In short, this marks a milestone in the country’s air defense modernization.

Regional Context and Smuggling Routes

The Super Tucano’s mission is rooted in the region’s geography. Paraguay is a transit point for smuggling between Bolivia, Brazil, and Argentina, and small planes often carry illegal cargo.

Therefore, having aircraft that can intercept these flights is vital. The new Super Tucanos are a direct response to this challenge.

A Boost for Air Defense

In addition to chasing drug flights, the Super Tucano serves as an advanced training aircraft. This dual role enhances the capabilities of the Fuerza Aérea Paraguaya.

Overall, the arrival of the fifth Super Tucano strengthens Paraguay’s air defense. It is a clear signal of the country’s commitment to securing its skies.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Super Tucano?

The Super Tucano is a Brazilian-made light attack and advanced training aircraft. It is small, propeller-driven, and designed to intercept other small aircraft.

How many Super Tucanos has Paraguay received?

Paraguay has received five Super Tucanos so far. The sixth and final aircraft is expected by the end of September 2026.

Why is Paraguay buying Super Tucanos?

The aircraft are intended to intercept illegal flights, including those used for drug trafficking. Paraguay sits on smuggling routes between Bolivia, Brazil, and Argentina.

How is the Super Tucano purchase financed?

The purchase is financed through a loan from Brazil’s development bank BNDES. Reported contract values differ, but the financing is known.

Sources: Fuerza Aérea Paraguaya; defence trade press; Paraguayan media.

World.title: Public Institutions Pull Out of Costa Rica’s Festival de la Luz
World.content:
Several major public institutions will not bring their traditional illuminated floats to San José’s Festival de la Luz this year, forcing organizers to rethink one of Costa Rica’s best-known Christmas celebrations. The Festival de la Luz 2026 remains scheduled for Saturday, December 12. However, the Municipality of San José has not released the final parade format or a complete list of participating floats.

Five public institutions have been identified as not participating: Banco de Costa Rica, Banco Nacional, Banco Popular, Grupo INS and Kölbi. The Junta de Protección Social has not confirmed whether it will take part. The Municipality said some public institutions had initially agreed to participate about two months ago but later backed out. According to Mayor Diego Miranda, some of those decisions were communicated informally.

The institutions that have spoken publicly have offered practical rather than political explanations. Banco Popular said it decided not to participate after reviewing its marketing plans and deciding where its money and activities could reach the most people. The bank is considering free family events in San José and other parts of Costa Rica during the holiday season.

Banco Nacional gave a similar explanation. It said it wants to spread its year-end activities across more communities, with a greater focus on local businesses and community events. The bank specifically denied that politics played any role in its decision. Grupo INS said its plans are based on budget limits and institutional priorities. The insurer entered a float in 2024 as part of its 100th anniversary celebration but it did not have its own float in 2025 however it participated in other Festival de la Luz activities.

For 2026, Grupo INS plans to illuminate Parque España, across from its offices in downtown San José. The institution also denied that its decision was political. Banco de Costa Rica offered a somewhat different account. The bank said the Municipality informed it that changes were being planned for the traditional float parade. Because of those changes, BCR said it would not take part this year and would instead consider other holiday activities.

Despite those explanations, Miranda has suggested that political disagreements between his administration and the national government may have influenced the withdrawals. The mayor said the timing comes after public disputes involving the treatment of homeless people in San José and other disagreements between the central government and the Municipality.

However, Miranda acknowledged that none of the institutions directly told him politics was the reason. He has not presented public evidence connecting their decisions to pressure from the government. The withdrawal of the public institutions does not necessarily mean the parade will have no floats at all. The Municipality is talking with private companies interested in participating, although it has not published a confirmed list.

City officials are also working on a new attraction featuring giant balloons similar to those used in New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The number of balloons, their designs and how they would be used have not yet been announced. The Municipality has promised a renewed version of the festival, but the final mix of private floats, marching bands, balloons and other displays remains unclear.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan Slips to Second in UN Race
World.content:
Costa Rican economist and former vice president Rebeca Grynspan has fallen to second place in the race to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations, but the contest remains far from decided. Grynspan received seven votes encouraging her candidacy during the second informal ballot held by the 15-member U.N. Security Council on Friday. She also received four votes discouraging her candidacy, while four council members expressed no opinion.

The results have not been formally released by the United Nations because the vote was secret. The figures were circulated among diplomats and widely reported after the closed-door meeting. Grynspan had led the first informal vote on July 30 with 10 encouraging votes, one discouraging vote and four members expressing no opinion. Her support therefore dropped by three votes during the latest round, while the number opposing her candidacy rose by three.

Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana moved into first place with eight “yes” votes, three “no” votes and four no-opinion. She had received nine “yes” votes in the first round, meaning her support also declined, but not as sharply as Grynspan’s. Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, who leads the U.N. nuclear watchdog, matched Grynspan with seven “yes” votes. However, Grossi received six “no” votes, compared with four for the Costa Rican.

The results do not mean Rodrigues-Birkett has won the position or that Grynspan has been eliminated. These early ballots are meant to show candidates how much support and opposition they have before the Security Council holds a formal vote. Council members mark each candidate as “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.” Several rounds are normally needed before the council reaches an agreement.

To advance, a candidate eventually needs at least nine of the council’s 15 votes. The candidate must also avoid a veto from China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom or the United States, the council’s five permanent members. The ballots used so far do not reveal whether any negative votes came from those five powerful countries. Later votes may use different-colored ballots to show whether a permanent member is blocking a candidate.

That means Grynspan’s four “discouraging “no” votes could become more important as the process continues, but it is currently impossible to determine whether any amount to a potential veto. Eight candidates are competing to replace António Guterres of Portugal, whose second five-year term ends on December 31, 2026. His successor is expected to take office on January 1, 2027.

Grynspan served as Costa Rica’s second vice president from 1994 to 1998 and has led the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development since 2021. She took temporary leave from that position while campaigning for the U.N.’s top job. Costa Rica formally nominated her on March 3. Her campaign focuses on strengthening the U.N.’s role in peace and security, making the organization work more effectively and preparing it for future global challenges.

The eventual candidate must first be recommended by the Security Council and then formally appointed by the 193-member U.N. General Assembly. The process could continue through September or October if council members remain divided.

World.title: Cincinnati Open 2026 Sets All-North American Semifinal
World.content:
An American man is guaranteed a place in the Cincinnati Open final after Frances Tiafoe and Brandon Nakashima won their quarterfinal matches on Friday. Tiafoe defeated Italy’s Lorenzo Musetti 7-6(2), 7-5 in a match that lasted two hours and 17 minutes. He will face Nakashima, who knocked out fellow American Taylor Fritz 7-6(9), 4-6, 6-3.

Their semifinal is scheduled for Saturday at 6 p.m. in Ohio, which is 4 p.m. in Costa Rica. It will be the first Cincinnati semifinal between two American men since Andy Roddick faced Mardy Fish in 2010. The winner will play either Italy’s Flavio Cobolli or France’s Arthur Fils in Sunday’s final.

Tiafoe had a chance to serve out his match against Musetti at 5-4 in the second set but could not finish the job. Instead of letting the missed opportunity derail him, he broke Musetti’s serve in the next game and closed the match on his fourth match point. “I just gotta play to win,” Tiafoe said after the match. “The guy who plays a little more brave at certain moments gets it.”

The 28-year-old is trying to win the biggest title of his career. He reached the Cincinnati final in 2024 but lost to Jannik Sinner. Tiafoe has beaten Nakashima in six of their seven previous meetings, giving him a clear advantage in their history. Nakashima, however, enters the semifinal in the best form of his career.

The 25-year-old reached his first Masters 1000 final earlier this month in Montreal. He has now followed that performance by reaching the final four in Cincinnati. A Masters 1000 tournament sits just below the four Grand Slam events in importance. Strong results at this level bring major ranking points, prize money and momentum.

Nakashima’s path through Cincinnati has included victories over Daniil Medvedev and Fritz. He saved three match points against Medvedev before winning in three sets, then recovered from a break down in the final set against Fritz. Fritz led 3-2 in the deciding set, but Nakashima won the final four games to take the match.

“Just getting a lot of confidence from all the matches I have been playing,” Nakashima said. “When it came down to the wire in the third set, I just tried to trust my game fully.” The Cincinnati Open has produced several major surprises this year. Argentina’s Thiago Agustín Tirante defeated Novak Djokovic and reached his first Masters 1000 quarterfinal before losing to Fils. Top men’s seed Alexander Zverev was eliminated by Tommy Paul, while Medvedev fell to Nakashima.

There is still a Latin American presence in the doubles competition. Brazilian pair Orlando Luz and Rafael Matos defeated Italians Simone Bolelli and Andrea Vavassori 7-6(7), 6-3 to reach the semifinals. Luz and Matos will face Hugo Nys and Édouard Roger-Vasselin on Saturday. The Brazilians are coming off their first Masters 1000 title together in Montreal.

The Cincinnati results carry added weight because the U.S. Open singles competition begins August 30 in New York. Players have only a short window to recover, adjust their games and build confidence before the year’s final Grand Slam. For Tiafoe and Nakashima, Saturday’s semifinal offers something more immediate: a place in one of the biggest finals of the tennis season.

World.title: International News: Europe endures scorching summer as heat waves push temperatures above 40°C
World.content:
International News: Europe endures scorching summer as heat waves push temperatures above 40°C

By Zoila Palma: Western Europe is experiencing an unusually hot summer, with a series of intense heat waves pushing temperatures above 40°C (104°F) across several countries.

The extreme heat began as early as May, when a heat dome shattered temperature records, and by mid-August, the region had experienced its fifth major heat wave of the season, NASA reports.

The prolonged heat has disrupted daily life across the region, contributing to increased hospitalizations and heat-related deaths while damaging roads and railway infrastructure.

Wildfires have also intensified in areas not typically accustomed to such severe conditions, while months of drought have lowered river levels and created challenges for agriculture, transportation, water supplies and energy production.

Temperature records have been broken repeatedly. London reached 35.1°C on May 26, surpassing the previous May record by 2.3°C, while Bordeaux, France, recorded 42.5°C on June 24 after breaking its maximum-temperature record for three consecutive days. According to Europe’s Copernicus climate monitoring service, combined temperatures across Western Europe in June and July were the highest on record.

The heat has been particularly dangerous because many European homes lack air conditioning, while some cities have limited green spaces and have experienced unusually high nighttime temperatures. Preliminary reports indicate that heat may have been associated with around 10,000 excess deaths across countries including the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Belgium. Experts warn that older adults and people with underlying health conditions are especially vulnerable to prolonged heat.

Scientists say Europe must prepare for increasingly frequent and severe heat events by expanding green spaces, planting trees, using reflective roofing materials and improving buildings and cooling systems.

World.title: International News: Argentina seeks to become Latin America’s Artificial Intelligence hub
World.content:
International News: Argentina seeks to become Latin America’s Artificial Intelligence hub

By Zoila Palma: Argentina is positioning itself to become a major artificial intelligence hub in Latin America as President Javier Milei’s administration pushes deregulation, investment incentives and technology infrastructure to attract billions of dollars in new investment.

The government is promoting data centers, high-speed connectivity and partnerships with technology companies as part of its broader strategy to expand the country’s digital economy, Digital Shield reports.

One initiative involves expanding satellite internet connectivity in rural and isolated areas through Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by SpaceX.

The government says improved connectivity could benefit thousands of remote schools while also creating opportunities for greater use of artificial intelligence and automation in agriculture and other sectors.

The government is promoting the Regime of Incentive for Large Investments, which offers tax, customs and foreign-exchange incentives to major projects, while initiatives involving AI, data centers and agricultural technology are being developed.

Among the projects being discussed are large-scale computing infrastructure investments, including the reported Stargate Argentina initiative involving OpenAI and Sur Energy.

World.title: International News: Infantino defies FIFA, attends Caribbean Youth football event
World.content:
International News: Infantino defies FIFA, attends Caribbean Youth football event

By Zoila Palma: FIFA President Gianni Infantino attended an Under-14 football tournament in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, despite a request from FIFA vice president Victor Montagliani to stay away amid growing tensions over Infantino’s controversial financial proposal.

Infantino posted photos from the Caribbean Football Union youth event, where he met with political and football officials, AP reports.

Montagliani had reportedly urged Infantino to reconsider attending, warning that the ongoing governance controversy surrounding FIFA could overshadow the youth competition.

The FIFA vice president said media attention would likely focus on Infantino’s failed FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal rather than the tournament and asked him to avoid becoming a distraction.

The dispute comes after Infantino faced criticism over a reported plan to transfer FIFA’s multibillion-dollar commercial activities to a subsidiary partly owned by private investors.

The proposal, which reportedly involved investors led by Joshua Kushner, was withdrawn on August 1 following backlash from football officials and fans.

Several FIFA vice presidents have since called for changes to Infantino’s leadership.

World.title: Belize Marketing and Development Corporation participates in Belize Climate Week 2026 in Punta Gorda
World.content:
Belize Marketing and Development Corporation participates in Belize Climate Week 2026 in Punta Gorda

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Marketing and Development Corporation (BMDC) is participating in Belize Climate Week 2026, being held in Punta Gorda, Toledo, highlighting its commitment to strengthening Belize’s agricultural sector and supporting local producers.

BMDC focuses on agriculture, food security, agro-processing and the development of Belizean producers.

BMDC says climate change makes it increasingly important to build a more resilient and sustainable agricultural sector that can adapt to changing conditions.

Throughout the week, participants are exploring opportunities related to climate-smart agriculture, innovation, technology, climate finance and the Orange Economy. The event also provides a platform for organizations and stakeholders to connect, exchange ideas and develop partnerships.

BMDC says its participation is aimed at identifying new opportunities to create greater value from Belizean agriculture while supporting producers and promoting sustainable development.

World.title: Hummingbird Agro-Producers Co-operative holds first Annual General Meeting
World.content:
Hummingbird Agro-Producers Co-operative holds first Annual General Meeting

By Zoila Palma: The Hummingbird Agro-Producers Co-operative Society Limited held its first Annual General Meeting on Thursday, August 20, 2026, bringing together its members to review the organization’s progress and plans for the future.

Based in Hope Creek Village, Stann Creek, the co-operative has 19 members, including 10 females and 9 males.

Its membership includes youths from communities and villages such as Hope Creek, Mullins River, Gales Point Manatee and Dangriga Town.

The members are engaged in the manufacture and processing of a wide variety of food products. During the meeting, guest remarks were delivered by Registrar of Co-operatives Gareth Murillo, while updates were also provided on the co-operative’s recent activities and financial status.

The meeting concluded with members pledging their continued support toward strengthening the organization, increasing its mobilization efforts and ensuring the long-term sustainability of the Hummingbird Agro-Producers Co-operative Society Limited.

World.title: BEL and government call press conference on energy issues
World.content:
BEL and government call press conference on energy issues

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Electricity Limited and the Government of Belize have called a press conference for Monday morning to address what they describe as topical issues within the energy landscape.

The briefing is set for Monday, August 24 at 10am at Toucan Hall, Belize Biltmore Plaza, 3 Miles Philip Goldson Highway, Belize City.

The announcement follows days of public complaints over sharp increases in electricity bills, with some consumers reporting their bills tripled.

Prime Minister John Briceño said on Friday that he had asked Minister Michel Chebat to meet with BEL Executive Chairman Young and the Public Utilities Commission, and to meet with the media early this week.

The complaints centre on the Cost of Power Adjustment, or COPA, approved by the PUC at 1.5 cents per kilowatt hour for August.

The United Democratic Party has demanded that the increase be rolled back and that government explain how close to $400 million invested in the energy sector has benefited consumers.

The press conference is expected to address those questions directly.

World.title: Evangelical association accepts pastor’s rape conviction and 10 year sentence
World.content:
Evangelical association accepts pastor’s rape conviction and 10 year sentence

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The National Evangelical Association of Belize has acknowledged the conviction and 10 year prison sentence handed down to Pastor Victor Hernandez on Monday, August 17.

In a press release signed by President Rev. Santie Valencia and the NEAB National Executive Team, the association said the situation is disturbing and saddening to the Church, but stressed that victims must come first.

“We fully accept the Court’s judgment and ruling and encourage the body of Christ to pray for the victim who bravely told her story,” the release states.

The association described the offence as unacceptable and criminal.

“Congregants place a sacred trust in Pastors and it is imperative that church leaders hold themselves, and each other, to a higher standard. This situation was a failure of that sacred principle of leadership in the Kingdom of God.”

NEAB is urging all pastors, churches, ministries and Bible study groups to discuss the issue with a view toward creating safe spaces and strong boundaries.

It also placed responsibility on leadership to build a culture that responds when the alarm bell goes off.

World.title: Six dollars an hour: who really wins and who could lose?
World.content:
Six dollars an hour: who really wins and who could lose?

By Horace Palacio:

On Friday, the Prime Minister said it again. His government remains committed to raising the minimum wage from five to six dollars an hour, a Plan Belize 2.0 promise, but the timing must wait on the wider economy and on what businesses can absorb. More talks with the Chamber of Commerce are promised. No date is given.

Readers of this column know I have written on this twice, once urging caution on the raise itself, once handing government ten things to do instead. I have had my say. So today I will do something different, and I believe more useful. I will lay out the full ledger, the case for six dollars now and the case for waiting, each argued at full strength, the way its own believers would argue it. Then the verdict goes where it belongs, to you.

First, the stakes, in numbers every Belizean should know by heart. The minimum wage has stood at five dollars since January 2023, when it jumped from the 3.30 that had held for a decade. A full legal week earns 225 dollars, roughly 975 a month. The median Belizean income sits near one thousand. So this debate is not about the edge of our economy. It is about its center.

Now, the case for six dollars, argued honestly.

Begin where the worker begins, at the end of the month that never reaches. Rent. The light bill, now carrying its new adjustment line. Bus fare. Butane. Then the grocery, where 90 percent of our inflation arrives imported and unbeatable. On 975 a month, the month is longer than the money, every month, forever. A dollar more per hour is 45 dollars a week, nearly 200 a month. To an economist that is a variable. To a minimum wage mother it is the light bill paid and shoes for September.

Second, the dignity argument, and it is not sentimental, it is foundational. A person who gives an employer 45 honest hours a week should not remain in poverty. If a business model only survives by paying wages a full-time worker cannot live on, the workers are subsidizing that business with their hardship. Work must pay. That is the whole social bargain.

Third, the raise feeds the very shops that fear it. Minimum wage earners save nothing, not by choice but by arithmetic. Every extra dollar goes straight back across Belizean counters, the corner store, the market, the bus. Raising the floor is partly a transfusion into small business’s own customer base.

Fourth, the erosion argument. Since 2023, prices have climbed while the five dollars stood still. A frozen wage in a rising market is a quiet pay cut, renewed monthly. Wait long enough for the perfect moment and inflation will have cancelled the last raise before the next one arrives.

And fifth, the precedent. In 2023 this country raised the wage 52 percent in one stroke, from 3.30 to five dollars, for more than thirty thousand workers. The sky did not fall. Businesses adapted. Against that history, a 20 percent step to six dollars is modest. We have done far bolder and survived.

Now, the case for waiting, argued just as honestly.

Begin with who actually pays, because it is not government. The wage order is signed in Belmopan but the cheque is written by the shopkeeper with four staff, the small restaurant, the farmer at harvest. The Prime Minister’s own words state the constraint plainly, businesses can only pay what they can pay. Command a payroll a small business cannot carry and it does not print money. It cuts hours, sheds its newest worker, or closes.

Second, the cruel selection of who gets hurt. A raise helps everyone who keeps their job and devastates whoever is priced out of one, and the priced-out are always the same people, the youngest, the least skilled, the last hired, the very Belizeans the policy means to rescue. Some slip into informality, off the books entirely, no Social Security, no protections, a worse world than five dollars ever was.

Third, the pass-through. Businesses facing higher payroll raise prices where they can. The worker wins at the pay window and loses a slice back at the counter, and in an economy whose inflation is overwhelmingly imported, a domestic wage push stacks a second layer of price pressure on top of the layer we cannot control.

Fourth, the weather has changed. That bold 2023 raise landed in a roaring rebound, when the economy was growing at historic double-digit paces. Today growth has cooled toward two percent, fuel has spiked, and the same power cost adjustment squeezing your home is squeezing every shop and factory harder. Stacking a labour cost rise on top of an energy cost rise, in a slowing economy, is how closures happen. Same policy, different weather, different risk.

And fifth, the floor is not the ladder. Six dollars is still not a living wage, roughly 1,170 a month, still short of the basket. The deeper fixes remain the ones this column has catalogued, cheaper power, cheaper food, skills that let workers climb past the floor entirely. A number on a wage order cannot outrun a grocery bill written abroad.

There is the ledger. Now, the Prime Minister’s alternative relief deserves its own honest audit, because he offers it as the answer in the meantime. Free secondary education has expanded to 23 schools, more than twelve thousand students, 95 percent of government secondary students paying nothing, and that is real, a genuine and large saving that reaches minimum wage families with teenagers directly. Credit it fully. The National Health Insurance expansion, likewise, reaches the poor where they live. But the income tax threshold raise, moved to 29,000 dollars, however sound a policy, by definition delivers zero to minimum wage workers, who earn far below it and never paid the tax. Relief that arrives above your head is not relief. So the alternative package is real but partial, strongest for families with students, weakest for the childless worker drowning in rent.

So what should Belizeans demand while deciding? One thing above all. A date, or a test. Further discussions is not a policy, it is a postponement without a calendar. If six dollars must wait for conditions, then publish the conditions, the growth rate, the inflation reading, the indicators that trigger the raise, so the promise cannot drift forever on the word timing. And consider the middle road both sides can live with, a phased step, fifty cents now, fifty cents on a named date, paired with the cost-cutting agenda that makes every dollar worth more. A commitment without a date is a wish. Workers cannot eat wishes, and businesses cannot plan around them.

Here, then, is the whole question, stripped to one sentence each way.

The worker’s month is longer than the money, and waiting taxes her daily. The shopkeeper’s margin is thinner than the slogan, and a misjudged raise closes his doors and her job together.

Both sentences are true. The question is which risk Belize chooses to carry, and who we trust to carry it.

You have the ledger now. The verdict is yours.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Residents of Cooper’s Pen stage protest as follow-up demolition looms
World.content:
Residents decked out in white and holding placards gathered along the North Coast Highway, which runs adjacent to the community, to declare their feelings on the matter.

Chanting “we need help” and “we need justice”, the residents were out from 7:00 am to drive home their concerns surrounding their current predicament.

Some residents say they have been on the property for over 30 years and describe the current situation as surprising and devastating.

Just over a week ago, residents woke up to the sounds of heavy machinery and workmen who began demolishing homes in the community.

Reports are that on August 11, the pre-dawn operation displaced between 20 and 40 families living in the area. This came as part of a long-running land dispute involving private interests that are said to own the land.

The allegedly unannounced operation drew widespread condemnation regarding the handling of the residents’ displacement, including news that several community members were detained by the police prior to the demolition exercise.

Since then, several individuals have been living in tents provided by the Social Security Ministry, while other help has been provided by the Member of Parliament, Tova Hamilton.

Meanwhile, the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP) has been calling for a halt to proceedings and for greater support for the residents.

World.title: US judge strikes down Trump’s 75-country immigrant visa ban
World.content:
US visa

WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — A United States (US) federal judge has struck down a government ban on visas to nationals from 75 countries, including Jamaica, who wish to settle in the country indefinitely, dealing a blow to President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

READ: Jamaica among 75 countries hit with suspension of US immigrant visa processing

In a ruling issued on Friday in the Southern District of New York, Judge Jeannette Vargas called the policy “contrary to law” and said Secretary of State Marco Rubio had exceeded his “statutory authority” in issuing it.

The policy, which came into force in January, suspended the processing of immigrant visas to nationals of 75 countries including Afghanistan, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and Yemen.

At that time, the State Department had said the decision was made “to ensure that immigrants from high-risk countries do not unlawfully utilise welfare in the United States or become a public charge.”

But Vargas ruled that consular officers were wrongly ordered to refuse immigrant visas solely based on an applicant’s country of origin, even if they had determined the applicant was otherwise.

Friday’s ruling vacates any visa denial based solely on the policy.

The government can appeal the ruling.

Trump campaigned for the White House on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken a number of actions since returning to the White House aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings.

World.title: ‘I’m going to fight it!’
World.content:
Seventy-five-year-old wood sculptor Walton Spence inside his craft shop at Jacob Taylor Beach in Trelawny, Friday morning. Spence says he will fight a removal notice issued by the Natural Resources Conservation Authority. Photo: Horace Hines

SILVER SANDS, Trelawny — A 75-year-old wood sculptor, who says he has made a living from a shop he erected at Jacob Taylor Beach 34 years ago, is vowing to fight a bid by Natural Resources Conservation Authority (NRCA) to remove him and other shop operators from the property.

Walton Spence was among about a dozen shop operators served with 30-day notices by the NRCA on Monday. The State agency, which identified itself as the owner of the property, said the land was needed “for a public purpose” and “for the purpose of being repaired and improved”.

But Spence said he will not leave without a fight. It is a common sentiment among other shop operators.

“My next move is not to leave. I’m going to fight it!” said the senior citizen.

He explained his history with the property locals often refer to as Silver Sands.

“I start to come down here from 1990 come demonstrate my work. What I used to do is carry them down in a box and carry them up back in the evening. But from 1992 I have been permanently based on this beach. I build a little shop and lock my things in from 1992,” Spence told the

Jamaica Observer Friday.

According to the existing legislation, a case can be made for adverse possession of government land if it is openly occupied, undisturbed for 60 consecutive years.

On Friday, Spence painted a grim picture of what will happen to him if he is forced to leave the location.

Wood carving, he said, is his only viable vocation. He said that years ago he worked as a mason, but had to abandon the trade because of ailments and challenges dealing with cement dust.

“I suffer with arthritis, blood pressure, [I’m] diabetic, and my sinus bother me. So less dust I can encounter with, me better off,” he explained.

Spence questioned being able to find employment at his age if he can no longer ply his wares at Silver Sands.

“My question to all of these people who trying to undermine my movement is to ask them, ‘What plans they got for me?’” he said.

“My question is, ‘After you lock me off with the one-month notice that you gave me, [are] you willing to start maintain my life from right there until God ready for me? Or you intend to really put me out there to suffer?” he asked.

Spence stressed that he is not seeking charity, just an opportunity to earn an honest living.

“I’m not looking for no handout or whatever. I’m a decent citizen of this land. I was born here, I grow here, and I’m intending to die here, but I have no intention of leaving Jamaica,” he said.

A day earlier, he and other shop operators had a meeting during which they decided to seek legal advice on how they can challenge the notices and secure their tenure on the beach.

“We will be seeking legal representation to fight this issue. This is our bread and butter,” one of the shop operators, who asked not to be identified by name, told the Observer.

Fisherman Leroy Gilzene, who runs a bar with his wife, Cordella, is among those refusing to leave without a fight. Cordella said Leroy has been operating there since 1984 and their business developed gradually from modest beginnings.

“This part of beach [was] full of nickel tree, lots of bush, before some of those shop made up there. So we’re coming from a long way. This is our livelihood. We don’t know anything more but this,” she explained.

Juliet, who has operated a cookshop on the beach for more than 20 years, said four generations of her family have occupied the area.

“My grandfather, my father they were also here. And my son grow here too. And now they want to come and take it from us,” she said.

Rohan Watson, a 39-year-old fisherman who also operates a craft shop, said he had seen businesses passed down through generations.

Rackquay Small, who is employed to Silver Moon Convenience Store, said the 30-day notice came at a difficult time, with back-to-school expenses approaching and some families still recovering from Hurricane Melissa which hit sections of the island last October.

“It will have a domino effect. It will affect everybody,” Small said.

“Back-to-school a week after next. Then they give people 30 days. What can we do in 30 days?” she asked.

Meanwhile, some fishermen who operate on the beach are now left wondering if after the shop operators are removed, the NRCA will turn its attention to them. But one fisher was unconcerned, saying fisherfolk were authorised to use the beach.

“Even if them have it in mind [to remove fishers], them nuh say nothing about that. And if they don’t say nothing about that, I will not assume because here was given to fishermen. It wasn’t given to no restaurant, no bar, nor no craft shop,” he insisted.

He was quick to add: “Don’t get me wrong, I am not against them, I’m just saying they did not give fishermen any eviction notice.”

World.title: Police defend Standpipe curfew as residents mourn cost
World.content:
Police on patrol in the Standpipe area on Wednesday.Photos: Karl Mclarty

HEAD of the St Andrew Central Police Division Superintendent Mark Harris is defending the imposition of curfew protocols in the eastern St Andrew community of Standpipe despite claims from residents that it is affecting their lives and livelihood.

The protocol has been in place since late last month following the killing of the still-unidentified owner of a restaurant in the community who went by the alias Whappa.

That was the second fatal incident in the Standpipe area in 72 hours, after 24-year-old Imani Richards was stabbed by an ex-girlfriend.

The police theorised that both incidents were related and immediately imposed a curfew in an attempt to prevent reprisals.

“Standpipe was under curfew on three separate occasions, each occasion the period lasted 48 hours and was approved by the Minister of National Security [Dr Horace Chang],” Harris told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

According to Harris, all the recent restrictions have been approved and the police are well within their rights to implement them.

“Curfew is imposed based on intelligence due to an increase in crimes, especially murders.

“The area is not under constant curfew but it can be applied for at any time and implemented if approved, so the residents will be inconvenienced at times when a curfew is imposed.

“All residents are safer when a curfew is imposed in any community. The police and the community need to work together in partnership to prevent crimes and ultimately save lives,” added Harris.

He told the Observer that while he understands the complaints of the residents he is urging them to cooperate with the police.

But the residents say they are struggling to adjust to this new normal which sees a ban on social events and the early closure of businesses in the usually vibrant community.

“Things have slowed down since they killed the guy down there named Whoppa. Because of the curfew people hardly come out again. Usually in the afternoon time is when I get most of my sales but everybody is afraid to come by this side now,” one shopkeeper told the Observer.

According to the shopkeeper, the police are in the community daily dispersing large gatherings and telling small shop owners to close their establishments.

One resident expressed concern that there was no notice of a curfew and the enforced early closure of businesses.

“Usually when we get a curfew they send some sort of announcement, but we didn’t get anything. All I know is, when six o’clock comes in the evenings they usually come and tell us to lock up or else we get charged,” claimed the resident.

He was supported by a neighbour who said she is not certain what the exact protocols are.

According to that resident, the “lock-off time” imposed by the police varies from 6:00 pm to 9:00 pm but others claim that the 6:00 pm shutdown time has been maintained by the cops.

The residents are also uncertain as to how long this will continue, with one woman telling the Observer that there is still doubt as to whether or not the curfew protocol should still even be in place.

“I don’t know when the curfew will be lifted, I don’t know, because you hear people say it was lifted and when you see police they say it is not, and then you have some other police who say it is lifted,” said the woman who asked not to be named.

Standpipe has seen the occasional outbreak of violence over the years, with much of that linked to gangsters who operated in the area and neighbouring communities.

But in recent years the killings have declined sharply, with domestic disputes believed to be behind most of the recent incidents.

World.title: Fuelling dreams
World.content:
Manager of human resource development and administration at Petrojam Colin Barnett looks on as the 2026 top PEP perfomer at St Andrew Primary School Neymar Pryce is greeted by guest speaker at the Petrojam awards ceremony Joan Davis-Williams, while other top performers (from third left) Kenzo Riley, Denesha Watson and Joe-Lee Gordon share in the moment.Naphtali Junior

THE parents of four students were on Thursday beaming with pride after their children were awarded full-ride scholarships by Petrojam for copping the top girl and top boy spots at St Andrew Primary School and Greenwich All-Age School in the 2026 Primary Exit Profile (PEP) exam.

Welcoming the scholarship valued at $60,00 per year for five years, Janelle East, mother of Neymar Price — who was named the top boy at St Andrew Primary — told the Jamaica Observer that her son’s acceptance to Excelsior High School and his selection for the award was not surprising.

“I am very, happy; words can’t even express how I feel, knowing where he’s coming from. I knew from the beginning that he had it in him. From basic school coming up, he was always the one topping the class. From class one to class three, he has always been the top boy, and then he went to St Andrew Primary School and he carried on that from grade one to grade six. I couldn’t expect anything less,” said East following the awards ceremony held at the Petroleum Corporation of Jamaica (PCJ) auditorium in New Kingston.

“I appreciate what Petrojam has been doing and what they will continue to do. This scholarship, will help my son in such a good way,” an emotional East added, citing financial burdens that often times worsens with her being Neymar’s sole provider.

These sentiments were shared by Gregory Gordon, father of the top girl at St Andrew Primary Joe-Lee Gordon.

He told the Observer that when he received news about his daughter’s performance in PEP he could not contain his emotions.

“I was at work when her teacher called me and told me she passed for Excelsior High. I was so happy that I had to stop working. Words can’t express how I feel. And she being the top girl, the highest achiever at her school in PEP,” said a beaming Gordon.

“I think it’s something good that Petrojam is doing, it is a good initiative. I just want to say give thanks to them and what they have been doing over the years,” added Gordon.

For Tashauna Swaby, mother of Denesha Watson who was named the top girl at Greenwich All-Age, her daughter’s success was grounded in sacrifice.

“I feel so proud to know a single mother like me that tries so hard in the streets, just to let her go to school and put food on her table. Thanks to Petrojam if it wasn’t for them, I don’t know how I would manage,” said Swaby, who smiled as she pointed out that her daughter has been placed at the highly regarded Merl Grove High School.

“The day that I heard that she passed for the school, I was so shocked, because she didn’t tell me it was Merl Grove, she told me it was STATHS, (St Andrew Technical High School) and I said, ‘Okay, no problem, I’m proud just the same’. And she said, ‘No, Mommy, it’s Merl Grove”. I was so happy,” said Swaby.

In the meantime, Shari-Gay Cowan, mother of the top boy at Greenwich All-Age Kenzo Riley, told the Observer that preparations leading up to the exams were challenging.

“It was very hard with him because he’s a child when I tell him about books, he wants to sleep, but when the time comes and he has to study he goes to study. I have to call him every minute, ‘Kenz, come and take up a book, Kenz, come do this, Kenz, come do that. Kenz, remember it’s PEP time, you need to focus now’, and so on. So, it was really a rough journey with him, but I’m glad when I heard that he’s a top boy for the school,” said Cowan as she shared that her son’s father is deceased.

“I just want to thank Petrojam for this programme that is going on. I’m a single mother, so it’s just me and him alone on the road. So, it means a lot to me. A lot of burden has been lifted off my shoulder with him, so I’m grateful for it, especially when you speak about the homework programme, because for me, it is very hard with him to say do your homework and so on, because sometimes I got frustrated, and so I’m here about the homework programme,” added Cowan.

Since 2006 the the State-owned oil refinery’s annual scholarship programme has been the cornerstone of its corporate social responsibility mandate which recognises education as key to its community development focus. Initially the programme, which was restricted to Greenwich All-Age, which is in the vicinity of the refinery. It was expanded to St Andrew Primary in 2014.

In his address to the awards ceremony, manager of human resource development and administration at Petrojam Colin Barnett underscored that the initiative extends beyond an award.

“So one of the most important things to understand from this is, [is that] this is not a one-off situation where we sit here, we celebrate, and then next year we come back. This is a programme. It goes through the entire year. And what we’re talking about is support to the students, not just those who are being awarded today, but remember, we have 10 students from each school right now at the secondary level, going through from grade seven onwards.

“And during the year, we would have a homework centre that we provide transportation to. We have a tutor and beyond that we have a mentorship programme that exists for the students,” Barnett explained.

World.title: Sean Paul, King Jammy première vid for Stand On Business
World.content:
Sean Paul(Photo: Fernando Hevia)

Dancehall superstar Sean Paul and legendary producer Lloyd “King Jammy” James continue the momentum behind Stand On Business with the release of the single’s official music video on August 21.

Released on August 7 and distributed by VP Records, Stand On Business is produced by King Jammy and brings Sean Paul’s unmistakable delivery to the legendary Sleng Teng rhythm, one of the most influential in reggae and dancehall history.

The official video now gives the collaboration a visual treatment, connecting an important piece of dancehall’s history with one of the genre’s most globally recognised artistes.

The Sleng Teng rhythm helped usher in the digital dancehall era after its emergence in 1985. Dancehall artistes had rushed to record on the up-tempo beat, notably Tenor Saw (Pumpkin Belly), Johnny Osbourne (Buddy Bye), John Wayne (What The Police Can Do), and Anthony Red Rose (Under Mi Fat Thing).

Since then, countless artistes and producers have reimagined the rhythm, extending its influence across generations.

For King Jammy, hearing Sean Paul bring his own approach to the rhythm represents another chapter in Sleng Teng’s enduring legacy.

“Sean Paul did exactly what I hoped he would do. He came to the Sleng Teng with his own style, his own energy, and his own history. This rhythm started a revolution in 1985, and now hearing Sean Paul riding it in 2026, and seeing the reaction from people all over the world, shows me that real music never gets old. Sleng Teng was built to last, and Sean Paul just gave it another life,” said King Jammy.

The collaboration also reinforces the lasting connection between dancehall’s foundation and its continued global evolution. King Jammy’s contribution to the development of digital dancehall remains embedded in the genre, while Sean Paul has spent more than two decades carrying Jamaican music to audiences around the world.

World.title: Youngsters code, build, and dream at 10th SVF Robotics Camp
World.content:
Embodying the ‘Build the Future’ theme, young innovators at the SVF Junior Creators Robotics Camp focus intently as they test their newly acquired coding and robotics skills at Caymanas Park.

EIGHTY young innovators from Portmore communities spent five days building, coding and imagining the future at the 2026 Supreme Ventures Foundation’s (SVF) annual Junior Creators Robotics Camp, held August 10-14 under the theme ‘Build the Future’.

Hosted on the grounds of Caymanas Park, the camp welcomed students from Waterford Primary School, Gregory Park Primary School, and Bridgeport Primary School, alongside children of Supreme Ventures staff.

The programme placed children aged nine to 12 at the centre of a high-energy science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) experience designed to build the skills, confidence and creative thinking that can support their educational journeys and future careers.

Facilitated by Marvin Hall, of Halls of Learning, the camp challenged participants to think through five practical, team-based activities. Students rotated through a new challenge each day, gaining hands-on exposure to artificial intelligence, robotics, coding and wearable technology.

By the end of the five-day programme, students had gained practical experience in training an artificial intelligence model to recognise patterns and make predictions; designing and coding playable games using a free app developed at MIT; building and programming robotic solutions to real-world problems; pitching their ideas as young innovators; creating sensor-based contraptions that responded to their surroundings; and programming wearable technologies, including step counters and movement-responsive light-up badges.

Heather Goldson, executive director of the Supreme Ventures Foundation, said she was pleased with the camp’s continued growth and impact.

“Every year, this camp reminds us why the foundation does this work,” Goldson said.

“When we first conceptualised this camp in 2016, our vision was simple but powerful: to expose young Jamaicans to the exciting world of STEM in a creative environment that encourages imagination, innovation and collaboration.

“Since then, we have proudly provided hundreds of children across Jamaica with opportunities to explore robotics, coding, LEGO engineering and other areas of STEM,” added Goldson.

Commenting on this year’s campers, Goldson expressed satisfaction with their development over the course of the week.

“It is a pleasure to see the growth in these children over just five days, and to know that some of them will carry these experiences forward into real careers is exactly the kind of impact we set out to create,” she said.

Hall echoed this sentiment, noting that the camp’s true impact is best measured by the students whose interest in STEM blossoms beyond the week-long programme.

He pointed to two former campers who have since returned to the programme as facilitators.

“What the camp has shown me is that if you do something in a child’s life, it can change their trajectory,” Hall said.

“It does not mean that they will learn everything they need to know, but they gain the inspiration to see a positive outcome in their lives and a broader horizon than they may have seen otherwise. For them to continue to develop and then return to give back shows the full-circle impact of the programme itself.” Added Hall.

Beyond the core robotics curriculum, campers also benefited from a financial literacy session with Carlton Stewart, host of

Let’s Talk Money, Kids! on

CVM TV, and a youth-development session with RISE Life Management Services focused on underage gambling prevention.

Caymanas Park proved to be a fitting and multi-purpose venue for this year’s camp. In addition to hosting the week’s STEM sessions, the property gave students an opportunity to learn about horses through a guided tour of the park and stables.

The camp culminated in an awards ceremony recognising outstanding participants. The top four achievers each received educational grants valued at $50,000 to support their continued learning and development.

Now in its tenth year, the Junior Creators Robotics Camp has become a defining part of the Supreme Ventures Foundation’s youth-development legacy.

Its 2026 staging also formed part of Supreme Ventures’ 25th anniversary celebrations, reinforcing the group’s long-standing investment in Jamaica’s young people and their potential to shape the country’s future.

World.title: SUPPORT THE YOUTH!
World.content:
MALABVER... maybe it is that you have to raid Ministry of Sports to get funds to invest in the infrastructure in many of our schools (Photo: Observer file)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Immediate past president of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA) Mark Malabver is calling on the Ministry of Education to place greater emphasis on developing sporting infrastructure in schools, arguing that Jamaica’s success on the international sporting stage must be matched by investment at the grass-roots level.

Malabver made the call on Wednesday during the final day of the JTA’s 62nd Annual General Conference at Ocean Coral Spring hotel in Trelawny, where he questioned whether the country was doing enough to provide schools with the facilities needed to identify and nurture sporting talent.

He noted that while considerable attention was being placed on the development of infrastructure for science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM) and science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM), sports should also form an important part of the development agenda.

“Minister, I see the STEM, I see the STEAM, where is the sports in all of this?” Malabver asked.

He said Jamaica had demonstrated repeatedly what could be achieved through sports, particularly in track and field, but argued that the country had not capitalised sufficiently on that success by building the infrastructure needed to develop young athletes.

Malabver suggested that funding could be redirected or shared across ministries to address deficiencies in sporting facilities at schools.

“Maybe it is that you have to raid Ministry of Sports to get funds to invest in the infrastructure in many of our schools,” he said, pointing to the need for facilities such as tracks at schools that currently lack them.

He highlighted the example of young sprint sensation Shanoya Douglas, who rose to prominence while attending Muschett Comprehensive High School in Trelawny before moving to Holland High for sixth form.

Malabver said Douglas’ success underscored the importance of ensuring that schools have adequate facilities to support talented youngsters, particularly those emerging from communities where sporting infrastructure is limited.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon, who was responding to questions from the floor, said the Government was already exploring ways to increase support for school sports through existing funding sources.

She said her ministry was in dialogue with the Sports Development Foundation (SDF), which has a mandate to support the development of sports, on how more of its resources could be directed towards schools.

“In terms of sports, one of the things I do is also look where other money is. If I don’t have it in education, it may be somewhere else,” Morris Dixon said.

She explained that discussions with the SDF were focused particularly on providing assistance to emerging schools and broadening support beyond track and field.

Morris Dixon noted that schools were increasingly participating in disciplines such as volleyball, hockey, lacrosse and netball, and said the Government wanted to encourage wider sporting development.

“We’re already in dialogue with SDF on that, so the sports side is absolutely important,” she said.

The JTA conference was held under the theme “Reformation Now: Rebuilding a Resilient Education System Buoyed by Eternal Father and Unrelenting Unionism.”

World.title: France to ramp up Ukraine support, says Macron
World.content:
President Emmanuel Macron is seen on the steps of the Elysee Palace in Paris on July 22, 2026. | Henrique Campos/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

BRUSSELS — French President Emmanuel Macron said on Saturday that Paris will strengthen its support for Ukraine after Russia’s deadly attacks on a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih on Friday.

Macron wrote on X that he called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday following the strikes, which killed 16 and left 130 injured. “I informed President Zelensky that we are stepping up our support with the delivery of interceptors and are continuing our cooperation,” he said.

Confirming the phone call during which the pair discussed “first and foremost, the need for air defense,” Zelenskyy also shared on social media that the two leaders had “agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles.”

World.title: Former EU Commissioner Siim Kallas dies at 77
World.content:
An economist by training, Kallas started his career as president of the Bank of Estonia in 1991, where he was one of the principal architects of the country’s monetary reform. In 1994, he founded the liberal-democratic Reform Party and was elected to the Estonian parliament the following year, when he became foreign affairs minister.

Kallas was also an important figure in the Baltic country’s European trajectory: After his appointment as foreign minister, he oversaw Estonia’s bid to join the EU. He was prime minister in 2002, when the country concluded negotiations to become a member and was invited to join NATO.



“I think of courage required to rebuild a state and introduce its own currency in the early 1990s, as well as the quiet conviction he brought with him to Brussels,” wrote European Parliament Roberta Metsola on social media in response to the news. “Estonia and Europe are better because of his life’s work.”



“Through his public career, [Kallas] helped shape Estonia’s EU path and key European policies,” stated the Commission.

His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was Estonia’s youngest-ever serving prime minister, holding office from 2021 to 2024. She is now the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s second term.

This story has been updated.

World.title: ‘Shameful’: Israel faces international backlash after closing probe into Gaza aid strike
World.content:
Warsaw escalated the diplomatic pressure Thursday night by summoning Israel’s ambassador. Polish aid worker Damian Soból was among the seven people killed in the strike.

Poland’s foreign ministry said in a post on X that it “does not accept the perpetrators’ evasion of legal and moral responsibility” and stressed that prosecutors in Przemyśl are still looking into the matter. Warsaw also demanded Israel provide “all necessary clarifications and materials” requested by Polish investigators.

Israeli drones struck the World Central Kitchen convoy as it delivered food to civilians in Gaza, killing three Britons, an Australian, Soból, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen and a Palestinian on April 1, 2024. The Israel Defense Forces described the attack at the time as a serious mistake and failure and pledged a thorough probe.

Closing the case this week, the IDF said it determined “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident.”

“Partnership requires mutual respect,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote on X Thursday evening, warning that the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and lack of accountability for the IDF’s “excessive use of force” were undermining public support “even in pro-Israel nations.”

World.title: France tackles dodgy condom problem
World.content:
A customer looks at condoms in the biggest French pharmacy in Paris. | Martin Bureau/AFP via Getty Images

Some recalled products carried “risk of bursting” and “the presence of perforations,” according to French authorities.

French health authorities warned Friday that more than 40,000 noncompliant condoms have been sold online in recent months, urging anyone who used affected products to get tested for sexually transmitted infections.

The products were “likely to pose serious risks to the health and safety of users,” including unwanted pregnancies and STIs, France’s consumer-fraud watchdog, the DGCCRF, and its general directorate for health, or DGS, warned Friday. Platforms selling the items were told to “immediately remove the ads,” with 36 listings taken down. Several sites have since promised to review their screening process.

According to the statement, investigators uncovered around 30 condom lines that lacked the EU’s required CE safety marking and third-party conformity checks. Most were sold by Asian vendors through major online marketplaces.

World.title: Poll: The older and richer you are, the more you like AI
World.content:
Compare the young adults to the 35 to 44-year olds, who use the tech as heavily as their younger counterparts, and a divergence is clear: only 19 percent of 18-24s think AI will improve both their own opportunities and society, whereas 28 percent of the older group does. The AI tools available are the same, but the older group already have career experience and expertise.

Among those who describe themselves as already very financially comfortable across all age ranges, 43 percent expect AI to improve their own circumstances further and also improve society. Of the poorest category, those who cannot afford essentials, only 18 percent share this view and 51 percent expect AI to harm both them and society.

The results do not prove that financial insecurity causes pessimism, note the study authors, but highlight that as young adults are entering the jobs market without the financial and professional security of older groups, their concerns around AI sit on top of their existing uncertainties.

This trend tracks into the future with similar results on questions around how AI affects people’s personal economic optimism.

World.title: Germany plans a €12B missile program to deter Putin
World.content:
They say the goal is to allow German forces to strike “far into the rear area of an adversary” and maintain the ability to respond with conventional weapons “below the nuclear threshold.”

The plan has four parts, with the first weapons due as early as next year and the most advanced systems built jointly with the U.K. and planned for the middle of the next decade.

Internal ministry talking points say “almost €12 billion” in budget funds are expected to be needed for the buildup.

The money has not yet been approved. Another ministry document says the costs have been estimated and submitted as part of the government’s budget planning process.

Germany’s defense ministry declined to comment on the figure or individual programs.

“The measures you refer to are generally subject to the approval of the German Bundestag,” a ministry spokesperson told POLITICO. The ministry can only comment after parliament considers them, the spokesperson added.

World.title: A German conservative mayor backed the AfD. Now Merz is on the spot.
World.content:
The letter prompted swift criticism from within his own party: “I don’t like it. I can say that very clearly,” Saxony-Anhalt CDU Premier Sven Schulze told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook Podcast on Thursday. “I think his approach is wrong. Definitely,” adding that he did not share Prange’s views “in any way.”

As for whether the mayor will remain a Christian Democrat, Schulze was in no rush to make a call: “We’ll deal with the issue after the election,” he said. “Right now, it’s campaign time.”

In an interview published earlier on Wednesday, Schulze had dismissed speculation about possible defections after the election: “No, someone switching from the CDU to the AfD will not happen,” he said. And while Prange hasn’t formally changed political allegiance, he said he wants Chancellor Friedrich Merz “removed” as CDU leader and accused him of running a party that is “giving up the conservative core of the Union.”

The episode hits the CDU at a perilous moment, as Merz struggles to maintain the country’s “firewall” against cooperation with the far right while support for the AfD surges across eastern Germany.

The AfD is polling between 41 and 43 percent in Saxony-Anhalt — almost twice the CDU’s 22 to 24 percent — putting the far right within striking distance of governing alone. Merz continues to rule out cooperation with the AfD, but September’s elections will put that under sustained pressure: Saxony-Anhalt votes on Sept. 6, followed by Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sept. 20.

World.title: Another eclipse over Spain on 28 August: where and how to see the Moon almost completely covered
World.content:
Just 16 days after the historic total solar eclipse of 12 August, the first visible from the Iberian Peninsula in more than a century, Spain will once again be looking to the skies to witness another major astronomical event.

 

On 28 August there will be a partial lunar eclipse with a magnitude of 0.93, which will be visible across the country. Unlike the solar eclipse, there will be no need for special glasses or any other form of protection to enjoy this event. The National Geographic Institute (IGN) says it can be observed with the naked eye without any risk and that no special instruments will be required.

The eclipse will be particularly deep. According to the IGN, it will reach a magnitude of 0.93, which means that at its peak the Earth’s darkest shadow, known as the umbra, will cover roughly 93% of the Moon’s diameter. This figure should not be confused with the percentage of the Moon’s surface that will be darkened.

Image of the lunar eclipse. IGN

A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon and our satellite passes through the shadow cast by the planet. When only part of the Moon enters the Earth’s umbra, as will happen on 28 August, the eclipse is classified as partial.

Where will the eclipse be seen best?

The event will be visible in some of its phases from Europe, Africa, the Americas and western Asia, according to IGN data. In Spain, the partial phase will be visible from the whole country before moonset, although there will be significant differences depending on where it is observed from.

In the centre and east of the peninsula, the Balearic Islands and Melilla, the Moon will set before the partial phase ends. In the rest of the peninsula, the Canary Islands and Ceuta, moonset will occur after this phase has finished.

Where the partial eclipse will be visible. IGN

This makes it particularly important to look for a place with good visibility towards the horizon where the Moon will set, as well as favourable weather conditions.
