Born in Beijing's mountainous Yanqing district, Li has spent much of her life moving — first from the north to the south of China, then Britain and finally New York. Every move brought another chance to start again.

"I've spent my whole life becoming an outsider," she says. "But every time I moved, I wasn't running away. I was searching for a freer life."

As she becomes more comfortable in American society, Li hopes to perform in English one day. But for now, Chinese remains the language through which she tells her stories.

Maizi Li

The former feminist activist now lives in Brooklyn, where she works with low-income Chinese migrant families, supporting children with autism, while also running what she describes as America's first independent Asian LGBTQ choir.

Long before Li performed stand-up in the US, she was already one of the most recognisable faces of China's young feminist movement. She helped pioneer a new generation of street activism that used performance, humour and spectacle to challenge gender inequality.

Wearing a blood-splattered wedding dress, Li joined the now-famous "Bloody Brides" campaign to protest domestic violence. She also helped organise the "Occupy Men's Toilets" movement in the southern city of Guangzhou, where women symbolically took over men's public toilets to highlight the chronic shortage of facilities for women. Following one of her advocacy campaigns, the Guangzhou municipal government increased the number of public toilets for women.

In March 2015, Li was detained for 37 days along with four other activists — known internationally as the "Feminist Five" — for planning to distribute anti-sexual harassment stickers on public transport ahead of International Women's Day. Their detention triggered an international campaign demanding their release including from then-US presidential candidate Hillary Clinton.

Unlike Alex Shi, who stumbled into comedy through Beijing's English-language open mics, Li first stepped onto a comedy stage using Chinese language after leaving China for New York with her partner three years ago.

Her first performance — at Women's Initiative, a platform that showcases women's stories and hosts annual Pride Month events — was deeply personal.

Rather than inventing fictional characters or telling observational jokes, Li drew directly from her life — her journey as a feminist activist, her same-sex marriage, and the experience of police disrupting her wedding celebration in China.

"The personal is political," she told me. "I've always tried to live by that."

For her second performance, Li chose a very different subject and continued to perform in Chinese to New York's large Chinese-speaking community. Instead of activism, she spoke about her grandmother.

Li's grandmother belonged to a generation of women whose lives were often overlooked. Yet Li credits her grandmother's quiet love with shaping the person she has become.

The audience cried.

Unlike the sharp, self-deprecating humour that filled Beijing's comedy clubs, Li's performance felt closer to a personal confession. Laughter came, but so did tears.

"It was the first time I'd publicly talked about my grandmother," Li says. "To realise that people connected with that story was incredibly moving."

Like Wong and Shi, Li believes that, in today's China, stand-up has become one of the cultural spaces where discussions about women's lives have flourished.

"Women's rights advocacy has become increasingly visible because it doesn't directly challenge political power or government policy," she says. "Female stand-up empowers women. Stand-up encourages women to step onto the stage."

Mixed messages

For decades, Chinese women have grown up with Mao Zedong's famous slogan that "women hold up half the sky". During the Mao era, women were encouraged to enter the workforce and participate in building the new socialist China. It represented an enormous shift from the traditional idea that women's primary place was inside the home.

The legacy of that change is still visible in everyday Chinese life. Most Chinese women, for example, keep their own surnames after marriage rather than adopting their husband's name. Some families even choose to give a child the mother's surname.

A consequence of China's Family (one-child) policy, for which I am personally grateful, is that as an only daughter my family's limited resources went into my education and eventually helped support master's degree. My father once told me that if I'd had a brother, I might have had to leave school early and work to help pay for his university education.

But government policy could not erase generations of son preference or traditional expectations about women's roles.

This is the contradiction facing many modern Chinese women. Society encourages them to become educated, financially independent and professionally successful. Yet older expectations can still demand that they marry at the "right" age, have children, care for their own parents and take responsibility for their husband's family.

Women face intense scrutiny over age and appearance and a woman who is highly successful or outspoken can still be described as "too strong".

The gap between the rhetoric of equality and political power is also striking: very few women make it into the senior ranks of Chinese politics.

Within these contradictions, female stand-up has found so much material.

Dating, marriage, divorce, children, beauty standards, mothers-in-law and disappointing boyfriends become punchlines because they are also familiar pressures in women's everyday lives. Female comedians can take expectations that have traditionally been directed at women and turn the gaze around.

That helps explain why one of Yang Li's most famous jokes — asking how men could be "so average, yet so confident" — struck such a nerve.

The rise of 'pǔxìn nán'

Before the American-style stand-up comedy arrived in China, audiences were already familiar with xiangsheng, or crosstalk, a traditional comic performance dating back to the Qing dynasty in the mid-19th century.

Typically performed by two comedians who exchange rapid-fire dialogue, wordplay, and satire, xiangsheng has long been one of China's best-known performing arts. And for most of its history, the stage was overwhelmingly dominated by men.

But in a reversal of long-standing stereotypes, the new generation of female comedians in China are turning the spotlight back on men.

Yang Li ( )

Yang Li became one of China's most recognisable comedians after joking that some men could "look so average, but can be so confident"—a line that quickly gave rise to the now-famous phrase, 普信男, pǔxìn nán.

It was more than a joke. Reminiscent of Sarah Hagi's English language gag: "God give me the confidence of a mediocre white dude" — Yang's line flipped a familiar script.

Yang turned scrutiny of women's appearance, age, career choices and marital status back on men, poking fun not at their looks alone, but at what many women saw as unquestioned confidence and entitlement.

The related Weibo social media hashtag attracted more than 210 million views and 84,000 discussions. Yang herself amassed more than 2 million followers on the platform.

Alex Shi believes comedy has become another way women are reshaping public conversations, alongside women rejecting the male gaze in cinema, challenging misogynistic double standards in news coverage and campaigning to break menstrual taboos, Growing visibility of women in comedy reflects broader social change and a much broader cultural shift, she believes.

Maizi Li agrees: "When women take the stage," she says, "they take ownership of the microphone."

Jiaoyang Summers ( )

Comedy star Jiaoying Summers, who moved to the US at 18, performs primarily in English and is the first Chinese comedian to headline New York's Apollo Theater, says stand-up has given Chinese women more opportunities for their voices to be heard.

"I think women's points of view have historically been overlooked, dismissed, or even ridiculed in many parts of society," Summers told me. "Audiences are realising that the female perspective isn't a niche perspective, it's half the world."

The cost of being funny

The growing visibility of China's female comedians has also brought growing scrutiny. For some, the consequences have come from authorities.

In 2022, comedian Dawn Wong said police took her away after a satirical performance about COVID-19 lockdowns attracted official attention. She later returned to the stage, but the incident served as a reminder that, in China, comedy can carry political consequences.

For others, the backlash has come from audiences.

Yang Li's popularity also came at a price. Despite becoming one of China's best-known stand-up comics, she faced fierce criticism from some male internet users who accused her of promoting sexism and "man-hating". In 2021, JD.com dropped her from an advertising campaign following an online backlash, illustrating the commercial risks that can accompany gender-related comedy in China.

Yang has consistently refused to apologise for her comedy, arguing many critics had only seen short clips of her routines rather than the full performances. She also rejects the label of feminist icon.

"I hope people won't make me an opinion leader or a pioneer for women," she told Chinese media. "I'm just an ordinary stand-up comedian writing jokes. I don't have a theory, nor can I carry such a big label."

That caution was something I encountered repeatedly while reporting this story.

Several female comedians declined interview requests. One industry insider suggested that speaking to Western media carried greater perceived risks because, unlike Chinese media, there is no domestic editorial review — what Western-style journalism might label "censorship" — before publication.

Ironically, the experience echoed the contradiction at the heart of this story. On stage, women joke about dating, marriage, family expectations and gender roles. Off stage, some become reluctant to discuss those same subjects in an interview.

Jiaoying Summers said that earlier in her career she worried about adjusting her material for different audiences, particularly when performing in more conservative parts of the United States. Eventually, she stopped trying to please everyone.

Today, Summers says, whether performing for Chinese, American or even Australian audiences (she will perform in Sydney in October), she concentrates on her own life.

"I talk about family, marriage, gender, culture, motherhood, all the things that affect me personally. I realised that I'm not onstage to make friends," she says. "My job is to be funny. People can love me or hate me, as long as I make them laugh, I've done my job."

Shi puts it even more simply: "Young Chinese women have things to say. And the funny ones make them into jokes."

Credits

Words: Cecily Huang

Illustrations: Kylie Silvester

Editing: Catherine Taylor

World.title: Missed out on a pay rise? Here’s how to guarantee one next year
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingPay Opinion Missed out on a pay rise? Here’s how to guarantee one next year Victoria Devine Money columnist August 23, 2026 — 5:01am

August 23, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every time a new financial year rolls around, most of us are hoping for a pay rise. Whether we’ve worked especially hard and are hoping to have those efforts recognised, want our loyalty to our company rewarded, or simply need more money to keep up with the cost of living, there are many valid reasons to be hoping for a salary bump come July. Though many people think that pay rises are only accessible via a promotion or through taking on extra responsibilities, that’s certainly not true of all industries. Often, pay rises are offered for doing the job you have exceptionally well, going beyond the remit of the position or when the company has had a successful year. It’s a huge mistake to think that pay rises happen on that one day you have a conversation with your manager. Dionne Gain But just as Rome wasn’t built in a day, pay rises aren’t awarded on a whim. So if you were among those lucky enough to score a pay rise recently, congratulations. If you weren’t, I’m genuinely very sorry. Getting turned down for a raise can really knock the wind out of your sails and sour how you feel about your job and your workplace. But with that disappointment comes three primary options: you can stay in the same job but change your behaviour, you can look for another job, or you can start laying the groundwork for next year’s promotion now.



For fairly self-explanatory reasons, I don’t recommend the first option. Over the years, I’ve seen many people respond to pay rise rejection by emotionally checking out and doing only the bare minimum as a form of protest. The logic is that if the company hasn’t financially rewarded your hard work and efforts, why should you go above and beyond for them? While feeling this way is entirely understandable, and I’m in no way recommending working well above your pay grade for free, I’ve never seen this stance have the long-term desired effect, mostly because it’s viewed by management as you having a tantrum. When you go to your boss with another offer, you have to be prepared that they may let you go. Holding this position also means you’re likely bringing a negative attitude into the office and increasing the workloads of your colleagues, and those things will be noticed by your bosses. It also doesn’t put you in a good position to get a raise next year, or be considered for promotions into the future. The second option, as I mentioned, is to look for a new job and secure a higher salary by moving to a new company. The main pro to this option is, of course, more money.



But another perk is that you can potentially use the offer as leverage with your current employer. If they value the work that you do and recognise your talent, another offer lets them know that they can’t be complacent. However, there are two things to consider with this approach. The first is that your current employer may want to keep you, but can’t match the offer you’ve received. So before you go to them, it’s worth having a list of non-financial benefits you’d be open to. For example, let’s say your new job offer is for $20,000 more, but your current employer can only offer you $10,000. Are there non-cash options you’d consider to make up a package, like working from home an extra day, undertaking training? Having some ideas of what this kind of package could include before you go into negotiations will help your employer see that you’re serious about staying at the company, and allows them to try and find a solution. The second thing to consider is that when you go to your boss with another offer, you have to be prepared that they may let you go. So if you are planning to use another job offer as leverage, know that they could call your bluff, so you should be fully willing to go through with leaving when you approach them.



Then we get to the third option, which is laying the groundwork now for pay rises that will be issued next year. Across most companies, HR will go to bosses each year with a designated amount that can be used for discretionary pay rises. Editor's pick Opinion

Elon Musk Why the richest man on Earth wants you to think money won’t matter Victoria Devine Money columnist Let’s say there’s a pool of $50,000 and 20 employees in the company. It’s extremely rare for a company to evenly spread that budget out and see everybody get a $2500 bump in their pay. Instead, a good boss will have spent months keeping an eye on who is performing well, and will divvy that amount out to five or 10 people when the time comes. And it’s this reason that it’s such a huge mistake to think that pay rises happen on that one day you have a conversation with your manager. Because in fact, those decisions are being made months ahead of time, and that conversation is merely the formality.



Now, let’s say you didn’t get approved for a pay rise this financial year. Now that a few weeks have passed since you received that news, it’s time to follow up with your manager, and really drill into how you can improve your chances between now and next July. Start by asking what they would need to see more of from you, and then specific examples of what that would look like in practice. While this conversation might come with some unpleasant feedback, if you can push through that what it will give you is a clear understanding of where the goal posts are and how to reach them – and that is essential. In this conversation, you also shouldn’t be afraid to make it clear that the reason you’re asking is that you are hoping to be eligible for a pay rise next year. Now that you have that list of what you need to be doing, let it be your north star. Check in with it on Monday mornings, and on Friday afternoons take five minutes to make notes from the week of any wins or successes you had. From there, schedule another check in for January and take the highlights from those notes along. At this point, you’re halfway through the financial year, and you can show them how you’re progressing, what you’ve done, and check in on those benchmarks they set. Ask them if they’re happy with your performance and if there’s more you can be doing between then and the time of pay rise decisions being made.



Hopefully, when next July rolls around, you’ll be among those being congratulated. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. World.title: I’m 64 and I just inherited $700,000. What should I do with it?
World.content:
August 23, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I have about $700,000 in cash from a recent inheritance and am unsure what to do with it. I’d like to be able to access some to help my adult children occasionally. I am a 64-year-old single female homeowner (no debt) working full-time, but I plan to reduce my weekly hours within 12 months. I have about $500,000 in super, including $340,000 invested in FY2026 through the three-year bring-forward provisions. I salary-sacrifice now to just under the maximum allowed for concessional contributions. It can be difficult to work out what to do with a large inheritance. Simon Letch Upon turning 65 years old, superannuation becomes completely accessible irrespective of whether you remain working or have retired. Throughout our working lives, the primary drawback of placing money in superannuation is loss of access, so this unlock is quite significant. With $500,000 in superannuation and the current transfer balance cap being $2.1 million, you have plenty of headroom to utilise the superannuation system. The reason the superannuation system stands out here is that while you are still accumulating, tax on earnings is only 15 per cent. And then once you retire and start drawing an income, the tax drops to 0 per cent.



So you have an environment where you can access your money whenever you like, and it receives extremely favourable tax treatment. It also has the benefit of being highly regulated, providing you with confidence. This investment could be left alone, hopefully for a few decades, and be available for any care needs that you may face later in life. Contribution caps are your problem, though. Given your use of the bring-forward provisions last financial year, we will need to wait until July 2028 (’28-29 financial year) before you can again make a lump sum contribution. At present, the maximum under this provision is $390,000, and it is reasonable to assume that will have been indexed up by the time you can next contribute. Let’s assume that come July 1, 2028 you want to be able to put $400,000 into your superannuation as a non-concessional contribution, once again using the bring-forward provisions, and allowing for a bit of indexation between now and then. I would establish an investment portfolio for your $700,000 now, breaking up the proceeds. I would place $400,000 in a balanced or conservative investment option to align with the two- to three-year time frame that we are facing here.



Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert We have $1.6m in an SMSF. Should we keep it, or move it to a standard fund? Noel Whittaker Money columnist If your inclination was towards conservativism, you could even simply place this money in a term deposit. For the remaining $300,000 that you won’t be able to get into superannuation, I would invest in something with a longer time horizon that aligns with your comfort around risk and volatility. Once retired, and with the super contribution made, I would be surprised if this investment in isolation would push you to the point of needing to pay and submit an annual tax return. This investment could be left alone, hopefully for a few decades, and be available for any care needs that you may face later in life. I am 56 and have insurance in my super than has gotten costly. Am I being irresponsible if I cancel it? The starting point with insurance is to consider your debts and dependents. If you have neither, your need for insurance diminishes significantly.



Next, you would consider how you would fare in the event of significant incapacity. If your balance sheet right now is strong, it is quite conceivable that you don’t need insurance for this either. Insurance does get more expensive as we age, and our financial position typically strengthens, so it is appropriate to consider scaling back, if not completely cancelling insurance later in life. World.title: Euthanasia laws are overdue for review. A former minister has ideas why
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Euthanasia laws are overdue for review. A former minister has ideas why Matt Dennien August 23, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When eligible terminally ill Queenslanders gained legal access to drugs to end their own lives at the start of 2023, a timer in the laws began. “As soon as practicable” after three years, the health minister would be required to review the laws’ effectiveness and eligibility criteria. Approaching nine months since that three-year milestone, the Crisafulli LNP government has said little publicly about a review. Former minister Jann Stuckey has an idea why. Former Liberal and LNP member for Currumbin, Jann Stuckey, pictured with then-AFL CEO Andrew Demetriou in 2013 while she was Tourism Minister in the Newman government. Matt Roberts “I don’t believe that the Crisafulli government will want to mention the word ‘voluntary assisted dying’,” she told this masthead by phone on Friday.



“Or anything that will raise any controversy amongst members – and we know that this will … I think they will avoid this release of this report or the review for as long as possible.” Behind-the-scenes, work to launch the review is under way. Loading Health Minister Tim Nicholls, approached by this masthead late last month, however, has declined to detail any of its planned shape. “The Queensland government is on the record that there will be no changes to voluntary assisted dying legislation,” a government spokesperson said in response, reiterating the LNP’s election vow.



“A review will be undertaken in accordance with the Act.” A parliamentary question on notice from independent Noosa MP Sandy Bolton late last year returned similar results. There, Bolton was pointed to an earlier response from Nicholls to a Labor opposition question in which he reiterated the government’s commitment to providing the service. “Queenslanders will be invited to contribute to the review at the appropriate time,” Nicholls said. When that might be remains the question for those wanting expansion – or winding-back. First elected to the Gold Coast seat of Currumbin as a Liberal, Stuckey remaining in parliament – through the party’s formal merge with the more dominate Nationals – until 2020. Bringing forward her retirement before that year’s election, Stuckey spoke out about the “cone-of-silence type of vilification” she felt after voting against party lines to decriminalise abortion in 2018.



She was one of only three LNP opposition figures to use the conscience vote to do so, including now-ministers Steve Minnikin and Tim Nicholls. A long-time advocate of voluntary assisted dying, she was among those involved with lobbying group Dying with Dignity to help push support for the laws brought to parliament in 2021. She was in the public gallery for the conscience vote that year when the laws passed, backed by 10 LNP MPs who broke with their partyroom’s majority opposition to them. In the parliamentary and public debate then, concerns were raised by both major party MPs and faith groups about the state of palliative care and need for church-run sites to allow the practice.



Within the next year came Stuckey’s pancreatic cancer diagnosis. For four years now, across multiple treatments and surgeries, 71-year-old Stuckey has had the “monster” – with a five-year survival rate of 12 per cent – come back four times. While Stuckey herself says she may not wish to use the laws, knowing they are there “is of enormous comfort”. So it is the fear it could be taken away likely “adds to the stress of many cancer patients”. And it is mostly used by people with a cancer diagnosis. The latest annual report of the state Voluntary Assisted Dying Review Board, for financial year 2024-25, put that figure at 76 per cent. In total from when the scheme began on January 1, 2023, to June 30 this year, the board’s data shows 3182 people have died after administering the drugs accessed through the multi-stage process.





Ultimately, after winning power and control of parliament, Crisafulli effectively gagged any debate of abortion laws, which Stuckey described to this masthead as an “astounding” move. No such restriction has been placed on parliamentary debate of voluntary assisted dying laws. Stuckey, who describes herself as Christian but says religion and politics should not cross, said she was concerned the voluntary assisted dying review could present an opportunity for parts of the party who have been blocked from pushing for changes to abortion. “I’ve been in the party room. I was there 16 years, you know, in opposition and as a minister. So I know how it works, and I and I know what the make-up of the parliament is and how they vote. I know, who’s hard-right Christian in the LNP,” she said. “So when they’re saying they’re not going to change it [assisted dying laws], I would just take that broadly as they’re not going to overturn it. But, I mean, they’ve got the numbers to overturn it easily”.



What’s really needed, though, according to Stuckey and other advocates – beyond even the state scheme review – is action from the federal Albanese government. While promising to review “carriage service” laws around suicide which have long been viewed as a barrier to access – particularly in regional areas – Albanese last month rejected a party push for action. David Muir, chair of the Clem Jones Group, said his group’s longstanding advocacy would include a submission to the upcoming review urging the state to use all influence it has to resolve the matter. In response to questions about any advocacy the state may have already taken up in this space since the election, Nicholls also declined to provide a direct answer.



“Any changes to the Commonwealth Criminal Code are a matter for the Commonwealth government,” a spokesperson for the health minister said. World.title: ‘No filter necessary’: Why 80-year-old women are fashion’s new secret weapon
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life ‘No filter necessary’: Why 80-year-old women are fashion’s new secret weapon Emily Cronin August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Charlotte Rampling: actor, forever fashion reference … octogenarian icon? The British actor, who turned 80 earlier this year, shared some of her feelings about reaching the milestone age in an interview with British Vogue. “I think I will be able to actually have a pretty good time [in my 80s]. I feel that I deserve it,” she said, going on to discuss her “loving friendship” with a new man. In the accompanying shoot, Rampling appears in a number of fashion-forward looks. Wearing outfits including a Saint Laurent blouse and biker jacket, Gucci tiger-print shearling coat and Louis Vuitton funnel-neck jumper and trousers, she appears edgy. Self-possessed. Even (dare we say it? Yes, we dare) hot. Eighty looks a little different than it used to. Make that very different. Along with Rampling, other women who’ve entered their 80s in recent years include Helen Mirren, mobbed by fans on her way into Erdem’s show during London Fashion Week earlier this year; Norma Kamali, still turning out bodycon dresses after almost 60 years; and Brenda Blethyn, star of the TV adaptation of A Woman of Substance. Joanna Lumley, who was surrounded by photographers as she took her seat in Burberry’s spring-summer 2026 front row, blew out 80 candles in May. Fashion front and centre: Helen Mirren, Charlotte Rampling, Jane Fonda, Vanessa Redgrave and Joanna Lumley. Launchmetrics Spotlight/Getty Images They join a cohort of 80-something women changing the face of ageing – women like Jane Fonda, 88, Vanessa Redgrave, 89, and Martha Stewart, 85.



Stewart in particular appears to be having an absolute ball. In 2023, aged 81, the domestic goddess and lifestyle mogul became the oldest cover star of Sports Illustrated’s annual swimsuit edition. Since then, she has covered the Olympics, partnered with friend and business partner Snoop Dogg on a gin venture and been the subject of a hit Netflix documentary. She also stars in the latest campaign for (denim brand) Mother in which she smoulders at the camera and purrs, “I love a nice package” and “No filter necessary”. “Martha is the ultimate muse,” says Lela Becker, the brand’s president and co-founder. “She knows what she wants, exudes confidence and isn’t afraid to challenge expectations. We wanted to celebrate that energy by presenting her in an unexpected way.” Martha Stewart, in Sydney this year, is living her best life after 80. Getty It should not be news that advanced age can correlate with advanced style. But ageing is changing. As Charlotte Rampling tells Vogue, “We’re all 10 years younger now.” Meaning that while the ninth decade might once have been a time to retreat to a comfortable armchair with the knitting, now it is a time for women to embrace life’s possibilities and do whatever they want, including declining great-grandchild babysitting opportunities in favour of travel, pursuing new relationships or, in Rampling’s case, starring in a Golden Lion-winning film. It is worth acknowledging that the group referenced here includes women renowned as some of the most stylish in the world for going on half a century. Of course Rampling, Lumley, Mirren et al were going to make ageing seem exciting rather than merely inevitable (if you’re lucky).



“The thing is, these women are so inspirational,” says Rachel Fanconi, a stylist who counts both Mirren and Lumley as longstanding clients. “They are the women who came up in the 1960s – they are the coolest girls.” Fanconi says that when preparing mood boards for photo shoots, the archive imagery she pulls from the ’60s and ’70s often references events or eras when “they were there – they were doing all of that”. She adds, “I think expectations around what women look like in their 80s are constantly evolving. The only surprise is that it seems to catch everybody by surprise. We all carry this idea of what each number looks like in our head from when we are very young. You have just got to let that go.” Taking a wider view, fashion designers seem to be embracing the power of older women on the catwalk and in advertising campaigns. Twiggy is in a Burberry campaign at 76. Gillian Anderson, 58, walked in the Miu Miu show at Paris Fashion Week (designer Miuccia Prada, at 77, remains at the peak of her power and influence). And one of the most talked-about models at Chanel’s recent shows has been 50-year-old Stephanie Cavalli and her beautiful curly grey hair (the destigmatisation of grey hair representing its own anti-ageist shift). It seems ageism may be on the way out – provided you have extraordinary bone structure and a runway-fashion-compliant frame.



By 80, most women will feel they have every clothing item they’ll ever need, and know how they like to dress. The key to facing the ninth decade in style lies not in imitating anyone mentioned above, but in having confidence and an awareness of what works. It is crucial to avoid stagnation, though. Rachel Fanconi’s advice? “Buy something new. Go somewhere great and buy one piece – the bag, the shoe, whatever it is – that goes with your clothes but gives it all an edge and helps you do something new, helps spark everything up a bit.” Surely Charlotte Rampling would approve. World.title: Specsavers told Nicole she needed glasses. Then, she had a car accident
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare Specsavers told Nicole she needed glasses. Then, she had a car accident Rachel Rasker August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three months after visiting Specsavers, wearing the bifocals she felt she was pressured into buying, Nicole Donovan had a car accident. “It could have just been from stress or hurrying,” the NSW mid-north coast resident said, “but I really couldn’t see properly”. When she called the store to ask why she was still having problems despite the new prescription, she was assured that she simply needed to get used to them. Nicole Donovan was frustrated Specsavers did not warn her about her cataracts. Matt Willis / Sitthixay Ditthavong “[The worker] was quite short on the phone with me,” Donovan said, and she wasn’t offered a follow-up appointment. “So I kept on trying, thinking it was me.” When Donovan sought a second opinion at an independent optometry clinic, she was promptly diagnosed with advanced cataracts which required urgent surgery.



She felt she had no choice but to travel five hours to Sydney for an $11,000 procedure: “I was frustrated that [Specsavers] didn’t pick it up, so that I may have been able to go on a public waiting list and get the surgery for free.” Related Article Investigation

Healthcare Revealed: The optometrists punished for putting patients before sales Donovan was one of the more than 70 people who contacted this masthead following its investigation into corporate optometry, which detailed how chains including Specsavers and OPSM pressured optometrists to hit sales targets, potentially jeopardising patient care. Professor Konrad Pesudovs, a leading optometrist researcher and clinician, said cataracts are to optometrists what high blood pressure is to GPs: “You can’t miss a cataract. It’s just so fundamental, it’s right there.” While he said it was possible that there had been a misunderstanding during Donovan’s initial appointment, her care should have been followed up: “What isn’t defensible is not seeing a patient when they’re unhappy, because that’s when you detect the problem.”



This masthead’s investigation found optometrists were routinely pressured to prioritise “convertible” appointments which would result in a glasses sales. Another Specsavers customer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said a manager “snatched the appointment card out of my hand” after he attempted to book a follow-up consultation because the glasses he was prescribed for a sudden vision change did not improve his eyesight: “My guess was that he wasn’t getting a sale, so he didn’t want to deal with me.” The patient instead visited a neighbouring independent optometrist, who escalated his concerns to an ophthalmologist. It was then – two weeks after his initial visit to Specsavers – that he was advised to go immediately to the emergency department, where it was confirmed that his sudden vision loss – diagnosed as hemianopia – was due to a stroke. Dr Tim Fricke, the director of research and education at the Australian College of Optometry, said while mistakes happen, a hemianopia should be picked up in a basic examination, during an initial consultation. He was also concerned by the refusal to book a patient in for a follow-up.



“Practitioners are paid for a health service through Medicare,” he said. “I don’t think it’s particularly [profitable for Specsavers], but there is an obligation to provide a health service.” In a statement, Specsavers said more than 5 million Australians trust the brand with their eye care each year, “a responsibility we take seriously, and in the rare instances where a patient believes their experience was not what it should have been, we have well-established clinical governance and review processes”. “We are proud of the professional standards of our optometrists in detecting and managing eye-threatening conditions,” the statement said. “These governance and review processes are designed to understand what occurred in these rare instances and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.” No longer a local operation A July 2026 report by industry research group IBISWorld highlighted the growing monopolisation of the sector, with Specsavers and EssilorLuxxotica (OPSM’s parent company) expected to account for just over half the industry’s revenue in 2026-27.



Specsavers opened its first Australian retail store in 2008 and now holds more than one-third of the market share, with $1.8 billion in annual revenue. Specsavers Australia represents the second-largest market by revenue for its global parent company, behind only the UK, where the chain originated. The brand’s “competitively priced products and services has forced other optical retailers to match”, the report found, with about 94 per cent of initial eye tests across the industry bulk-billed. The report noted that other outlets – which included a mix of independent optometrists and smaller chains such as Oscar Wylee, George & Matilda, and Bailey Nelson – still hold a 48.7 per cent market share, with $2.51 billion in revenue.



The true cost of bulk billing Across the industry, costs for rent and equipment have skyrocketed while Medicare rebates have remained stagnant. “The squeeze has been on for decades,” Fricke said. “You get less payment per unit of time than you used to, and all your costs [have gone] up. So something has to give at some point.” Optometry Australia chief executive Mark Nevin said the peak body has consistently advocated for higher rebates, which he said were “unsustainably low” and needed to be cross-subsidised by sales of spectacles and contact lenses to remain viable. However, Nevin said financial KPIs that compromise clinical autonomy, including the quality and safety of care, were unacceptable: “We can assure the public that care provided by optometrists is safe and high quality, evidenced by the very low level of complaints to our regulator.”



Nigel Chesterfield-Evans, who has been an optometrist since 1978 and ran five independent practices before converting them to Specsavers franchises, said public expectation around bulk billing had damaged the industry: “People do not appreciate what they don’t pay for.” “I have sat in a consulting room, found a retinal tumour, photographed it, sent it to the GP and then sent it to the ophthalmologist. The fee that I got from Medicare for that was less than the lady at the nail salon,” he said. Shereen Kassir is calling for award recognition for optometrists. Health Services Union Optometrist and Health Services Union (HSU) delegate Shereen Kassir said the government should “step up” to ensure MBS fees matched both current inflation and optometrists’ scope of practice. “It’s not just affecting the optometrists under these really strong KPI pressures, but it’s also impacting the patient care,” she said. “Medicare disincentivises being a clinical-focused eye care provider.”



Related Article Healthcare ‘It’s really debilitating’: The hidden danger in your daily screen time driving a surge in disease A spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said in a statement that optometry services are indexed every year on July 1. The spokesperson said changes to MBS optometry services came into effect in March 2025, including creating two new MBS items for glaucoma patients at high risk, amending low vision assessment items to align with contemporary best practice, and increasing schedule fees for domiciliary visits. Clinicians, not retail staff Last month, the HSU lodged a bid at the Fair Work Commission which called for optometrists to be explicitly covered under the Health Professionals and Support Services Award, to ensure industry recognition and improved pay, breaks and rosters. “We know Specsavers have said: You fall under the retail award, you are not a health professional,” HSU president Kate Marshall said. “Simply knocking that argument out means that we can legitimately have a go at these companies.”



Kassir said the award will allow optometrists to work under an enterprise agreement, and if needed, participate in protected industrial action: “That gives [us] the power back.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: Women have always feared becoming invisible as they age. But with travel, it’s a gift
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Women have always feared becoming invisible as they age. But with travel, it’s a gift Julietta Jameson August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I was little, someone asked me what superpower I’d most like to have. I chose invisibility. To my young mind, it meant freedom. The ability to go anywhere, eat anything and do whatever I wanted without asking permission or worrying what anyone thought. As the youngest of six children in a chaotic household, disappearing into the background felt like a delicious kind of independence. Of course, like many childhood ideas, invisibility became more complicated as I grew older. I learned there are people for whom invisibility isn’t a superpower but a sentence. People pushed to the margins because of their race, disability, sexuality or age. I also absorbed the familiar warning handed to women: enjoy being noticed while it lasts because one day you’ll be invisible, too. Invisibility after a certain age is actually a superpower. Michela Ravasio / Stocksy United When I was travelling through Italy in my 40s, I remember the first time someone addressed me as signora instead of signorina. It was only a word, but it rocked me. I’d crossed a threshold, and I soon began to mourn the woman I’d apparently left behind, especially when menopause began to wreak havoc and my body told me it had crossed its own personal Rubicon. My 50s arrived, and my menopausal symptoms started to subside, but the predicted invisibility didn’t arrive. Men still flirted with me, often at moments I’d have preferred they didn’t. The world hadn’t suddenly stopped looking. But the way I responded to it was changing.



Now that I’m in my 60s, I’m contemplating all this from a different perspective. Is society really rendering older women invisible? Or have I, after years of feeling scrutinised, judged and assessed, stepped into a different relationship with visibility? I suspect the answer is both. I’m starting to believe invisibility after a certain age is actually the superpower I craved as a kid. JULIETTA JAMESON There’s no denying that ageism exists. Women over 50 encounter it in obvious and subtle ways, from job interviews to everyday interactions that leave us feeling overlooked or patronised. But somewhere between the cultural warnings and my own experience, I’m starting to believe invisibility after a certain age is actually the superpower I craved as a kid. As a travel writer, I spend much of my life moving through places where nobody knows me. Every new destination offers a potential reset. I’m not somebody’s daughter, sister, colleague, neighbour or patient. Nobody knows my history. Nobody knows my age, unless I choose to tell them – though as an au naturel girly, experience is proudly writ large on my face, albeit with a dash of mascara and a slick of lippy. Putting aside the so-called telltale signs of ageing, every morning I wake up with complete freedom to decide how visible I want to be. Some days I embrace anonymity. I find a corner table in a cafe, order a coffee, open a book and happily disappear into my own company for an hour or two. There can be an enormous luxury in being left alone. Just ask any mum.



On other days, I decide to be rampantly visible. I’ll chat to the woman beside me on a train – if she seems approachable and up for it. I love to compliment people. If I see a hairstyle I like, or a coat that’s particularly great, I let the wearer know. Honestly, it makes their day and ends up making mine, too. I’ll strike up a conversation with a market vendor – usually by butchering the local language, and everyone usually gets a laugh. I’ll stop to pat every dog that will let me, though this did get me into a bit of trouble in Barcelona recently. There I was, cooing to a pretty doggo called Sophia at a set of traffic lights when her owner, Marco, decided my admiration for Sophia extended to himself. It took me several blocks of walking to shake Marco off. Even in my 60s, it seems, men can still pick up the wrong signals from me. Related Article Sunday Life Unpack once, see three countries: Why this is one of the best ways to see Europe Generally though, those small acts of openness have led to some of my favourite travel memories, and they have very little to do with the destination itself. It’s about who I choose to be at that moment. It’s about exercising my freedom to do so. Travel isn’t the antidote to feeling discarded, disrespected and disappeared. I know how societal pressures can prey on our vulnerabilities. I’ve felt tired, flat, flustered and lonely during my journeys, and in those moments, the impossible standards and ageism of the world at large can bear down on me with an awful force.



But it’s on my travels where I practise choosing when to step into the light and when to enjoy the freedom of remaining blessedly in the background. And I’ve brought that lesson home. I’m far less concerned with whether other people notice me than whether I’m noticing the world around me. As a child, I thought invisibility would let me move freely through the world. It turns out I was right. And like every good superhero, I get to decide when to use my power. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: When animal activist Pam Ahern had to choose her partner or a pig, her choice was clear
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life When animal activist Pam Ahern had to choose her partner or a pig, her choice was clear Robyn Doreian August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Animal activist Pam Ahern is best known as the founder of Edgar’s Mission, a refuge in Victoria. Here, the 64-year-old talks about the important men in her life, including her father and her friendship with Hollywood actor James Cromwell. Pam Ahern: “I didn’t have a boyfriend at high school – I was much happier at the pony club.” Peter Tarasiuk My father, Bernie, had an incredible influence on my life. He used to call me “Itsy” after the nursery rhyme about the spider. He passed away around 17 years ago but lives on in so much more than my genes. Dad left school early. He got a billycart and used to go to the tip to collect bottles and sell them for money – his first little empire. Later on, he created his trucking business, BJ Ahern. Dad loved fancy cars but he also loved animals. He could have bought pedigree dogs but he got rescues. He had a little golden Labrador, Sandy, who wore these booties so she wouldn’t damage the seat of his Rolls-Royce. Dad taught me to value what I have and to never have what you can’t afford – I’ve never owned a credit card. He also taught me gratitude. Dad valued education, logic and justice.



My parents split when I was eight years old. Initially, I lived with my mum, Sylvia, but in my teen years, I lived with Dad. I didn’t have a boyfriend at high school – I was much happier at the pony club or being out in the backyard playing with the dog and watching bees. In my 20s, I read [Australian moral philosopher] Peter Singer’s book, Animal Liberation, after which I turned vegan. I have met Peter several times. I like the way he stays really composed and thinks deliberately before he answers questions. Even if he disagrees, he doesn’t get rattled. He gave me an ultimatum – him or the pig. I chose the pig so I could live an authentic life. It was the best call. In 2003, I was living in Woodend [Victoria] on a five-acre property. At that time, I enjoyed a successful equestrian career. I was also involved in caring for wildlife and finding homes for them. I started taking abandoned, homeless and mistreated farm animals as well. That year, I worked with Animals Australia on the “Save Babe” campaign to highlight the plight of factory-farmed pigs. We needed a pig for a photo shoot. The day before, I had got Edgar Alan Pig, a tiny, poop-covered rescue piglet.



Actor James Cromwell was in Melbourne making the film Babe and we thought he’d bring significant media attention to our message, so I got in touch. He suggested an action on the steps of Parliament House to demand a better deal for pigs. I took Edgar on a lead and walked him around. People would stop and rub Edgar’s tummy when I took him for a walk. He wormed his way into people’s hearts, reminding them where these animals really belong. I loved Edgar and I wanted to create somewhere for him to live out his days [Edgar died in 2010]. So the idea for Edgar’s Mission came from my involvement with James. Ahern’s beloved Edgar Alan Pig at Parliament House in 2003. Farifax Archives I took James to dinner at this tiny vegan restaurant that had butchers paper for tablecloths. While we were eating, this lady came up to me: “Your dad looks just like James Cromwell.” I told her he wasn’t my dad, it was James. She refused to believe me. James is an incredible man. In America, not only does he work on behalf of animals but also for Native Americans displaced off their land. Dad loved hearing about the antics Edgar got up to. They were similar in that they both disliked vegetables and could be pig-headed. When Dad died, he left me a bequest. It enabled me to buy the 62-hectare Lancefield property, 72 kilometres north of Melbourne, where Edgar’s Mission is now located. I am so grateful. I hope he’s looking down and smiling; the animal sanctuary is his legacy.



I’ve had two significant relationships. The longest, which was for eight years, ended in 2007. He gave me an ultimatum – him or the pig. I chose the pig so I could live an authentic life. It was the best call. Related Article Sunday Life ‘Unhinged and gloriously crazy’: What Pussy Riot’s Maria Alyokhina looks for in a partner Even as a kid, getting married and having children was never on my agenda. I’m happy doing my own thing. Someone once commented that I was missing out on so much, to which I replied, “Maybe by your measure I am, but I think I’m gaining so much.” I would never judge anyone. It’s an enormous responsibility to have children. And just like animals, children are very vulnerable. I have made the right decision for me. World.title: Missed out on a pay rise? Here’s how to guarantee one next year
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingPay Opinion Missed out on a pay rise? Here’s how to guarantee one next year Victoria Devine Money columnist August 23, 2026 — 5:01am

August 23, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every time a new financial year rolls around, most of us are hoping for a pay rise. Whether we’ve worked especially hard and are hoping to have those efforts recognised, want our loyalty to our company rewarded, or simply need more money to keep up with the cost of living, there are many valid reasons to be hoping for a salary bump come July. Though many people think that pay rises are only accessible via a promotion or through taking on extra responsibilities, that’s certainly not true of all industries. Often, pay rises are offered for doing the job you have exceptionally well, going beyond the remit of the position or when the company has had a successful year. It’s a huge mistake to think that pay rises happen on that one day you have a conversation with your manager. Dionne Gain But just as Rome wasn’t built in a day, pay rises aren’t awarded on a whim. So if you were among those lucky enough to score a pay rise recently, congratulations. If you weren’t, I’m genuinely very sorry. Getting turned down for a raise can really knock the wind out of your sails and sour how you feel about your job and your workplace. But with that disappointment comes three primary options: you can stay in the same job but change your behaviour, you can look for another job, or you can start laying the groundwork for next year’s promotion now.



For fairly self-explanatory reasons, I don’t recommend the first option. Over the years, I’ve seen many people respond to pay rise rejection by emotionally checking out and doing only the bare minimum as a form of protest. The logic is that if the company hasn’t financially rewarded your hard work and efforts, why should you go above and beyond for them? While feeling this way is entirely understandable, and I’m in no way recommending working well above your pay grade for free, I’ve never seen this stance have the long-term desired effect, mostly because it’s viewed by management as you having a tantrum. When you go to your boss with another offer, you have to be prepared that they may let you go. Holding this position also means you’re likely bringing a negative attitude into the office and increasing the workloads of your colleagues, and those things will be noticed by your bosses. It also doesn’t put you in a good position to get a raise next year, or be considered for promotions into the future. The second option, as I mentioned, is to look for a new job and secure a higher salary by moving to a new company. The main pro to this option is, of course, more money.



But another perk is that you can potentially use the offer as leverage with your current employer. If they value the work that you do and recognise your talent, another offer lets them know that they can’t be complacent. However, there are two things to consider with this approach. The first is that your current employer may want to keep you, but can’t match the offer you’ve received. So before you go to them, it’s worth having a list of non-financial benefits you’d be open to. For example, let’s say your new job offer is for $20,000 more, but your current employer can only offer you $10,000. Are there non-cash options you’d consider to make up a package, like working from home an extra day, undertaking training? Having some ideas of what this kind of package could include before you go into negotiations will help your employer see that you’re serious about staying at the company, and allows them to try and find a solution. The second thing to consider is that when you go to your boss with another offer, you have to be prepared that they may let you go. So if you are planning to use another job offer as leverage, know that they could call your bluff, so you should be fully willing to go through with leaving when you approach them.



Then we get to the third option, which is laying the groundwork now for pay rises that will be issued next year. Across most companies, HR will go to bosses each year with a designated amount that can be used for discretionary pay rises. Editor's pick Opinion

Elon Musk Why the richest man on Earth wants you to think money won’t matter Victoria Devine Money columnist Let’s say there’s a pool of $50,000 and 20 employees in the company. It’s extremely rare for a company to evenly spread that budget out and see everybody get a $2500 bump in their pay. Instead, a good boss will have spent months keeping an eye on who is performing well, and will divvy that amount out to five or 10 people when the time comes. And it’s this reason that it’s such a huge mistake to think that pay rises happen on that one day you have a conversation with your manager. Because in fact, those decisions are being made months ahead of time, and that conversation is merely the formality.



Now, let’s say you didn’t get approved for a pay rise this financial year. Now that a few weeks have passed since you received that news, it’s time to follow up with your manager, and really drill into how you can improve your chances between now and next July. Start by asking what they would need to see more of from you, and then specific examples of what that would look like in practice. While this conversation might come with some unpleasant feedback, if you can push through that what it will give you is a clear understanding of where the goal posts are and how to reach them – and that is essential. In this conversation, you also shouldn’t be afraid to make it clear that the reason you’re asking is that you are hoping to be eligible for a pay rise next year. Now that you have that list of what you need to be doing, let it be your north star. Check in with it on Monday mornings, and on Friday afternoons take five minutes to make notes from the week of any wins or successes you had. From there, schedule another check in for January and take the highlights from those notes along. At this point, you’re halfway through the financial year, and you can show them how you’re progressing, what you’ve done, and check in on those benchmarks they set. Ask them if they’re happy with your performance and if there’s more you can be doing between then and the time of pay rise decisions being made.



Hopefully, when next July rolls around, you’ll be among those being congratulated. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: I’m 64 and I just inherited $700,000. What should I do with it?
World.content:
August 23, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I have about $700,000 in cash from a recent inheritance and am unsure what to do with it. I’d like to be able to access some to help my adult children occasionally. I am a 64-year-old single female homeowner (no debt) working full-time, but I plan to reduce my weekly hours within 12 months. I have about $500,000 in super, including $340,000 invested in FY2026 through the three-year bring-forward provisions. I salary-sacrifice now to just under the maximum allowed for concessional contributions. It can be difficult to work out what to do with a large inheritance. Simon Letch Upon turning 65 years old, superannuation becomes completely accessible irrespective of whether you remain working or have retired. Throughout our working lives, the primary drawback of placing money in superannuation is loss of access, so this unlock is quite significant. With $500,000 in superannuation and the current transfer balance cap being $2.1 million, you have plenty of headroom to utilise the superannuation system. The reason the superannuation system stands out here is that while you are still accumulating, tax on earnings is only 15 per cent. And then once you retire and start drawing an income, the tax drops to 0 per cent.



So you have an environment where you can access your money whenever you like, and it receives extremely favourable tax treatment. It also has the benefit of being highly regulated, providing you with confidence. This investment could be left alone, hopefully for a few decades, and be available for any care needs that you may face later in life. Contribution caps are your problem, though. Given your use of the bring-forward provisions last financial year, we will need to wait until July 2028 (’28-29 financial year) before you can again make a lump sum contribution. At present, the maximum under this provision is $390,000, and it is reasonable to assume that will have been indexed up by the time you can next contribute. Let’s assume that come July 1, 2028 you want to be able to put $400,000 into your superannuation as a non-concessional contribution, once again using the bring-forward provisions, and allowing for a bit of indexation between now and then. I would establish an investment portfolio for your $700,000 now, breaking up the proceeds. I would place $400,000 in a balanced or conservative investment option to align with the two- to three-year time frame that we are facing here.



Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert We have $1.6m in an SMSF. Should we keep it, or move it to a standard fund? Noel Whittaker Money columnist If your inclination was towards conservativism, you could even simply place this money in a term deposit. For the remaining $300,000 that you won’t be able to get into superannuation, I would invest in something with a longer time horizon that aligns with your comfort around risk and volatility. Once retired, and with the super contribution made, I would be surprised if this investment in isolation would push you to the point of needing to pay and submit an annual tax return. This investment could be left alone, hopefully for a few decades, and be available for any care needs that you may face later in life. I am 56 and have insurance in my super than has gotten costly. Am I being irresponsible if I cancel it? The starting point with insurance is to consider your debts and dependents. If you have neither, your need for insurance diminishes significantly.



Next, you would consider how you would fare in the event of significant incapacity. If your balance sheet right now is strong, it is quite conceivable that you don’t need insurance for this either. Insurance does get more expensive as we age, and our financial position typically strengthens, so it is appropriate to consider scaling back, if not completely cancelling insurance later in life. Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. Questions to: paul@financialautonomy.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Euthanasia laws are overdue for review. A former minister has ideas why
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Euthanasia laws are overdue for review. A former minister has ideas why Matt Dennien August 23, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When eligible terminally ill Queenslanders gained legal access to drugs to end their own lives at the start of 2023, a timer in the laws began. “As soon as practicable” after three years, the health minister would be required to review the laws’ effectiveness and eligibility criteria. Approaching nine months since that three-year milestone, the Crisafulli LNP government has said little publicly about a review. Former minister Jann Stuckey has an idea why. Former Liberal and LNP member for Currumbin, Jann Stuckey, pictured with then-AFL CEO Andrew Demetriou in 2013 while she was Tourism Minister in the Newman government. Matt Roberts “I don’t believe that the Crisafulli government will want to mention the word ‘voluntary assisted dying’,” she told this masthead by phone on Friday.



“Or anything that will raise any controversy amongst members – and we know that this will … I think they will avoid this release of this report or the review for as long as possible.” Behind-the-scenes, work to launch the review is under way. Loading Health Minister Tim Nicholls, approached by this masthead late last month, however, has declined to detail any of its planned shape. “The Queensland government is on the record that there will be no changes to voluntary assisted dying legislation,” a government spokesperson said in response, reiterating the LNP’s election vow.



“A review will be undertaken in accordance with the Act.” A parliamentary question on notice from independent Noosa MP Sandy Bolton late last year returned similar results. There, Bolton was pointed to an earlier response from Nicholls to a Labor opposition question in which he reiterated the government’s commitment to providing the service. “Queenslanders will be invited to contribute to the review at the appropriate time,” Nicholls said. When that might be remains the question for those wanting expansion – or winding-back. First elected to the Gold Coast seat of Currumbin as a Liberal, Stuckey remaining in parliament – through the party’s formal merge with the more dominate Nationals – until 2020. Bringing forward her retirement before that year’s election, Stuckey spoke out about the “cone-of-silence type of vilification” she felt after voting against party lines to decriminalise abortion in 2018.



She was one of only three LNP opposition figures to use the conscience vote to do so, including now-ministers Steve Minnikin and Tim Nicholls. A long-time advocate of voluntary assisted dying, she was among those involved with lobbying group Dying with Dignity to help push support for the laws brought to parliament in 2021. She was in the public gallery for the conscience vote that year when the laws passed, backed by 10 LNP MPs who broke with their partyroom’s majority opposition to them. In the parliamentary and public debate then, concerns were raised by both major party MPs and faith groups about the state of palliative care and need for church-run sites to allow the practice.



Within the next year came Stuckey’s pancreatic cancer diagnosis. For four years now, across multiple treatments and surgeries, 71-year-old Stuckey has had the “monster” – with a five-year survival rate of 12 per cent – come back four times. While Stuckey herself says she may not wish to use the laws, knowing they are there “is of enormous comfort”. So it is the fear it could be taken away likely “adds to the stress of many cancer patients”. And it is mostly used by people with a cancer diagnosis. The latest annual report of the state Voluntary Assisted Dying Review Board, for financial year 2024-25, put that figure at 76 per cent. In total from when the scheme began on January 1, 2023, to June 30 this year, the board’s data shows 3182 people have died after administering the drugs accessed through the multi-stage process.





Ultimately, after winning power and control of parliament, Crisafulli effectively gagged any debate of abortion laws, which Stuckey described to this masthead as an “astounding” move. No such restriction has been placed on parliamentary debate of voluntary assisted dying laws. Stuckey, who describes herself as Christian but says religion and politics should not cross, said she was concerned the voluntary assisted dying review could present an opportunity for parts of the party who have been blocked from pushing for changes to abortion. “I’ve been in the party room. I was there 16 years, you know, in opposition and as a minister. So I know how it works, and I and I know what the make-up of the parliament is and how they vote. I know, who’s hard-right Christian in the LNP,” she said. “So when they’re saying they’re not going to change it [assisted dying laws], I would just take that broadly as they’re not going to overturn it. But, I mean, they’ve got the numbers to overturn it easily”.



What’s really needed, though, according to Stuckey and other advocates – beyond even the state scheme review – is action from the federal Albanese government. While promising to review “carriage service” laws around suicide which have long been viewed as a barrier to access – particularly in regional areas – Albanese last month rejected a party push for action. David Muir, chair of the Clem Jones Group, said his group’s longstanding advocacy would include a submission to the upcoming review urging the state to use all influence it has to resolve the matter. In response to questions about any advocacy the state may have already taken up in this space since the election, Nicholls also declined to provide a direct answer.



“Any changes to the Commonwealth Criminal Code are a matter for the Commonwealth government,” a spokesperson for the health minister said. If you or anyone you know needs help, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 (and see lifeline.org.au) or Beyond Blue on1300 22 4636 (and see beyondblue.org.au). World.title: ‘No filter necessary’: Why 80-year-old women are fashion’s new secret weapon
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life ‘No filter necessary’: Why 80-year-old women are fashion’s new secret weapon Emily Cronin August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Charlotte Rampling: actor, forever fashion reference … octogenarian icon? The British actor, who turned 80 earlier this year, shared some of her feelings about reaching the milestone age in an interview with British Vogue. “I think I will be able to actually have a pretty good time [in my 80s]. I feel that I deserve it,” she said, going on to discuss her “loving friendship” with a new man. In the accompanying shoot, Rampling appears in a number of fashion-forward looks. Wearing outfits including a Saint Laurent blouse and biker jacket, Gucci tiger-print shearling coat and Louis Vuitton funnel-neck jumper and trousers, she appears edgy. Self-possessed. Even (dare we say it? Yes, we dare) hot. Eighty looks a little different than it used to. Make that very different. Along with Rampling, other women who’ve entered their 80s in recent years include Helen Mirren, mobbed by fans on her way into Erdem’s show during London Fashion Week earlier this year; Norma Kamali, still turning out bodycon dresses after almost 60 years; and Brenda Blethyn, star of the TV adaptation of A Woman of Substance. Joanna Lumley, who was surrounded by photographers as she took her seat in Burberry’s spring-summer 2026 front row, blew out 80 candles in May. Fashion front and centre: Helen Mirren, Charlotte Rampling, Jane Fonda, Vanessa Redgrave and Joanna Lumley. Launchmetrics Spotlight/Getty Images They join a cohort of 80-something women changing the face of ageing – women like Jane Fonda, 88, Vanessa Redgrave, 89, and Martha Stewart, 85.



Stewart in particular appears to be having an absolute ball. In 2023, aged 81, the domestic goddess and lifestyle mogul became the oldest cover star of Sports Illustrated’s annual swimsuit edition. Since then, she has covered the Olympics, partnered with friend and business partner Snoop Dogg on a gin venture and been the subject of a hit Netflix documentary. She also stars in the latest campaign for (denim brand) Mother in which she smoulders at the camera and purrs, “I love a nice package” and “No filter necessary”. “Martha is the ultimate muse,” says Lela Becker, the brand’s president and co-founder. “She knows what she wants, exudes confidence and isn’t afraid to challenge expectations. We wanted to celebrate that energy by presenting her in an unexpected way.” Martha Stewart, in Sydney this year, is living her best life after 80. Getty It should not be news that advanced age can correlate with advanced style. But ageing is changing. As Charlotte Rampling tells Vogue, “We’re all 10 years younger now.” Meaning that while the ninth decade might once have been a time to retreat to a comfortable armchair with the knitting, now it is a time for women to embrace life’s possibilities and do whatever they want, including declining great-grandchild babysitting opportunities in favour of travel, pursuing new relationships or, in Rampling’s case, starring in a Golden Lion-winning film. It is worth acknowledging that the group referenced here includes women renowned as some of the most stylish in the world for going on half a century. Of course Rampling, Lumley, Mirren et al were going to make ageing seem exciting rather than merely inevitable (if you’re lucky).



“The thing is, these women are so inspirational,” says Rachel Fanconi, a stylist who counts both Mirren and Lumley as longstanding clients. “They are the women who came up in the 1960s – they are the coolest girls.” Fanconi says that when preparing mood boards for photo shoots, the archive imagery she pulls from the ’60s and ’70s often references events or eras when “they were there – they were doing all of that”. She adds, “I think expectations around what women look like in their 80s are constantly evolving. The only surprise is that it seems to catch everybody by surprise. We all carry this idea of what each number looks like in our head from when we are very young. You have just got to let that go.” Taking a wider view, fashion designers seem to be embracing the power of older women on the catwalk and in advertising campaigns. Twiggy is in a Burberry campaign at 76. Gillian Anderson, 58, walked in the Miu Miu show at Paris Fashion Week (designer Miuccia Prada, at 77, remains at the peak of her power and influence). And one of the most talked-about models at Chanel’s recent shows has been 50-year-old Stephanie Cavalli and her beautiful curly grey hair (the destigmatisation of grey hair representing its own anti-ageist shift). It seems ageism may be on the way out – provided you have extraordinary bone structure and a runway-fashion-compliant frame.



By 80, most women will feel they have every clothing item they’ll ever need, and know how they like to dress. The key to facing the ninth decade in style lies not in imitating anyone mentioned above, but in having confidence and an awareness of what works. It is crucial to avoid stagnation, though. Rachel Fanconi’s advice? “Buy something new. Go somewhere great and buy one piece – the bag, the shoe, whatever it is – that goes with your clothes but gives it all an edge and helps you do something new, helps spark everything up a bit.” Surely Charlotte Rampling would approve.
