World.title: Specsavers told Nicole she needed glasses. Then, she had a car accident
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare Specsavers told Nicole she needed glasses. Then, she had a car accident Rachel Rasker August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three months after visiting Specsavers, wearing the bifocals she felt she was pressured into buying, Nicole Donovan had a car accident. “It could have just been from stress or hurrying,” the NSW mid-north coast resident said, “but I really couldn’t see properly”. When she called the store to ask why she was still having problems despite the new prescription, she was assured that she simply needed to get used to them. Nicole Donovan was frustrated Specsavers did not warn her about her cataracts. Matt Willis / Sitthixay Ditthavong “[The worker] was quite short on the phone with me,” Donovan said, and she wasn’t offered a follow-up appointment. “So I kept on trying, thinking it was me.” When Donovan sought a second opinion at an independent optometry clinic, she was promptly diagnosed with advanced cataracts which required urgent surgery.



She felt she had no choice but to travel five hours to Sydney for an $11,000 procedure: “I was frustrated that [Specsavers] didn’t pick it up, so that I may have been able to go on a public waiting list and get the surgery for free.” Related Article Investigation

Healthcare Revealed: The optometrists punished for putting patients before sales Donovan was one of the more than 70 people who contacted this masthead following its investigation into corporate optometry, which detailed how chains including Specsavers and OPSM pressured optometrists to hit sales targets, potentially jeopardising patient care. Professor Konrad Pesudovs, a leading optometrist researcher and clinician, said cataracts are to optometrists what high blood pressure is to GPs: “You can’t miss a cataract. It’s just so fundamental, it’s right there.” While he said it was possible that there had been a misunderstanding during Donovan’s initial appointment, her care should have been followed up: “What isn’t defensible is not seeing a patient when they’re unhappy, because that’s when you detect the problem.”



This masthead’s investigation found optometrists were routinely pressured to prioritise “convertible” appointments which would result in a glasses sales. Another Specsavers customer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said a manager “snatched the appointment card out of my hand” after he attempted to book a follow-up consultation because the glasses he was prescribed for a sudden vision change did not improve his eyesight: “My guess was that he wasn’t getting a sale, so he didn’t want to deal with me.” The patient instead visited a neighbouring independent optometrist, who escalated his concerns to an ophthalmologist. It was then – two weeks after his initial visit to Specsavers – that he was advised to go immediately to the emergency department, where it was confirmed that his sudden vision loss – diagnosed as hemianopia – was due to a stroke. Dr Tim Fricke, the director of research and education at the Australian College of Optometry, said while mistakes happen, a hemianopia should be picked up in a basic examination, during an initial consultation. He was also concerned by the refusal to book a patient in for a follow-up.



“Practitioners are paid for a health service through Medicare,” he said. “I don’t think it’s particularly [profitable for Specsavers], but there is an obligation to provide a health service.” In a statement, Specsavers said more than 5 million Australians trust the brand with their eye care each year, “a responsibility we take seriously, and in the rare instances where a patient believes their experience was not what it should have been, we have well-established clinical governance and review processes”. “We are proud of the professional standards of our optometrists in detecting and managing eye-threatening conditions,” the statement said. “These governance and review processes are designed to understand what occurred in these rare instances and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.” No longer a local operation A July 2026 report by industry research group IBISWorld highlighted the growing monopolisation of the sector, with Specsavers and EssilorLuxxotica (OPSM’s parent company) expected to account for just over half the industry’s revenue in 2026-27.



Specsavers opened its first Australian retail store in 2008 and now holds more than one-third of the market share, with $1.8 billion in annual revenue. Specsavers Australia represents the second-largest market by revenue for its global parent company, behind only the UK, where the chain originated. The brand’s “competitively priced products and services has forced other optical retailers to match”, the report found, with about 94 per cent of initial eye tests across the industry bulk-billed. The report noted that other outlets – which included a mix of independent optometrists and smaller chains such as Oscar Wylee, George & Matilda, and Bailey Nelson – still hold a 48.7 per cent market share, with $2.51 billion in revenue.



The true cost of bulk billing Across the industry, costs for rent and equipment have skyrocketed while Medicare rebates have remained stagnant. “The squeeze has been on for decades,” Fricke said. “You get less payment per unit of time than you used to, and all your costs [have gone] up. So something has to give at some point.” Optometry Australia chief executive Mark Nevin said the peak body has consistently advocated for higher rebates, which he said were “unsustainably low” and needed to be cross-subsidised by sales of spectacles and contact lenses to remain viable. However, Nevin said financial KPIs that compromise clinical autonomy, including the quality and safety of care, were unacceptable: “We can assure the public that care provided by optometrists is safe and high quality, evidenced by the very low level of complaints to our regulator.”



Nigel Chesterfield-Evans, who has been an optometrist since 1978 and ran five independent practices before converting them to Specsavers franchises, said public expectation around bulk billing had damaged the industry: “People do not appreciate what they don’t pay for.” “I have sat in a consulting room, found a retinal tumour, photographed it, sent it to the GP and then sent it to the ophthalmologist. The fee that I got from Medicare for that was less than the lady at the nail salon,” he said. Shereen Kassir is calling for award recognition for optometrists. Health Services Union Optometrist and Health Services Union (HSU) delegate Shereen Kassir said the government should “step up” to ensure MBS fees matched both current inflation and optometrists’ scope of practice. “It’s not just affecting the optometrists under these really strong KPI pressures, but it’s also impacting the patient care,” she said. “Medicare disincentivises being a clinical-focused eye care provider.”



Related Article Healthcare ‘It’s really debilitating’: The hidden danger in your daily screen time driving a surge in disease A spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said in a statement that optometry services are indexed every year on July 1. The spokesperson said changes to MBS optometry services came into effect in March 2025, including creating two new MBS items for glaucoma patients at high risk, amending low vision assessment items to align with contemporary best practice, and increasing schedule fees for domiciliary visits. Clinicians, not retail staff Last month, the HSU lodged a bid at the Fair Work Commission which called for optometrists to be explicitly covered under the Health Professionals and Support Services Award, to ensure industry recognition and improved pay, breaks and rosters. “We know Specsavers have said: You fall under the retail award, you are not a health professional,” HSU president Kate Marshall said. “Simply knocking that argument out means that we can legitimately have a go at these companies.”



Kassir said the award will allow optometrists to work under an enterprise agreement, and if needed, participate in protected industrial action: “That gives [us] the power back.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: Women have always feared becoming invisible as they age. But with travel, it’s a gift
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Women have always feared becoming invisible as they age. But with travel, it’s a gift Julietta Jameson August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I was little, someone asked me what superpower I’d most like to have. I chose invisibility. To my young mind, it meant freedom. The ability to go anywhere, eat anything and do whatever I wanted without asking permission or worrying what anyone thought. As the youngest of six children in a chaotic household, disappearing into the background felt like a delicious kind of independence. Of course, like many childhood ideas, invisibility became more complicated as I grew older. I learned there are people for whom invisibility isn’t a superpower but a sentence. People pushed to the margins because of their race, disability, sexuality or age. I also absorbed the familiar warning handed to women: enjoy being noticed while it lasts because one day you’ll be invisible, too. Invisibility after a certain age is actually a superpower. Michela Ravasio / Stocksy United When I was travelling through Italy in my 40s, I remember the first time someone addressed me as signora instead of signorina. It was only a word, but it rocked me. I’d crossed a threshold, and I soon began to mourn the woman I’d apparently left behind, especially when menopause began to wreak havoc and my body told me it had crossed its own personal Rubicon. My 50s arrived, and my menopausal symptoms started to subside, but the predicted invisibility didn’t arrive. Men still flirted with me, often at moments I’d have preferred they didn’t. The world hadn’t suddenly stopped looking. But the way I responded to it was changing.



Now that I’m in my 60s, I’m contemplating all this from a different perspective. Is society really rendering older women invisible? Or have I, after years of feeling scrutinised, judged and assessed, stepped into a different relationship with visibility? I suspect the answer is both. I’m starting to believe invisibility after a certain age is actually the superpower I craved as a kid. JULIETTA JAMESON There’s no denying that ageism exists. Women over 50 encounter it in obvious and subtle ways, from job interviews to everyday interactions that leave us feeling overlooked or patronised. But somewhere between the cultural warnings and my own experience, I’m starting to believe invisibility after a certain age is actually the superpower I craved as a kid. As a travel writer, I spend much of my life moving through places where nobody knows me. Every new destination offers a potential reset. I’m not somebody’s daughter, sister, colleague, neighbour or patient. Nobody knows my history. Nobody knows my age, unless I choose to tell them – though as an au naturel girly, experience is proudly writ large on my face, albeit with a dash of mascara and a slick of lippy. Putting aside the so-called telltale signs of ageing, every morning I wake up with complete freedom to decide how visible I want to be. Some days I embrace anonymity. I find a corner table in a cafe, order a coffee, open a book and happily disappear into my own company for an hour or two. There can be an enormous luxury in being left alone. Just ask any mum.



On other days, I decide to be rampantly visible. I’ll chat to the woman beside me on a train – if she seems approachable and up for it. I love to compliment people. If I see a hairstyle I like, or a coat that’s particularly great, I let the wearer know. Honestly, it makes their day and ends up making mine, too. I’ll strike up a conversation with a market vendor – usually by butchering the local language, and everyone usually gets a laugh. I’ll stop to pat every dog that will let me, though this did get me into a bit of trouble in Barcelona recently. There I was, cooing to a pretty doggo called Sophia at a set of traffic lights when her owner, Marco, decided my admiration for Sophia extended to himself. It took me several blocks of walking to shake Marco off. Even in my 60s, it seems, men can still pick up the wrong signals from me. Related Article Sunday Life Unpack once, see three countries: Why this is one of the best ways to see Europe Generally though, those small acts of openness have led to some of my favourite travel memories, and they have very little to do with the destination itself. It’s about who I choose to be at that moment. It’s about exercising my freedom to do so. Travel isn’t the antidote to feeling discarded, disrespected and disappeared. I know how societal pressures can prey on our vulnerabilities. I’ve felt tired, flat, flustered and lonely during my journeys, and in those moments, the impossible standards and ageism of the world at large can bear down on me with an awful force.



But it’s on my travels where I practise choosing when to step into the light and when to enjoy the freedom of remaining blessedly in the background. And I’ve brought that lesson home. I’m far less concerned with whether other people notice me than whether I’m noticing the world around me. As a child, I thought invisibility would let me move freely through the world. It turns out I was right. And like every good superhero, I get to decide when to use my power. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: When animal activist Pam Ahern had to choose her partner or a pig, her choice was clear
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life When animal activist Pam Ahern had to choose her partner or a pig, her choice was clear Robyn Doreian August 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Animal activist Pam Ahern is best known as the founder of Edgar’s Mission, a refuge in Victoria. Here, the 64-year-old talks about the important men in her life, including her father and her friendship with Hollywood actor James Cromwell. Pam Ahern: “I didn’t have a boyfriend at high school – I was much happier at the pony club.” Peter Tarasiuk My father, Bernie, had an incredible influence on my life. He used to call me “Itsy” after the nursery rhyme about the spider. He passed away around 17 years ago but lives on in so much more than my genes. Dad left school early. He got a billycart and used to go to the tip to collect bottles and sell them for money – his first little empire. Later on, he created his trucking business, BJ Ahern. Dad loved fancy cars but he also loved animals. He could have bought pedigree dogs but he got rescues. He had a little golden Labrador, Sandy, who wore these booties so she wouldn’t damage the seat of his Rolls-Royce. Dad taught me to value what I have and to never have what you can’t afford – I’ve never owned a credit card. He also taught me gratitude. Dad valued education, logic and justice.



My parents split when I was eight years old. Initially, I lived with my mum, Sylvia, but in my teen years, I lived with Dad. I didn’t have a boyfriend at high school – I was much happier at the pony club or being out in the backyard playing with the dog and watching bees. In my 20s, I read [Australian moral philosopher] Peter Singer’s book, Animal Liberation, after which I turned vegan. I have met Peter several times. I like the way he stays really composed and thinks deliberately before he answers questions. Even if he disagrees, he doesn’t get rattled. He gave me an ultimatum – him or the pig. I chose the pig so I could live an authentic life. It was the best call. In 2003, I was living in Woodend [Victoria] on a five-acre property. At that time, I enjoyed a successful equestrian career. I was also involved in caring for wildlife and finding homes for them. I started taking abandoned, homeless and mistreated farm animals as well. That year, I worked with Animals Australia on the “Save Babe” campaign to highlight the plight of factory-farmed pigs. We needed a pig for a photo shoot. The day before, I had got Edgar Alan Pig, a tiny, poop-covered rescue piglet.



Actor James Cromwell was in Melbourne making the film Babe and we thought he’d bring significant media attention to our message, so I got in touch. He suggested an action on the steps of Parliament House to demand a better deal for pigs. I took Edgar on a lead and walked him around. People would stop and rub Edgar’s tummy when I took him for a walk. He wormed his way into people’s hearts, reminding them where these animals really belong. I loved Edgar and I wanted to create somewhere for him to live out his days [Edgar died in 2010]. So the idea for Edgar’s Mission came from my involvement with James. Ahern’s beloved Edgar Alan Pig at Parliament House in 2003. Farifax Archives I took James to dinner at this tiny vegan restaurant that had butchers paper for tablecloths. While we were eating, this lady came up to me: “Your dad looks just like James Cromwell.” I told her he wasn’t my dad, it was James. She refused to believe me. James is an incredible man. In America, not only does he work on behalf of animals but also for Native Americans displaced off their land. Dad loved hearing about the antics Edgar got up to. They were similar in that they both disliked vegetables and could be pig-headed. When Dad died, he left me a bequest. It enabled me to buy the 62-hectare Lancefield property, 72 kilometres north of Melbourne, where Edgar’s Mission is now located. I am so grateful. I hope he’s looking down and smiling; the animal sanctuary is his legacy.



I’ve had two significant relationships. The longest, which was for eight years, ended in 2007. He gave me an ultimatum – him or the pig. I chose the pig so I could live an authentic life. It was the best call. Related Article Sunday Life ‘Unhinged and gloriously crazy’: What Pussy Riot’s Maria Alyokhina looks for in a partner Even as a kid, getting married and having children was never on my agenda. I’m happy doing my own thing. Someone once commented that I was missing out on so much, to which I replied, “Maybe by your measure I am, but I think I’m gaining so much.” I would never judge anyone. It’s an enormous responsibility to have children. And just like animals, children are very vulnerable. I have made the right decision for me. World.title: Firefighters working on large vegetation fire in Invercargill
World.content:
Firefighters are working to put out a 600 metre long blaze on Oreti Beach in Invercargill.

The south shift manager said vegetation fire is rather large, with firefighters working against the wind and rain.

Officials have been working to extinguish the fire for more than three hours, after they were alerted just after 3am.

World.title: Firefighters investigating cause of large Wānaka blaze
World.content:
Firefighters are investigating the cause of a ferocious fire that blazed through trees and scrub in Wānaka, sending flames leaping metres into the air and forced the evacuation of 22 homes.

The blaze broke out near Lagoon Avenue at 7.30pm on Saturday night and tore through steep hillsides close to houses, fanned by strong winds.

Fire and Emergency said no houses had caught fire on Saturday, although emergency services initially thought seven to eight properties were under threat.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) crews brought the flames under control using eight trucks and three support vehicles, but were still dealing with hotspots, flare-ups and flying embers late into the night.

In McLellan Place, Marty Lohrey said he had been shocked to open the curtains to see flames tearing through kānuka behind his house.

"Very quickly they just flared up, within a few moments, probably 10-20 metres in the air. Quite quickly the wind just whipped them down the terrace. It was really hot, noisy, and all the embers were blowing across the houses. It made you think of the forest fires we've seen, everyone was pretty scared," he said.

Lohrey said neighbours were knocking on each other's doors and calling 111.

"I think we've dodged a bullet because there's no property damage. The fire boys were all here pretty quickly. The response by the fire brigade and police has been fantastic," he said.

Corey Young said he saw a bright glow in the sky from his living room and raced out to help the firefighters.

"They got on top of it pretty quickly but it was very, very close to a number of houses, it was pretty scary actually," he said.

"It was looking pretty grim there for a little bit until they arrived on the scene.

"I could feel the heat from the fire. Some of the flames got probably a good 20 metres high at times. It was just making sure that the people in those houses were safe."

Young said people were ready to use garden hoses and buckets of spa pool water to try to protect their properties.

"It was pretty touch and go there. There was smoke billowing everywhere," he said.

Hunt Place resident Del Tubb told RNZ the fire started with a roar: "[We] looked out the window and it was like a blazing inferno right across the garden. Everything was bright red and there were embers. It was pretty scary stuff," he said.

He quickly grabbed warm clothes to go out into the night and moved two cars. Talking on Saturday night he was relieved a woodshed just over the fence from the flames had not gone up in flames.

Strong winds and fire a bad mix, firefighter says

Fire and Emergency NZ Queenstown Lakes manager Nic McQuillan in Albert Town, on Saturday night. RNZ/ Katie Todd

FENZ assistant district commander Nic McQuillan told RNZ that dry, windy weather was problematic, even in winter.

"We don't know how the fire started but I would just ask people to be conscious of the fact that even though it's still coming out of winter, everything is dry, the wind is a real problem when it comes to a spark or an ember that gets out of control," he said

McQuillan said people getting rid of ashes from fires should make sure they are completely cool before disposing of them and check if conditions are safe before lighting a fire.

World.title: Polytechs resisting attempts to keep single collective agreement for sector, union says
World.content:
The Tertiary Education Union says polytechnics are resisting its attempts to retain a single collective employment agreement covering the entire sector.

It has asked the Employment Relations Authority to provide facilitated bargaining for a multi-employer collective agreement, or MECA.

The union's assistant national secretary - industrial, Daniel Benson-Guiu, said for the past four years its members were covered by a single agreement negotiated while the polytechnics were campuses of the national skills and training institute Te Pūkenga.

The institute was winding up and Benson-Guiu said there was no reason they couldn't shift to a multi-employer collective covering 11 employers - the 10 independent institutes and the group of four that remained within Te Pūkenga, but would next year function as a federation of individual institutions.

"We know that the employers may have slightly different interests, but we also know that the sector has not drastically changed over the last few years, especially when it comes to what it takes to employ staff and retain staff and make sure that they're well remunerated for the work that they do," he said.

A single agreement was in place while polytechnics were all part of Te Pūkenga. Peter de Graaf

But the union was struggling to negotiate a MECA.

"Currently each employer is claiming they're so different from each other that they couldn't possibly be in one agreement. That's even though the agreement right now continues to be in force and there doesn't appear to be a problem on a day-to-day basis," Benson-Guiu said.

"Right now, effectively, they're stalling in terms of negotiations. We had our claims from day one. We've seen no claims at all from any of the polytechnics about the MECA specifically and we've been in negotiations for over six months," he said.

"From what we can see, there is no money and there's an attitude that each employer should go it alone."

One of the polytechnics, Ara, said it was engaged in collective bargaining with the union and remained committed to bargaining in good faith.

"Our preference is for a single employer collective agreement because we believe it provides greater flexibility to reflect Ara's specific operating environment and the needs of our kaimahi," it said.

Ara Institute of Canterbury in Christchurch RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Existing terms and conditions remain an important foundation for those discussions. As bargaining is ongoing, we are unable to comment further."

Meanwhile, the union said it was seeking a six percent pay rise for its members at six universities.

Benson-Guiu said the universities had made offers but the union's members wanted to see more money on the table.

The universities were Auckland, Waikato, Massey, Victoria, Canterbury and Otago.

Benson-Guiu said universities and polytechnics were under-funded and could not meet the needs of staff or students.

World.title: Black Ferns find their ruthless side
World.content:
Coach Whitney Hansen called for ruthlessness from her side, and unfortunately for the Wallaroos in their 100th test, the Black Ferns delivered.

New Zealand ran riot in Auckland with a 66-19 rout of the Wallaroos, scoring 10 tries to retain the O'Reilly Cup in emphatic style.

The relentless nature of the performance was particularly pleasing for Hansen.

"That's one of the things we've been searching for. We're pretty proud of the fact that it wasn't just a 40 minute effort, it was 80."

Ticking further boxes was the trio of debutants Elinor Plum-King, Shyrah Tuliau-Tua'a and Amarante Sititi all seamlessly stepping up on the international stage.

"None of them let us down today. Pretty exciting to see two of them score, and that's off the back of King getting three last week too. I think they came in and they did their roles well and, to be able to be really confident in the black jersey, we've gained some real confidence in them, too."

Hansen said after a brutal domestic season, the players are primed for test rugby.

"We have competition in Aupiki that is the most physical internationally and that's a brand of rugby we want to play and we absolutely show that today. We are pretty proud of what we did do, but we also know there's lots out there that we can be better at too."

Skipper Ruahei Demant said the competition for places in the squad is fierce.

"I thought this week our girls who didn't get the opportunity to strip up really challenged us in every single training that we had. The girls respected the opposition, we respected each other and the ball, and we stayed really disciplined to stick to our game plan right from the start."

She said the senior members in the team have been sure to make the rookies welcome.

"I think that that is always the mark of a very healthy environment. Environments where people can be themselves. So for young players coming through, the future of our Black Ferns team, being able to be their authentic selves off the field, you see how that confidence translates into performances like today."

Demant again led a stirring haka prior to kick off, one which the Australians responded to by getting into boomerang formation and walking forward.

"We knew Aussie was going to be tough and we saw that with the response of the haka today, they were going to bring it and so I'm super proud of the physicality we brought in the first 20 minutes and then continue to do throughout the game.

"It's cool to see that they accept the challenge and respect our culture and respect our haka. I was really proud of the mana that the girls brought, you could feel that. The team feels that, and we use that to strengthen us as we lay down our challenge."

Despite the domination on display, Demant said they are still far from the finished product.

"There's lots of things that still need to be better and we'll dig into those because it's our next chance to do that will be South Africa. So getting really clear on what went well, where we can be better on."

A slight blight on the afternoon was the noticeably sparse crowd, numbering only around 6000.

Hansen however felt the game was still in a strong position in Aotearoa.

"I think it's growing in New Zealand and we've seen that our game can capture numbers .. across Aupiki and a couple of different times and our team's worked really hard to bring this one to life.

World.title: Warriors go top - for now - after thrilling win over South Sydney
World.content:
The Warriors have surged clear of South Sydney to win 45-26 to notch a fourth-straight win in the NRL and climb provisionally to the top of the standings.

After dominating the first half to lead 26-8 in Sydney, the Warriors needed to withstand a fightback from the Rabbitohs before late tries to Jacob Laban and Alofiana Khan-Pereira made the result safe.

Luke Hanson, introduced in the halves for just his second start because of a host of injuries in the Warriors playmaker ranks, then calmly slotted a field goal in the last play of the match.

It was enough to lift the Warriors one point ahead of the Panthers on points differential.

The Sydney Roosters could yet leapfrog both teams if they are victorious against the Wests Tigers on Sunday.

Either way, the Warriors are well-placed to push for a valuable top two finish, with their remaining regular season games both at home - against mid-table opponents Newcastle and Manly.

The Warriors unleashed another bright attacking display, although it was clouded by a shoulder injury suffered by Dallin Watene-Zelezniak.

Dallin Watene-Zelezniak holding an injured shoulder after scoring against South Sydney. photosport

The speedy winger was forced from the field after diving to score a try early in the second half, with initial reports suggesting it could be an AC joint injury.

Hanson slotted neatly into the Warriors patterns while once again Chanel Harris-Tavita shone, this time wearing the less-familiar No.7 jersey.

Harris-Tavita scored the last try of a dominant Warriors first half display, having also set up another to Leka Halasima via a towering bomb.

Mitchell Barnett of the Warriors scores a try against South Sydney. photosport

Front-rower co-captains James Fisher-Harris and Mitchell Barnett were the other early try-scorers, both off subtle playmaking from hooker Wayde Egan.

It was the first loss at Accor Stadium this season for the Rabbitohs and completed a memorable week for coach Andrew Webster.

World.title: Strong winds hampering firefighters at large Wānaka blaze
World.content:
A large fire that forced evacuations in Wānaka has been brought under control, but strong winds and steep terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to reach the remaining flames.

About 22 homes were evacuated in Wānaka's Albert Town on Saturday night, as the huge flames burned close to residential streets.

Fire and Emergency NZ said they were alerted to the vegetation fire in an area made up of gullies and steep hills, just before 7:30pm on Saturday, and had been attacking it from "multiple points".

In a briefing after 10pm on Saturday, Fire and Emergency District Assistant Commander Nic McQuillan said the fire was in about one kilometre of trees and scrub "alongside houses".

While it was now controlled, "firefighters are still dealing with hotspots, flare-ups and ember transfers," and firefighters would be at the scene working on it all night into Sunday, he said.

"No houses have caught fire, although initially it was thought seven to eight properties were threatened and Police evacuated 22 homes."

It was not known what caused the fire, or when people who were evacuated would be able to return home, he said. But a reporter at the scene said there were signs some people may have been allowed home shortly after that briefing.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz with information or images

Fire crews from right across central Otago, including Hawea, Tarras and Cromwell, had responded to the blaze, along with three support vehicles.

Fire and Emergency Queenstown Lakes group manager Nic McQuillan, on Saturday night. RNZ/ Katie Todd

Fire trucks could be seen in various streets around the Lagoon Avenue area, just minutes from central Wānaka and the Clutha River.

"We can contain the fire, but we are having to reposition to reach each spot ... But we are dealing with it," McQuillan told RNZ earlier in the night.

Del Tubb said the fire had come right up against his woodshed, near the back of his property:

"We were watching telly and there was a huge roar, which I thought was wind and thought - my God that's strong. Then [his companion] looked out the window - and it was like a blazing inferno."

"It was right across the garden - everything was bright red and it was embers. It was pretty scary stuff at that time, and you don't know what to do, you think 'shall I get out, shall I get my stuff out, move the cars' - all those things. It's really serious, you know."

Tubb said they quickly put on warm gloves and beanies before going out into the cold night, and he was able to move two cars away from the fire area.

RNZ/ Katie Todd

Michael Frankton, who uses a wheelchair, said it was a terrifying sight: "I looked out the window and I could see a raging fire heading towards our house, up the bank in the kānuka".

Sarah Dawson said neighbours acted quickly: "It just went up like these enormous, raging, high flames, just roaring towards us. It was absolutely terrifying," she said.

"All the neighbours rushed out and people were knocking on each other's doors and checking. People looked after Michael and gave him blankets."

RNZ/ Katie Todd

Images posted online showed huge flames rising into the night near houses.

Police were at the scene carrying out evacuations and controlling traffic. A cordon on the corner of Hunt-Lagoon-Sherwin was lifted earlier in the night.

Rain had been minimal this week, residents told RNZ, but by 10:30pm it was raining heavily.

Supplied/ Bernie Hewson

World.title: Late Hanson field goal puts Warriors atop NRL
World.content:
Rookie five-eighth Luke Hanson has slotted a last-minute field goal to put NZ Warriors atop the NRL table with a 45-26 win over the South Sydney Rabbitohs in Sydney.

With one eye on the scoreboard and the other on the points-differential column of the ladder, the visitors almost lost their way in a contest they were in complete control of at halftime on Saturday, but gathered themselves with a late rally for a convincing victory.

A fast start, with tries to skipper James Fisher-Harris and centre Leka Halasima, put the Warriors 12-0 ahead in the opening 10 minutes, and while Souths grabbed a couple of first-half tries, they were unable to stem the onslaught, as co-skipper Mitch Barnett and halfback Chanel Harris-Tavita scored tries before the break.

With incumbent fullback Charnze Nicoll-Kolkstad suspended, Taine Tuaupiki was handed the No.1 jersey and the kicking tee, and he responded with a perfect display that may keep him in the line-up long term.

The 26-8 halftime lead had the Warriors level with Penrith Panthers on the top of the live ladder and they grabbed the outright advantage, when wing Dallin Watene-Zelezniak was first to score after the restart.

Watene-Zelezniak aggravated a shoulder injury in the process and left the field, throwing the backline into disarray, with centre Adam Pompey moving out and second-rower Eddie Ieremia-Toeava into the midfield.

Souths began to take full toll of that confusion, with centre Tallis Duncan, wing Alex Johnson and halfback Cody Walker all scoring down that left side.

Back within six points, the home side seemed on the verge of a dramatic comeback, but Harris-Tavita produced the decisive moment of the game, putting up a high kick on the last tackle, chasing it and gathering to bounce, to put second-rower Jacob Laban over for a try that swung momentum back.

Wing Alofiana Kahn-Pereira scored next and the Warriors were again level with Penrith in the closing moments.

Hanson had also been called into action for his second first-grade game, after star halfback Luke Metcalf tweaked a hamstring last week.

As the final seconds ticked down, the Warriors entered the redzone and set up for the field goal. The ball initially came to Harris-Tavita, but he offloaded to Hanson, who made no mistake, bisecting the uprights for the competition lead.

Sydney Roosters can still reclaim the top spot, when they host struggling Wests Tigers on Sunday, but the result virtually cements a top-four position for the Warriors.

Fifth-placed Cronulla Sharks are now six points behind with three games to play, but lag 130 points behind on differential countback.

Kick-off was 7.30pm Saturday.

World.title: Three hurt in Lindis Pass crash
World.content:
Police are seeking witnesses after three people have been critically injured following a crash on Lindis Pass.

Emergency services were called to State Highway 8, between Lindis Pass-Tarras Road and Birchwood Road, at about 7.40am on Saturday.

Oamaru Police Sergeant Tony Woodbridge said two vehicles were involved in the crash, which happened near Dalrachney Station.

On Saturday evening Woodbridge gave an update: "Three people were transported to hospital, where they remain in critical condition, and our thoughts are with their families at this extremely difficult time".

The Omarama-Lindis Pass Road had reopened after it was closed for several hours after the crash while a scene examination was carried out, but police were still seeking more information, he said.

"Police would like to hear from anyone who witnessed the crash or who might have dashcam footage of it.

"In particular, Police are hoping to speak with a man we believe witnessed the crash and was one of the first people on scene.

"He left before Police arrived, and we are hoping he will come forward and speak with us to help us build a picture of what occurred."

Woodbridge also thanked the people who stopped at the scene of the crash to help and carry out first aid on the injured.

World.title: Zolani Tete shot dead outside his home in South Africa
World.content:
Former world boxing champion Zolani "Last Born" Tete has been shot dead outside his home in South Africa's Eastern Cape province, police and the country's sports minister said.

The 38-year-old was arriving at his residence in Mdantsane township when two armed men wearing balaclavas got out of a vehicle and opened fire.

"I will not speculate about who did this or why," Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said in a statement.

Tete's killing will renew attention on violent crime in South Africa, which continues to have one of the world's highest murder rates despite recent declines in homicides.

The killing was condemned by Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabunyane. (Reuters)

The murder of the world champion has also struck a chord in Mdantsane, the Eastern Cape township that has produced some of South Africa's most successful boxers.

SABC, the South African public broadcaster, reported that Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabuyane expressed shock and sadness at Tete's killing.

A spokesperson for the premier said: "It is heartbreaking that a life that brought so much pride to our province has been ended through such a brutal act of violence," according to SABC.

"We call on law enforcement agencies to leave no stone unturned to establish what happened and bring those responsible to book. Anyone with information must assist the police.

"On behalf of Premier Mabuyane and the EC provincial government, we extend our deepest condolences to the Tete family, his friends, the boxing fraternity and the community of Mdantsane.”

A woman travelling with Zolani Tete was also shot during the attack. (Reuters)

A 27-year-old woman travelling with Tete was shot multiple times and taken to hospital. Police have started investigations and the motive remains unclear.

Tete won the IBF junior bantamweight world title in 2014 after defeating Japan's Teiru Kinoshita in Kobe. He later won the WBO bantamweight crown.

He tested positive for the steroid stanozolol after a fight against British boxer Jason Cunningham in 2022 and was given a four-year suspension from competing, which expired in July this year.

He is best remembered internationally for his 11-second knockout of fellow South African Siboniso Gonya in Belfast in November 2017, the fastest stoppage in a world title fight.

Reuters

World.title: Mackay makes cricket history as day one of inaugural Test match sells out
World.content:
Barry Jansen mortgaged his house to help buy land for a cricket arena and didn't tell his wife for five years.

More than 40 years later, history is being made on the same field as the Queensland city of Mackay hosts its first international Test cricket match.

Mr Jansen said in the late 1980s the cricket association wanted to expand but needed financial backing.

Three members took an extraordinary personal risk and mortgaged their homes to help make it happen.

"We couldn't afford to pay our groundsmen without extending our facility. We didn't have the finance. We had park land with some value and that was all," he said.

Mackay cricket stalwart Barry Jansen in the commentary box. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

A government grant and a bank loan guaranteed by three members' homes helped fund the expansion.

Mr Jansen said there were a "couple of quiet moments" about five years later when he told his wife he'd mortgaged their home.

"I was very, very fortunate. I always say, it [Harrup Park] is like one of the family," he said.

"My wife always says it was part of the family because we'd sunk so much in it."

Nicolas Jones and Joe Brayshaw are on safari from Brisbane for the test. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

In 1939 the field was a cow paddock, purchased by local farmers for 1,000 pounds to start a cricket club.

"It was definitely a risk but those people then created the vision and we had to do it," Mr Jansen said.

'True cricket lovers'

Grandstands and hills at Harrup Park's Great Barrier Reef Arena were packed out with Bangladeshi locals waving flags and placards, with a "tiger" or two in the mix.

Shagufta Hasan, who described herself as a "true cricket lover", said Mackay's Bangladeshi community was cricket obsessed.

Members of Mackay's Bangladeshi community were out in force to support their team. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

"It doesn't matter if Bangladesh are playing or not, we're always watching," she said.

"We have 32 Bangladeshi families in Mackay so when the news came we all are very excited."

Scoring dream

Mackay resident Mel Dwyer, one of two Cricket Australia official scorers at the game, said it was a dream come true to score a Test in her home town.

She made her Test scoring debut at the Gabba in 2024 for Australia vs West Indies.

Mel Dwyer says scoring a Test match in her home town of Mackay was a dream come true. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Matches are scored on paper and she said the slower pace of a Test made the job "a little bit easier" than a T20 match.

"There are plenty of sets of eyes watching and there's lots of talking going on as far as what happens with every ball. We have to confirm everything," she said.

Ms Dwyer started scoring about 12 years ago when her youngest child started playing representative cricket.

"I just put my hand up to help out with those games because I found that if I sat on the sideline with the other parents, I would be too engrossed in conversations with them and miss what was actually going on the field," she said.

Cricket fans from Sydney flew in for the test match. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Ms Dwyer grew up in a family of cricket lovers in a house full of memorabilia celebrating Sir Donald Bradman and the Invincibles.

"I never thought in my wildest dreams that I would be working in cricket and scoring Test matches. A five-day test match would be absolutely amazing," she said.

Strong pitch

Peter Kazakoff, head curator of Great Barrier Reef Arena, said perfect weather and just the right amount of rain earlier in the week combined for a strong pitch.

The wicket in Mackay has the same clay soil profile as the Gabba.

"We source it from the same paddock down in Peak Crossing just at the back of Ipswich," he said.

Mr Kazakoff said selectors, coaches and players had been "blown out of the water" by the playing surface.

"We've gone from being a country cricket ground to an international test cricket venue. It's quite remarkable."

World.title: Quick hits: Stunning Shoriful rivals Starc's staggering spell, Hazlewood fumes
World.content:
Two lethal left arm quicks combine for 12 wickets, Australia comes close to snaring the rarest of dismissals, and a Harrup Park specialist fails on his return to the team.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Sensational Starc's first-ball strike

Mitchell Starc claimed a first ball wicket in both of this first two overs. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

We've seen this play before: Four times, in fact.

Mitch Starc steaming in, an opening batter studiously preparing for a lengthy stay at the crease, only to succumb to the very first challenge.

Shadman Islam was the unfortunate batter on this occasion, looking to clip Starc into the leg side but misjudging the pace and sending a leading edge to Cameron Green at gully.

He is, incredibly, the fourth batter to fall to Starc with the very first ball of a Test match.

Sri Lankan opener Dimuth Karunaratne was his first such victim back in 2016.

England's Rory Burns was famously bowled around his legs at the Gabba in the 2021/22 Ashes series.

And then, in 2024 at Adelaide Oval, Yashavi Jaiswal was trapped LBW with a pink ball.

Oh, and he wasn't done there, either.

2. Starc's five-fa comes in just 22 balls

Mitchell Starc tore through the top order. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Mitch Starc would not be contained or limited with just one wicket in his first spell.

Incredibly, he took five, tearing through the Bangladesh top order like a cyclone of ill-intent.

Shadman Islam's wicket was the only one to fall in the first over.

But in his second, he took two in the first two balls, accounting for Tanzid and Shanto in consecutive balls.

Mominul survived the first ball of the third over, but shouldn't have let down his guard as he fell later in the very same over to make it 4 in 3 for the big left-hander.

And then, in his fourth over, he made it five, Litton Das falling LBW for yet another duck, his five wickets coming in just 22 balls.

It should have been just 21 balls, had Beau Webster not shelled the sort of ball that you'd toss up to a toddler in the backyard.

It didn't matter though, Starc could not be contained, ending his six-over spell with figures of 5-5 and four maidens, leaving Bangladesh 5-15.

It was the sixth fastest five-wicket haul in Test history, but remarkably, it wasn't Starc's fastest in the format — that came in just 15 balls against the West Indies last year.

3. Obstructing the field?

Hazlewood was unimpressed with Taskin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Fans of obscure dismissals were almost gifted a rare instance of a player obstructing the field in the later stages of Bangladesh's batting innings.

Hazlewood came in and Taskin swiped across the line, sending the ball straight up in the air.

Hazlewood raced towards the ball, as Taskin took off for a run, before he then realised Hazlewood was baring down on him.

Taskin attempted to cover up, Hazlewood barged into him and the ball fell safe.

The crowd in Mackay felt aggrieved and there was more than a small suggestion of obstructing the field.

Hazlewood's eyes were in danger of having to be registered as dangerous weapons such was the ferocity of the daggers he was giving the unfortunate batter, as Pat Cummins engaged in a discussion with umpire Nitin Menon.

There was no appeal though that we could see, and Taskin was reprieved.

Only one player has ever been given out obstructing the field in Test cricket, Len Hutton for England against South Africa at The Oval in 1951.

Incredibly, later in the over, it appeared there was an (inadvertent) case of a double hit too as an attempted pull shot went awry.

4. Renshaw out cheaply on Test return

Renshaw was dimissed cheaply on his return to the Test arena. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

If Matt Renshaw could have chosen any ground in the world to make his Test return, it may well have been Harrup Park.

The Queenslander is the leading First Class run scorer at the venue, and is the only man to have scored two Sheffield Shield centuries in Mackay.

He's also coming off an impressive domestic summer, during which he scored three red-ball centuries at an average flirting with 50.

And it was under porcelain blue skies and in what looked to be perfect batting conditions that he made his way back to the Test-match crease, with the pitch having flattened out since Starc's new-ball demolition job.

The southpaw made an assured start to his innings, working a few attractive runs through the off-side, but it wasn't long before he was back in the sheds, having edged one into the slips.

Renshaw was out for 8 and Bangladesh, in desperate need of an early wicket after being bundled out for just 64, had their breakthrough.

5. Shoriful's dream day

The towering Shoriful made an instant impact at the bowling crease. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Forced to sit out the first Test with a side strain, exciting fast bowler Shoriful Islam wasted no time in making an impact in Mackay.

The 25-year-old left-armer is just that little bit quicker than his more workmanlike pace-bowling colleagues, and at over 190 centimetres tall, provides a different challenge in terms of release point.

Coming into the attack at first change, Shoriful took just two deliveries to claim his first Test wicket in Australia.

Pitching on a good length and seaming into Travis Head, the Australian opener was caught trying to play a shot that was never there, and was out chopping on for the third innings in a row.

Three balls later, and Shoriful had his second.

This time, he was aided by thigh pad rather than willow, with the ball rolling onto the stumps after thudding into Marnus Labuschagne.

Labuschagne was in disbelief, Shoriful was in dreamland, and Bangladesh was making a fist of things in Mackay.

And the towering left-armer wasn't done there.

First, he produced a beauty to dismiss Smith, who was well set on 42, LBW midway through the evening session.

Then, he tore through the Australian lower order, conjuring three more moments of magic to dismiss Beau Webster and Cummins for ducks, and Starc for 1.

World.title: Pendlebury could miss rest of season with his playing future undecided
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury's glittering Collingwood career could be over after the AFL/VFL games record holder suffered a hamstring injury.

The 38-year-old will miss up to three weeks, ruling him out of at least next week's historic wildcard match.

In an added blow for the Magpies, tough defender Brayden Maynard suffered a knee injury at training and is in doubt to return this season, no matter how far Collingwood progress in finals.

"These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden," Collingwood football boss Charlie Gardiner said.

"These are unfortunate setbacks especially at this time of year, but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible."

Pendlebury was ruled out in the second quarter of Friday night's 63-point thrashing by Brisbane at the MCG with what Collingwood described as a "knee bursa".

But scans on Saturday revealed a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two or three weeks.

It comes at a critical time for the 21-season veteran, who is waiting until the end of the year to decide if he plays on in 2027.

McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

If he does not retire, Pendlebury has also received an offer from Gold Coast to be effectively an on-field playing coach next year.

Collingwood are carefully balancing how they deal with an iconic player contemplating his football mortality.

Pendlebury was also substituted four-and-a-half minutes into last year's preliminary-final loss to Brisbane with calf tightness.

Collingwood would likely err on the side of caution, desperate to avoid a repeat, even if the Magpies are still in premiership contention when he is available.

The Magpies would have to play five straight weeks of knockout finals to claim the most unlikely of premierships.

"That'll all be weighed up," coach Craig McRae said.

"He (Maynard) might be right to go, but then do we want to take that risk?"

The Magpies were conservative with Isaac Quaynor, Patrick Lipinski and Maynard on Friday night.

All three were expected to return next week, but Maynard is now no chance.

"Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade-one MCL strain," Gardiner said.

"This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury."

Collingwood also managed the game time of Nick Daicos and Darcy Cameron against the Lions in anticipation of the wildcard game, which McRae insisted felt like a final.

AAP

World.title: By the narrowest margin possible, the Warriors are top of the NRL
World.content:
Rookie Luke Hanson has booted a field goal to give the Warriors a 45-26 win over South Sydney that sent the Kiwi outfit to the top of the NRL ladder by the barest of margins.

With hooker Wayde Egan pulling all the strings at Stadium Australia, Andrew Webster's side joined Penrith and the Sydney Roosters on 38 points with a 19-point victory.

The win — the first by the scoreline in premiership history — helps the Warriors (+295) move past the Panthers (+294) on points differential after Hanson nudged a one-point goal from 30m out on the buzzer in just his second NRL game.

The third-placed Roosters (+163) have a game in hand and will play Wests Tigers on Sunday.

"As a team we weren't saying let's go kick a field goal because we need to," Webster said.

"We said every point's going to matter from here to the end.

"Once we kicked it we knew as staff, but I don't know if the players knew — you'd have to ask Luke, he's a pretty smart guy."

The Warriors host Newcastle and Manly over the final two rounds, while Penrith face Canterbury and Wests Tigers.

After Sunday's meeting with the Tigers, the Roosters square off with the Dolphins and Souths to round out their regular season.

The Warriors defied another change at halfback to run up a big score. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

"It might not be for too long and you only want to be on top at the end," Webster said.

"That's why we didn't mention for and against between now and then — we could win all our games and it could look different at the end."

While Webster's club bolstered their chances of a first minor premiership since 2002, and the chance to have a home final in week one, Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett was left frustrated.

A win would have locked up a top-eight finish for Bennett's Bunnies, who must now beat Gold Coast or the Roosters in their last two fixtures to qualify for the finals.

"What's between their ears? We're not real smart at different times out there," said Bennett, who all but confirmed Latrell Mitchell would return against the Titans.

"I'm talking about the game generally — a lot of things put us under pressure, but I'm never disappointed in the effort."

Canterbury ran up their highest score of the season against the Dragons. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Meanwhile, Canterbury have kept their NRL finals hopes alive with a 44-14 thrashing of St George Illawarra, who are all but certain to collect their first wooden spoon as a joint venture.

Shifted to right centre, Matt Burton grabbed a try-scoring double to help the ninth-placed Bulldogs to a 24-0 halftime lead at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday night.

The Dogs bit back at concerns over their attack with their highest score of the season, halfback Lachlan Galvin setting up two tries and scoring one to seal a comfortable win.

Canterbury's clearest path into finals is to win both their remaining games, hope North Queensland lose one of theirs and then leapfrog the Cowboys on for-and-against.

That scenario relies on the Bulldogs beating premiership heavyweights Penrith next week and the eighth-placed Cowboys losing to either Wests Tigers or Canberra, neither of whom will play finals in 2026.

But for now the Dogs remain a top-eight chance, some 12 weeks since languishing in the bottom four.

The win may have come at a cost as veteran Kurt Mann picked up a groin issue after winger Enari Tuala (knee) dropped out before kick-off.

Earlier, Newcastle were left sweating on a Dom Young hip-drop tackle charge after he was sin-binned and their hopes of a home final were put in jeopardy in a shock 44-24 capitulation to Manly.

On a humbling Old Boys' Day in Newcastle, the Knights blew an 18-6 lead early to leave themselves potentially needing to beat the Warriors next week to stay sixth.

Making matters worse is Young being at risk of missing the start of the finals, over a hip-drop tackle that left Sea Eagles star Tolu Koula with a syndesmosis injury.

Koula will require scans, but a grade-three charge would be enough to rule the star Newcastle winger out of the opening week of finals given they have a last-round bye.

AAP

World.title: Tex farewells Adelaide Oval in style as Crows, Cats lock in top six
World.content:
Taylor Walker has a perfect farewell to Adelaide Oval as the Crows and Geelong seal top-six spots, and Melbourne's loss to the Bulldogs re-shapes the finals.

Adelaide beat GWS by 56 points, with Walker kicking six and Izak Rankine four. The win saw the Crows temporarily jump above Hawthorn, who will finish third or fourth if they beat West Coast tomorrow.

In Geelong, the Cats beat Richmond by 57 points, with Jeremy Cameron returning to the side after injury. The Cats are fourth going into the final day of the home-and-away season.

Marcus Bontempelli recorded 27 touches and kicked two goals as the Bulldogs claimed a 16.12 (108) to 12.15 (87) win over the Demons, setting up a wildcard clash against Collingwood.

The Bulldogs win came at a cost though as star forward Aaron Naughton left the ground at the end of the third quarter with an ankle injury.

Earlier on Saturday, Carlton continued its hot form, recording a 37-point win over ladder-leaders Fremantle at Docklands Stadium.

After trailing by 23 points early in the first quarter, the Blues turned the tables in sensational fashion, running out 18.11 (119) to 12.10 (82) winners as Francis Evans kicked five goals.

Meanwhile, former Sydney Swans assistant Josh Francou says the club's scandal "wouldn't have unfolded" under previous coach John Longmire.

Look back at all the action in our live blog.

World.title: Wallaroos hammered in historic 100th Test by ruthless Black Ferns
World.content:
The Wallaroos' 100th Test match, and the Test debut of Australia's all-time leading rugby 7s try-scorer, has been soured by a dominant New Zealand performance in Auckland.

The Black Ferns maintained their unblemished record against the Wallaroos in Test rugby, with a 66-19 win at Mt Smart Stadium.

New Zealand came into Saturday's Test having not lost to Australia in all 30 Tests between the two nations, and a 10-try haul ensured that streak would continue.

The Wallaroos scored three tries, including a score from Waiaria Ellis who started at fly half for the first time.

Maddison Levi, Australia's all-time leading rugby 7s try scorer, made her Wallaroos debut with a 30-minute stint off the bench. Meanwhile, Emily Chancellor became the first woman to represent the Black Ferns and Wallaroos in Test rugby when she made her Australian debut off the bench.

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said her team was disappointed in the result, but was pleased the Australians continued fighting, managing to score two of the game's final three tries.

"New Zealand started off really fast, so we were on the back foot," she said.

"But you could see towards the end that we can get back, it's just a matter of starting well."

Highlights were few and far between for the Wallaroos as the Black Ferns dominated from the opening whistle.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' As the Wallaroos prepare for their 100th Test, past and present players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching this milestone.

A brilliant counter ruck inside Australian territory gave the home side possession, and the Black Ferns then methodically worked their way to the goal-line before fullback Braxton Sorensen-McGee scored on the right flank in the fourth minute.

The Black Ferns continued their early dominance. The Wallaroos were forced to scramble on their goal line to hold out a rampant home side, with New Zealand lock Maiakawanakaulani Roos held up over the line from a line-out maul.

That was just a reprieve for the Wallaroos, as the Black Ferns continued to attack, with prop Chryss Viliko charging over from close range for the second try.

The Black Ferns had a third try in the 24th minute, with lock Maama Mo'onia Vaipulu making a big line break up the middle of the field before passing to fly half Ruahei Demant, who scored under the posts.

New Zealand's one blemish in the first half was Vaipulu being sent to the sin bin, not lowering herself enough in a tackle and making head-on-head contact with Wallaroos' flanker Lily Bone.

Being down to 14 women did not seem to matter to the Black Ferns, who scored a fourth try when Liana Mikaele-Tu'u touched down in the 35th minute.

The Wallaroos were able to take momentum into half-time with their first try of the afternoon. A free kick against the Black Ferns from their own line-out, gave the Wallaroos the ball near the opposition goal-line. The visitors seized the opportunity, with left winger Desiree Miller scoring and then converting her own try.

Down 26-7 at half-time, any hope the Wallaroos had of making a famous comeback was doused quickly.

After being held up early in the first half, Roos finished off a nice passage of play to score New Zealand's fifth try just three minutes into the second half.

By the time Australia's Rugby 7's all-time leading try scorer Levi came on for her Wallaroos debut, the game was not a contest.

Tries to Ayesha Leti-I'iga in the 50th minute and reserve hooker Vici-Rose Green in the 56th minute piled on more misery for the Wallaroos.

The Black Ferns crossed the half-century mark with a try to Maia Joseph, then Shyrah Tuliau-Tua'a charged down a kick from Wallaroos fullback Faitala Moleka inside the Australian in-goal, and grounded the ball.

A lovely side-step from Wallaroos fly half Waiaria Ellis sliced open the Black Ferns defensive line for a try in the 67th minute.

That was the start of a bright spot for the Wallaroos, who produced a driving maul from close range, with reserve hooker Brittany Merlo scoring Australia's third try.

World.title: Third woman engages lawyer over 'incredibly traumatic' Sydney Swans scandal
World.content:
A lawyer representing a third woman involved in the Sydney Swans sexual assault scandal says a potential civil lawsuit is being looked at.

Slater and Gordon senior lawyer, Jackson Pannam, has been engaged to represent a woman who he said contacted police immediately following the alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne in the early hours of Monday, August 17.

"Our client has had her entire world turned upside down and is now trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience," he said.

He said the firm's lawyers "see the profound and long-lasting impact that serious injury, loss and abuse can have on people's lives".

Jackson Pannam says the woman's world has been "turned upside down" by the incident. (ABC News)

On Friday, Carbone Lawyers announced separately that it was representing two women, believed to be adult entertainers involved in the incident, and looking into launching a civil claim.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at the Pullman Hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' victory against Essendon last Sunday night.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following the match in Melbourne.

Mr Pannam said following her initial contact with police, his client was continuing to speak to them as part of their investigation into the incident.

"Everyone deserves to be safe going about their life, at home, at work, and in public spaces without risk of being assaulted or harmed," Mr Pannam said.

"We're standing with our client to give her support at this difficult time, and to help her get the justice she deserves."

Mr Pannam described the woman as "extremely distressed" by what had occurred, and asked for her privacy, and that of the other women involved, to be respected.

He said his client had not spoken to the media.

A police investigation is still underway, but they have not made any arrests or laid charges.

On Saturday, police provided an update about the investigation being undertaken by detectives from the Sexual Crimes Squad.

"The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established, and a number of people have been spoken to," the statement read.

"As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further, including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken."

In a statement, the Sydney Swans said the club "supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today's statement regarding the investigation".

The club's statement also addressed comments relating to other men, beyond the five players identified by the club, being present in the hotel room at the centre of the allegations.

"The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation," it read.

"The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage."

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham told The Age the club would "thoroughly" look into how the events of Monday morning took place, adding the club's standards were not the problem, but rather the fact they were breached.

A club representative later clarified there were no plans for an official inquiry.

Tech.title: Doodle generative compositions in your browser with Musical Spirograph
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

I remember having a Spirograph as a kid and being obsessed with it. Its geometric patterns are hypnotic and gorgeous. I also love generative music composition. So bringing those two things together in a browser tab, I’m hooked. Musical Spirograph is a relatively simple concept. A set of points dash around the screen according to mathematical equations, generating hypotrochoids and epitrochoids. Those points pass through a series of concentric rings which trigger specific notes.

Honestly, that alone is fun enough, but you can customize it quite a bit. There are six different virtual rotors to pick from, you can have up to three arms drawing simultaneously, and there are a bunch of other parameters to tweak the pattern. Then there are six different scale options, or you can completely customize the notes, and there are six different synth presets. Plus you can change the quantization and BPM, or even expand the number of rings out to two octaves.

Sure, the sound engine isn’t great, and it’s prone to clipping and artifacts. And I really wish there was a way to get MIDI out of it to control other instruments. But it’s still a ton of fun to get lost in for a while.

Tech.title: W. Kamau Bell has the most practical ‘most indispensable tool’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

W. Kamau Bell is one of those people who has always just seemed to be there. From Totally Biased, to Politically Re-Active, United Shades of America, and We Need to Talk About Cosby, his blend of comedy, social commentary, and political activism has helped him stand out. He’s won a Peabody and four Emmys, been a Celebrity Jeopardy! champion, received honors from the ACLU, and been crowned the Ambassador of Fishbone by founding member Chris Dowd. Bell is, if nothing else, a busy man.

So we’re very grateful that he took time between episodes of his podcast Who’s With Me, his comedy tour, and Substack of the same name, promoting his upcoming children’s book Rock Paper Scissors Cheese (out October 27th), and, of course, being a dad, to answer our weekly questionnaire.

What is your most indispensable tool?

A charger. All of this is just shiny paperweights without a charger.

Which app is the most underappreciated?

I probably use the map app every day. I wish MapQuest’s app was better, so I didn’t have to use the Trump Billionaire guys’ apps. You know who I’m talking about. The map apps that have the Gulf of Mexico listed as the Gulf of America. SOOOOOOOOO EMBARRASSING!!!

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

It’s been a long, loooong time since I had a phone that didn’t just transfer my old apps over, but I would guess that if I had a clean phone with only the basic apps on it, I would quickly install YouTube. What do you expect me to do? Just think my own thoughts all day? I need somebody constantly telling me something about something. Or singing me something about something.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

Just come in a hard case with that piece of plastic that claims it stops your screen from cracking already on the phone. I just bought it. I don’t need a project, and I’m not comfortable asking the person at the cellphone place to do it for me. Also, I’m sure it is a scam, but I just put it on there anyway.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I have 17 windows open across two different browser windows. That’s light work. When I’m writing a Substack article, I can get to 30 windows… easy. I only close them when I hit “publish” on an article. I have to earn the right to close a window.

Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?

I really want to thank Elon Musk for breaking my addiction to Twitter. It wasn’t healthy, so I can say that he really improved my life by ruining Twitter. These days, I’m an Instagram and Threads guy. Not that Zuckerberg is significantly better than Elon, but as a public-facing person, I do need these platforms. But Zuckerberg better be careful. My generation isn’t afraid to leave social media platforms. We left MySpace and Friendster, just like I left Twitter.

What is your happy place online?

Watching the latest Japanese video on YouTube or watching Lionfield videos with my 8-year-old on Instagram

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

Afro pick with extra-long metal teeth with a fist as the handle.

Which was the most disappointing?

A brush that claimed it could effectively comb Afros. I bought it because of Shark Tank. But I think my hair is just too long. Or the X-ray specs they used to sell in comic books.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

It is a tie between Civilization on the PC and NBA Live on Sega Genesis. I’m talking like NBA Live ‘95. I’M SOOOOO OLD!

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

AI.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Flappy Bird. But I would have let it rock instead of deleting it. Maybe because I have three kids, I can’t look a gift app in the mouth like that. You all would have had at least eight Flappy Bird movies by now. It would have out-Minioned the Minion movies.

What creation are you most proud of?

My three daughters. It was a collab project.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

“Don’t think you are going to make it just by doing stand-up comedy. You need to learn how to write other things,” – Kevin Kataoka.

What is your current obsession?

The NBA off-season. It is way better than the actual season, even with the Knicks winning.

What do you do when you need to focus?

Coffee and extreme quiet… like leave me the eff alone… so I can listen to YouTube while I work. Middle of the night is the best time to work, but I can’t do that as often as I like… those three kids like it when both their parents are awake at the same time. My wife likes that better, too.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

Change the song or play a silly cellphone game for four hours. Do you know YouTube has games now for free???

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

Excuse me? EXCUSE ME??? WHY WOULD I DO THAT?

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

I’m a middle-aged-dad-who-buys-records-years-old. The guy at the shop (Mars Records in Oakland) holds things for me. I bought Fishbone’s first EP recently. I should really buy a record player.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

If you need a new computer, GET A NEW COMPUTER!

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Doing the best he can.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Amazon just hiked the prices for Echo, Fire TV, and Kindle products by up to 60 percent
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Citing “significant increases in memory and storage component costs,” Amazon has raised prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs, and Eeros by up to 60 percent, as first reported by Fortune.

The cheapest products in Amazon’s lineup were hit hardest, with the Echo Dot smart speaker jumping from $49.99 to $79.99. The Fire TV Stick 4K Max also rose by over 40 percent to $84.99, and the base level Kindle now costs $149.99, a nearly 37 percent increase.

In a statement to The Verge, Kristy Schmidt, senior communications manager of Amazon’s Devices & Services divison, said, “The consumer electronics industry is facing significant increases in memory and storage component costs. After absorbing these increases for as long as we could, we recently adjusted pricing across our product lines. Our approach has always been to offer great products at accessible prices, and that commitment hasn’t changed.”

Amazon’s flagship Echo Dot Max smart speaker, which launched last year, now costs $119.99, up from $99.99. Apple increased the price of its comparable HomePod Mini this summer to $129 from $99.99, also in response to rising costs. The Google Home Speaker remains at $99.99 for now.

Amazon hardware products apparently not affected include its line of Ring cameras and video doorbells, and the Echo Studio, its higher-end $219.99 smart speaker.
